events.overview: The first contact flight is about surviving the cockpit setup and launch cleanly, then proving you can transition into basic airwork without getting behind the aircraft. Be ready to brief seat and start discipline, takeoff and departure flow, and the first core maneuvers that set the tone for the rest of FAM.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Seat and canopy-fracturing knowledge come before any flying in this event. You should be able to brief pin discipline, seat envelope, CFS and ISS logic, and the immediate priorities after leaving the aircraft.

children.text: Respect the seat every time you approach the aircraft.
Before entering the cockpit, confirm both CFS and ejection-seat safety pins are installed and use the standard pin calls between cockpits.
Before leaving the wing, confirm both pins are back in and the cockpit is left in the required safe configuration. If solo mode applies, ISS mode selection must match the brief.
The aircraft uses the Martin-Baker Mk 16 seat with the GQ5000 parachute, and both emergency oxygen and CFS activate automatically on ejection.
The published escape envelope runs from 0/0 up to about 35,000 feet and 370 KIAS.
Controlled ejection minimum altitude is 2000 feet AGL. Break out PCL and complete as many steps as time permits.
Uncontrolled ejection minimum altitude is 6000 feet AGL.
CFS can activate automatically during ejection or manually through the CFS handle.
Each internal CFS handle fractures only that cockpit transparency, so both may be required if both canopies need to be cleared.

ISS mode logic matters: SOLO ejects only the initiating seat, BOTH ejects both seats with the rear seat leaving first, and CMD FWD lets the front cockpit command both seats while the aft cockpit ejects only itself.
After ejection, inspect the canopy and suspension lines, inflate the LPU, release the raft as required, and work through the remaining post-ejection priorities.
Over land, steer into the wind and execute a proper PLF. Over water, release the upper Koch fittings at the surface and execute ADR.
Grasp the ejection handle and pull sharply toward the abdomen with elbows against the body.
The emergency escape system is explosive. Exposed skin should be covered, with O2 mask on and visor down before actuating CFS or ejecting.
If ejecting over mountainous terrain above 8000 feet MSL, use the MOR handle to separate from the seat and deploy the parachute.
At low speed, one or both riser sets may remain together after separation, producing a slightly higher descent rate or an uncommanded turn.

items.text: Abnormal starts are a recognition-and-abort problem. Know the start types, the abort criteria, and what has to happen after fuel has been introduced.

children.text: Hot start: ITT is likely to exceed 1000 C, or ITT remains between 871 and 1000 C for more than 5 seconds.
Hung start: N1 stops increasing normally or stagnates below 60 percent, often around 30 percent.
No start: no ITT rise within 10 seconds of fuel flow.
Loss of ST READY, red BAT BUS, or low oil pressure during start all drive you toward an abort.
Abort if ITT is likely to exceed 1000 C.
Abort if ITT remains between 871 and 1000 C for more than 5 seconds.
Abort if N1 increase halts, if there is no ITT rise within 10 seconds of fuel flow, if BAT BUS appears, or if ST READY extinguishes during start.
Use PCL OFF or STARTER AUTO/RESET as required by the PCL position when the abort is called.
If an overtemperature occurred, record both the degree and the duration.
Any aborted start with fuel introduced requires a motoring run with PCL OFF, ignition NORM, prop area clear, and STARTER MANUAL for 20 seconds before returning the switch to NORM.
ST READY confirms the PMU is armed and should remain illuminated for at least 3 seconds after the PCL is moved toward IDLE.
PMU auto-aborts for no ITT rise, excessive ITT, or poor N1 acceleration.
Weak battery, high OAT, high pre-start ITT, high density altitude, and tailwind battery starts are common PMU-abort contributors.

items.text: Brake failure can range from a simple reapplication problem to a directional-control problem on landing. Brief who has braking authority and what the runway plan becomes if a brake is lost.

children.text: If braking pressure fades or there is no brake response, fully release the brakes in both cockpits and then re-apply.
Braking force is determined by the pilot applying the greater pedal pressure.
Land on the side of the runway corresponding to the failed brake.
Use the opposite brake, rudder, and ailerons to maintain directional control.
If both cockpits are occupied, the pilot with the effective brake becomes the braking authority.
Plan for a firm, centered, on-speed touchdown.
Use rudder and ailerons to maintain directional control.
Be ready to transition immediately to aircraft-departs-prepared-surface logic if runway departure becomes likely.
Top red band only visible means the reservoir needs servicing.
Red-green visible means the reservoir is adequately serviced.
Red-green-red visible means the reservoir is overserviced.

items.text: Treat any strike of a ground object as aircraft damage until maintenance proves otherwise, even if the contact felt minor.

children.text: A strike of a ground object is contact with any ground obstacle during taxi, takeoff, or landing.
Stop immediately, execute emergency engine shutdown on the ground as required, notify Ground or Tower, and do not continue taxi without maintenance direction.
Use judgment conservatively: even minor contact can create damage that makes a later takeoff unsafe.
Ensure the strike is documented for maintenance action.

items.text: Takeoff in this event is about disciplined setup, smooth rotation, and an organized cleanup. If the launch is rushed on the ground, the rest of the sortie starts behind the aircraft.

children.text: Switch to Tower as required before hold short, read back lineup or hold-short instructions correctly, and align on centerline only after clearing final.
Run the lineup checklist from memory, and if held in position, stop the checklist at the published hold point until cleared.
Call the crosswind direction and set the flight controls appropriately before brake release.
Bring torque up to about 30 percent and verify the engine instruments before releasing the brakes.
Release brakes, center the nosewheel, and advance PCL to MAX over about 2 to 3 seconds while using rudder for directional control.
At 60 KIAS, verify minimum power and acceptable fuel flow.
Use aileron into the wind for crosswind correction and do not use aileron to solve yaw.
At 90 KIAS, apply smooth back stick to set about 7 to 10 degrees nose high and let the aircraft fly off.
For gusts, add one-half the gust factor to rotation speed, not more than 10 knots.
Confirm two positive rates with airspeed below 150 KIAS, then call for gear.
Above 110 KIAS, call for flaps up and trim as required.

Maintain the initial climb picture, then transition to the briefed climb attitude and airspeed as the aircraft accelerates. Best-rate climb is about 140 KIAS, but the departure profile you brief is what governs the sortie.
Improper rudder causes immediate directional-control problems.
Late, early, or excessive rotation turns the takeoff into a pitch-control problem.
Students often forget rudder trim or the gear/flaps cleanup calls once the aircraft starts accelerating.

items.text: Departure knowledge here is about flying a clean climbout and understanding which parts of the plan are universal versus local. The goal is to leave the field safely without memorizing a base-specific route as if it applied everywhere.

children.text: Call for departure only when number one, and read back hold-short, lineup, or takeoff instructions correctly.
If using a departure option or practice abort option, ensure that has already been coordinated with ATC.
Do not turn before the briefed safe altitude or departure condition.
Fly the takeoff climb picture first, then transition to the briefed climb and level-off airspeeds as you leave the pattern.
Know when the sortie transitions from runway control to the next agency or frequency in the brief, and do not let the radio call interrupt aircraft control.
Runway-specific headings, named VFR routes, class D exit points, transition gates, and local frequencies are location-specific and must come from the current SOP or day-of brief.
The transferable knowledge is understanding why those items exist: obstacle clearance, traffic deconfliction, airspace transition, and proper radio handoff timing.

items.text: Basic transitions are the building blocks for changing between climb, cruise, and descent without fighting trim or chasing the airspeed after the fact.

children.text: Advance PCL to MAX, raise the nose to about 12 to 15 degrees nose high, and trim as required.
At 180 KIAS, lower to the normal climb picture at about 8 degrees nose high, retrim, and center the ball.
For climbs greater than 1000 feet, use 180 KIAS. Shorter climbs can stay at cruise airspeed with MAX power.
About 200 feet prior to level-off, start lowering the nose toward the level picture.
About 5 knots prior to cruise airspeed, reduce power to cruise, set the level attitude, trim, and center the ball.
Reduce power to about 20 percent and lower the nose to about 5 degrees nose low.
Trim for the power reduction, clear as required, and retrim once the descent stabilizes.
About 100 feet prior to level-off, add cruise power and raise the nose to the level picture.
Trim for the power addition, then retrim and center the ball once level.

items.text: Trim keeps the aircraft from becoming a control-force workout. The correct habit is always Power, then Attitude, then Trim.

children.text: Lead with the power change, set the new attitude picture, then use trim to remove the control pressure you are holding.
Trim in order: rudder first, then elevator, then aileron only if the aircraft still wants to roll.
Rudder trim is controlled on the PCL and is used to center the ball.
Elevator trim relieves stick force after the correct nose attitude is already set.
Aileron trim physically repositions the ailerons and is used only after rudder trim if a roll tendency remains.
The Trim Aid Device commands rudder trim only.
It becomes active once the aircraft is above 80 KIAS and weight off wheels.
It helps with rudder trim, but it does not remove the pilot's responsibility to trim the aircraft correctly.
Power addition usually needs right rudder trim and down elevator trim.
Power reduction usually needs left rudder trim and up elevator trim.
Acceleration usually trends toward left rudder trim and down elevator trim.
Deceleration usually trends toward right rudder trim and up elevator trim.

items.text: The turn pattern is your first deliberate contact-airwork energy exercise. Smooth roll rate, coordinated rudder, and early trim matter more than muscling the airplane back to altitude after each turn.

children.text: Establish level flight on a numbered heading at about 200 KIAS and the briefed cruise power setting.
Clear the area before the pattern and keep scanning outside throughout the maneuver.
For 30 degrees AOB, turn 90 degrees left and right with minimal power or back-stick change.
For 45 degrees AOB, turn 180 degrees left and right while adding a little power and slight nose-up attitude to maintain energy.
For 60 degrees AOB, turn 360 degrees left and right with noticeably more back pressure and power.
Use the one-third rollout or reversal rule, maintain trim, and prevent the nose from dropping or ballooning through the rollout.
Return to the original heading with altitude and airspeed under control, reset cruise power, and retrim the aircraft.
Abrupt control inputs and inconsistent nose attitude create most altitude and airspeed errors.
Students often fixate inside or stop clearing the area once the turn starts.
Unbalanced flight and late corrections make the steep turns look much worse than they started.

items.text: Level speed change teaches how configuration, airspeed, power, and trim all move together while you stay level and ahead of the aircraft.

children.text: Start from normal cruise at about 200 KIAS and cruise power on a numbered heading, then clear the area before the configuration changes begin.
Reduce to IDLE and trim while decelerating.
Below 150 KIAS, lower the gear. At about 130 KIAS, set about 31 percent power and stabilize at 120 KIAS.
Select landing flaps, immediately increase power to about 52 percent, hold 120 KIAS, and complete the Before Landing Checklist.
To recover, set PCL to MAX, raise gear and flaps below 150 KIAS as allowed, raise flaps fully at or above 110 KIAS, then reduce to about 54 percent as airspeed approaches 200 KIAS.
Stabilize back at normal cruise with the aircraft level, trimmed, and the ball centered.
Poor rudder trim causes heading drift through the whole demonstration.
Trying to do the Before Landing Checklist mid-transition usually ruins the basic airwork.
Improper nose attitudes and poor elevator-trim discipline cause most of the altitude-control errors.

items.text: Slow flight teaches you to stay ahead of the aircraft when it is trimmed, configured, and powered close to the landing regime. The goal is controlled, coordinated maneuvering without letting AOA or trim get away from you.

children.text: Complete the maneuver above 6000 feet AGL.
Slow below 150 KIAS, lower the landing gear, and complete the Before Landing Checklist and the pre-stall / spin / aerobatic checklist.
Clear the area, lower flaps to LDG, reduce to about 85 KIAS, and set power to about 45 percent torque.
Perform a coordinated 30-degree AOB turn for about 180 degrees, then return with a coordinated 30-degree AOB turn the opposite direction.
Add power and trim as required to hold altitude and the slow-flight airspeed.
Advance PCL to MAX, raise the gear below 150 KIAS, move flaps from LDG to TO, raise flaps fully at or above 110 KIAS, accelerate to about 200 KIAS, reduce to about 54 percent power, and retrim.
Students usually get behind on trim first, then try to fix the slow-flight picture with large pitch changes instead of small power and trim corrections.
Letting bank angle creep up or rushing the cleanup sequence turns the recovery into a configuration-management problem instead of a basic-airwork recovery.

items.text: HUD knowledge is introductory in this event. You should know what the major cues are doing, but the outside picture remains primary from brake release through the basic maneuver set.

children.text: The HUD and repeater present flight, navigation, steering, and master-mode information in front of the pilot.
Know the master modes NAV, A/A, and A/G, and understand what Flash, Limit Cross, and invalid symbology are telling you.
The basic symbols to recognize early are the waterline reference, flight path marker, climb dive marker, climb dive ladder, bank references, sideslip, and heading scale.
You do not need to brief every symbol from memory yet, but you should know the big-picture job of the major flight cues.
In this event, the HUD should support takeoff, climb, scan-pattern work, trim demonstration, AGSM discussion, and TCAS integration without dragging your eyes off the outside picture.
If the HUD cue conflicts with what the airplane is obviously doing outside, re-anchor to the outside attitude picture first and then use the HUD as a cross-check again.

events.overview: This event turns basic contact flying into real landing work. You should be ready to recognize and recover from stall cues, fly a disciplined pattern in each flap configuration, and wave off instead of trying to salvage a landing that is already going bad.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A tire failure changes whether you stop now or continue to a controlled landing. Directional control is the constant priority either way.

children.text: If the decision is to stop, execute the abort immediately.
If the takeoff continues, do not change gear or flap position. Fly a straight-in approach and land on the side of the runway with the good tire so the drag stays toward centerline.
Maintain directional control with rudder, brakes, and nosewheel steering as required, and expect the airplane to feel more sensitive on rollout above 80 KIAS.
Main tire pressure is 225 +/- 5 PSI or 185 +/- 5 PSI, depending on tire installation. Nose tire pressure is 120 +/- 5 PSI.
The aircraft has no anti-skid or anti-lock braking. Do not apply wheel brakes until weight is firmly on wheels.
Most blown tires occur before tire spin-up or below about 40 knots. Excessive brake pressure below about 20 knots can also lock a wheel and fail a tire.

items.text: An aborted takeoff is an early stop decision, not a last-second attempt to save a bad rollout. Keep the aircraft straight first, then stop it with a smooth braking application.

children.text: PCL - IDLE.
BRAKES - AS REQUIRED with one smooth application; do not pump or slam them.
Maintain directional control with rudder and nosewheel steering. The abort call comes after the aircraft is under control, not before.

Abort for any unsafe condition before the briefed max-abort point: blown tire, smoke or fuel leak, chip or fire light, bird strike, runway obstacle, rising ITT, fluctuating oil pressure, or engine/system malfunction.
For this event, the local gouge teaches the decision as an early takeoff-roll problem, commonly briefed around 60 KIAS or 1500 feet remaining unless the day-of brief is more restrictive.
Above 80 KIAS, braking is less effective because lift is still unloading the wheels, so do not let aggressive braking create a skid or blown tire problem.
After maximum-effort braking, do not set the parking brake or taxi into a congested area until the brakes cool.
If an arresting cable is lowered, release the brakes before crossing it and resume braking once clear.
If the aircraft cannot taxi clear safely, transition to Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground and Emergency Ground Egress as required.

items.text: Power-on stalls teach recognition and recovery when thrust is available. The goal is to break the stall cleanly and recover with minimum altitude loss, not to force the airplane to hold an impossible pitch picture.

children.text: Establish the aircraft clean above 6000 feet AGL and complete the Three Cs.
Begin at about 150 KIAS. For the straight-ahead entry, set PCL to achieve about 30-60% torque and raise the nose to about 15-40 degrees nose high.
For the turning entry, use the same setup but add 20-30 degrees of bank and hold that bank with coordinated rudder and aileron.
Hold the pitch and bank constant until uncommanded nose drop or unplanned rolling motion occurs. Do not chase the exact full-stall point.
Recover with RELAX, MAX, LEVEL, BALL. Reduce AOA first, advance PCL to MAX, level the wings, and use rudder to keep the ball centered.
Once the stall is broken, keep scanning AOA and BALL. As airspeed rebuilds, re-adjust the stick to stay near maximum recovery AOA instead of over-pitching into a secondary stall.
The maneuver is complete when the aircraft is wings level with two positive rates of climb and the recovery is stabilized without entering a secondary stall.
Failing to hold a constant pitch or bank attitude prior to loss of control effectiveness.
Late recognition of the stall break or late transition from stall recovery back to level flight.
Recovering with less than maximum recovery AOA, or pulling too soon and inducing a secondary stall.
Torque above 60% in the stall can induce a left torque roll. Be especially cautious in turning entries.
If the aircraft condition is in doubt or a departure develops, stop trying to fly a normal stall recovery and transition to the applicable departure recovery.
If the aircraft is in an unrecoverable descent below 6000 feet AGL, eject.

items.text: Landing pattern stalls are pattern-specific stall recoveries. Recover at the first stall cue with minimal altitude loss; do not let the maneuver turn into a full stall or a low-altitude salvage attempt.

children.text: Establish the aircraft in downwind configuration at 120 KIAS, gear down, flaps as required, and complete the PSSA and Before Landing Checklists.
Clear the area, then simulate the abeam transition with about 20% torque and a descending 30-degree AOB turn at 120/115/110 KIAS based on flap setting.
Once stabilized in the turn, raise the nose to about 5-10 degrees nose high, retard PCL to idle, maintain 20-45 degrees AOB, and increase back-stick pressure to hold the pitch attitude.
At first indication of stall, recover with RELAX, MAX, LEVEL, BALL and return to a controlled downwind picture with minimal altitude loss.
Set up a simulated final approach at 5-10 knots above final approach speed for the selected flap setting.
Retard PCL to idle, execute a simulated landing transition, and hold the landing attitude constant until the first indication of stall.
Recover at the first cue. If the nose is already within about 5-10 degrees nose high, maintain that attitude to preserve altitude. If it rises above that range, lower it enough to avoid a full stall.
The maneuver is complete when the aircraft is wings level with two positive rates of climb and 120 KIAS downwind configuration is regained.
Releasing instead of relaxing back-stick pressure, or delaying power long enough to create needless altitude loss.
Cycling rudder to chase the ball before flying speed is regained.
Lowering the nose too far in a landing-attitude recovery and turning the exercise into a prop-strike or porpoise setup.
Recover at the first indication of stall. Do not intentionally enter a full stall in the landing pattern.
Use maximum recovery AOA, about 14-17.9 units, and keep scanning AOA and BALL throughout the recovery.
If recovery appears unlikely in the pattern, eject.

items.text: Power-off stalls are ELP-profile stalls. The real lesson is not just stall recovery; it is protecting glide profile and not wasting altitude once the airplane gets slow.

children.text: Start clean above 6000 feet AGL at about 150 KIAS or at the IP's discretion, and complete the Three Cs.
Retard PCL to 4-6% torque. If at or below 150 KIAS, decelerate directly to best glide. If above 150 KIAS, zoom glide to capture best glide.
As airspeed approaches 125 KIAS, lower the nose to the best-glide attitude and verify roughly 1350-1500 FPM sink rate.
Simulate high key, lower the gear, re-trim for 120 KIAS glide, start a 15-20 degree AOB turn to low key, and complete the Before Landing Checklist.
Raise the nose to about 5-10 degrees nose high and let the airspeed decay to the first indication of stall.
Maintain the turn or profile ground track, then recover by lowering the pitch attitude until the prop arc is on the horizon, about 8 degrees nose low, until 120 KIAS is regained.
Re-trim and stabilize the glide instead of letting the recovery turn into a dive-and-chase exercise.
The maneuver is complete when 120 KIAS glide is reestablished, the aircraft is trimmed, and the profile is back under control.
Failure to recognize the first approach-to-stall cue.
Lowering the nose too far and giving away excessive altitude.
Failing to recapture 120 KIAS or re-trim the aircraft after recovery.
Expect to lose at least 800 feet in the recovery and another 1000-2000 feet in the setup. Give yourself room before starting.
Best glide is about 125 KIAS clean and about 120 KIAS with the gear down in the simulated ELP portion.

items.text: The landing pattern is a disciplined racetrack, not a loose traffic pattern. Good patterns build good approaches, and good approaches build good landings.

children.text: Pattern interval should already be established in the break or upwind. Do not try to invent interval corrections late in the approach turn.
A normal pattern is built from the break, downwind, approach turn, final, and landing. The goal is to arrive at each checkpoint already trimmed and on-speed.
Enter at 200 KIAS and the briefed break altitude and initial point. Use local SOP or the day-of brief for field-specific altitude, IP, and traffic-flow requirements.
Use a 30-60 degree AOB break, slow to 120 KIAS, lower the gear below 150 KIAS, and adjust to arrive downwind at about 3/4 to 1 WTD.
Approaching 120 KIAS, use about 31% torque if staying level, or about 20% and a descending picture if coming down to pattern altitude.
Once on downwind, select the desired flaps setting, level at pattern altitude with the PAT principle, and complete the Before Landing Checklist.
Fly downwind at 120 KIAS and a WTD that supports a 25-30 degree AOB approach turn. If more than 45 degrees AOB is required, wave off.
Initiate transition no sooner than abeam the intended point of landing. Transition power is about 20% for all flap settings; the no-flap pattern delays that power reduction until the 180.
At the 180, lower the nose to the 120/115/110 KIAS approach picture for NF/TO/LDG. Stay balanced and do not allow the aircraft to slow below on-speed AOA.
Aim to arrive in the groove about 1200-1500 feet from the threshold and about 200 feet AGL with a fixed aim-point and a stable scan.
Not flying all checkpoints or arriving at the 90 and final off altitude and airspeed.
Poor trim and scan discipline, especially in the approach turn.
Overshooting, spotting the deck, or ignoring wave-off cues until too late.

items.text: The no-flap landing is the least forgiving landing picture in this event. It stays clean longer, carries more energy, and punishes students who get slow or wait too long to recognize a bad approach.

children.text: Fly the normal pattern at 120 KIAS on downwind with the aircraft clean and about 31% torque.
Unlike the flapped patterns, a no-flap approach normally delays the transition power reduction until the 180.
Use a WTD and turn picture that still supports a 25-30 degree AOB final turn without forcing the bank past 45 degrees.
At the 180, lower the nose to the no-flap approach picture and hold about 120 KIAS in the turn and about 110 KIAS on final.
Expect the flap-up picture to look flatter and to require more precise power reduction and bank management to make the same checkpoints.
Do not allow the aircraft to slow below on-speed AOA. If the green chevron appears, trim nose down and add power as required.
The maneuver is complete when the aircraft lands in the touchdown zone on centerline without an excessive float, late flare, or long landing.
Carrying the no-flap pattern too slow and falling behind the AOA picture.
Using too little bank or too much power in the turn and ending up wide, long, or both.
Trying to salvage a long float instead of waving off.

items.text: The takeoff-flap landing is the middle-ground landing picture. It gives more drag and a slower final than no-flap, but it still asks you to manage energy deliberately.

children.text: Set takeoff flaps on downwind, hold 120 KIAS, and expect about 42% torque once stabilized.
This configuration is often a good answer for gusty or moderate crosswind conditions because it preserves control margin without forcing the full landing-flap picture.
Initiate the transition no sooner than abeam with about 20% torque and lower the nose to the takeoff-flap approach picture.
Fly about 115 KIAS in the approach turn and about 105 KIAS on final, adjusting power early enough to stay on the correct glide path.
In crosswinds or gusts, stay ahead of the wing-low correction and do not wait until the flare to start fixing drift.
The maneuver is complete when the aircraft touches down in the zone, aligned with the runway, with no unresolved drift or long float.
Flying no-flap airspeeds in a takeoff-flap pattern.
Failing to anticipate the drag change once flaps are set and ending up low or slow.
Waiting too long to wave off a drifting or unstable final.

items.text: The landing-flap landing is the standard landing picture in this event. It offers the easiest slow-speed picture, but only if the pattern is trimmed and stabilized early.

children.text: Set landing flaps on downwind, complete the Before Landing Checklist, hold 120 KIAS, and expect about 52% torque once established.
Use the normal 3/4 to 1 WTD downwind spacing and be ready to trim right rudder as the higher power setting comes in.
Transition no sooner than abeam with about 20% torque and lower the nose to the landing-flap approach picture.
Fly about 110 KIAS in the approach turn and about 100 KIAS on final, keeping the aim-point fixed and the aircraft balanced.
In the flare, keep shifting the eyes down the runway, increase back-stick smoothly, and move PCL to idle once the landing is assured.
The maneuver is complete when the aircraft lands on the main mounts in the touchdown zone, aligned with runway centerline, and the nose is lowered smoothly below 80 KIAS.
Carrying too much power or too much airspeed into the flare.
Flattening the landing attitude and touching nose gear first.
Applying brakes at touchdown instead of waiting for weight on wheels and airspeed below 80 KIAS.

items.text: Landing irregularities are usually recoverable early and ugly late. The rule for this event is simple: correct small errors early, and wave off before a landing error becomes a runway problem.

children.text: High flare comes from flaring too early or with too much pitch. Ease off a small amount of back-stick and re-establish a normal flare. If the approach is steep or the flare is too high to salvage safely, wave off.
A late or rapid flare creates firm touchdown or an accelerated stall. Hold landing attitude, add power, and wave off rather than forcing the touchdown.
Porpoising comes from a flat landing and nosewheel-first contact. Set takeoff attitude immediately, add power, and wave off. Do not chase each bounce with opposite stick.
Floating usually comes from late power reduction, excess airspeed, or the wrong flap setting. A slight float may settle out; a long landing should become a wave-off.
Ballooning comes from a rapid flare with too much airspeed. Hold landing attitude through a slight balloon, but wave off a pronounced balloon.
A slight bounce can often be continued with correct landing attitude and direction control. A severe bounce or crosswind bounce should become a wave-off.
Landing in a drift or crab creates side loads and can start a swerve. If proper wing-low correction is not established before touchdown, wave off.
If the upwind wing rises after touchdown, keep adding aileron into the wind and use rudder to maintain direction. Do not make an aggressive correction back toward centerline.
In a hard landing, do not raise the gear.

items.text: A wave-off is a planned discontinuation of the approach, not a stall recovery. The earlier you recognize a bad landing picture, the safer and cleaner the wave-off becomes.

children.text: Wave off for any unsafe approach picture: unsafe airspeed or altitude, overshooting final, unresolved drift or crab, a high transition likely to bounce, or traffic conflicts that are not fixing themselves.
If you roll out in the straightaway before the preceding aircraft has landed, wave off immediately.

If a stall cue occurs in the pattern, recover the stall first with minimal altitude loss. Once the aircraft is under control and safety permits, reestablish normal wave-off procedures and ground track.
ELP traffic has the right-of-way over normal touch-and-go traffic.
Advance PCL as required; MAX power is common, but not every wave-off requires full power if traffic or deconfliction demands otherwise.
Level the wings if conditions permit, center the ball, raise the nose to climb attitude, and climb at 120 KIAS. Re-trim.
If flaps were lowered, raise them once safely airborne at or above 110 KIAS with two positive rates of climb, then accelerate to 120 KIAS and reduce power to about 60-70%.
Follow the required ground track for traffic deconfliction and make the radio call after the aircraft is under control.
When number one upwind with interval, make the crosswind or departing call.
Initiating too late and then treating the wave-off like an emergency.
Forgetting to maintain 120 KIAS, raise the flaps, or keep sight of other traffic.
Making the radio call before the aircraft is actually under control.

events.overview: This sortie is about getting between the working area, outlying fields, and home field without letting radios, checkpoints, or pattern flow get ahead of you. Show up ready to brief how you enter an OLF, stay disciplined on course rules, recover back to home field with a clean plan, and explain what SCATSAFE teaches about low-speed handling.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: OLF work is a standardization problem. Safety comes from every aircraft using the same duty runway, initial point, break interval, and radio flow instead of improvising the pattern.

children.text: Determine the duty runway before arrival and get on the correct field frequency early enough to build the picture before the initial.
Arrive at the published initial point on or parallel to extended centerline, wings level, on runway heading, at the locally briefed break altitude and airspeed.
Visually acquire traffic, confirm wind information, and make the initial call before you commit inbound.
Do not continue inbound for the break without the required two-way communications or pattern acknowledgement.
Establish proper interval before the break, not halfway through it. If the aircraft ahead is not where it should be, fix interval early or discontinue.
If the pattern is saturated, the preceding aircraft is not in sight, or communications are not working by the briefed gate, reset or hold as directed instead of forcing the entry.
After a touch-and-go, stay straight ahead until number one upwind with interval and any required clearance before turning crosswind or departing.
Practice PEL or other nonstandard entries must be coordinated early enough that everyone in the pattern understands your plan.
The exact distances, checkpoints, and holding points are field-specific. Brief the current local SOP and day-of gouge instead of memorizing one field's place names.

items.text: Course rules are the deconfliction system that gets you between fields, MOAs, and home field without guesswork. Treat them like a published procedure, not like loose local knowledge.

children.text: Know the route you are joining, the controlling agency, the required check-in point, and the altitude and airspeed that keep you separated from other training traffic.

Hold the assigned side of the route, respect any altitude step-downs or speed changes before entering controlled airspace, and do not assume a direct shortcut is approved just because it looks convenient.
If weather, traffic, or aircraft configuration makes the standard recovery unrealistic, call early and request a direct recovery or alternate entry rather than drifting off the published flow.

items.text: What course rules are really doing:

children.text: Brief the departure option, first radio handoff, route checkpoints, expected termination point, and what you will do if communications degrade.
Expect local procedures to define specific reporting points, route names, and runway-dependent turns. Those details change by base and must be confirmed from the current SOP or day-of brief.
What does not change is the logic: stay predictable, stay on altitude and airspeed, make required calls on time, and never let administrative tasks outrun aircraft control.
Late frequency changes, climbing or descending before cleared, and showing up fast to the next control point all create avoidable traffic problems.
Do not fixate on route names. What matters is understanding the purpose of the route, the sequence of control agencies, and the conditions that trigger a reroute or reset.

items.text: Home-field arrival should feel pre-briefed before you reach the arrival gate. The student mistake is waiting until the checkpoint to decide which entry, runway, or recovery plan makes sense.

children.text: Remain on the published arrival route and transit profile until the arrival gate or controlling agency directs something different.
If weather, traffic, or gear/flap configuration prevents the normal recovery, make that call early and request a direct recovery or alternate entry before the airplane gets busy.
Know whether you want an overhead, straight-in, base, or downwind entry before the check-in call so the request sounds deliberate instead of improvised.
At the home-field arrival gate, slow to the published entry speed, contact the proper controlling agency, and state the recovery type you want.
For overhead recoveries, be at the published entry altitude and airspeed, slightly offset to the pattern side, and ready to report initial and numbers as required.
For straight-ins, be slowed and configured before intercepting final. Gear-down and base/final calls should help tower and other traffic understand exactly what picture you are building.
If the setup is wrong, ask for a reset to initial or a different entry early instead of trying to salvage a rushed arrival close to the field.
The field-specific arrival gates, landmarks, and runway-dependent turns will vary. The transferable skill is arriving configured, predictable, and ahead of the radio timeline.

items.text: SCATSAFE is an instructor demonstration of how the T-6B behaves near stall speed. The point is to build pattern-relevant sight pictures and coordination habits before a student sees them the hard way close to the runway.

children.text: Complete the maneuver above 6000 feet AGL.
Slow below 150 KIAS, lower the gear, complete the Before Landing Checklist and the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist, and clear the area.
Lower flaps to LDG, continue slowing to about 80 KIAS or 15 units AOA, and set about 45% torque.

Straight and Level: recognize the pitch, torque, and rudder picture required to hold level flight on the back side of the power curve. This is the same slow-flight picture that matters near rotation and just before touchdown.
Coordination Exercise: use 15-20 degrees of bank and coordinated rudder to keep the ball centered. The airplane needs noticeably more right rudder in right turns than in left turns.
Adverse Yaw: without rudder, the nose initially yaws opposite the turn and overshoots rollout; coordinated rudder makes the nose track and stop where you expect.
Torque and Turns: a rapid advance to MAX power from slow flight will pitch, yaw, and roll the aircraft left unless you hold proper pitch and coordinated rudder.
Steep Turns: increasing bank toward 60 degrees at slow airspeed rapidly drives AOA up and can push the airplane into an impending stall.
Abrupt Control Movement: a sudden flare-like pull quickly increases AOA without fixing sink rate and can produce the exact hard-landing or stall sequence students create in the pattern.
Flap Retraction: retracting flaps too early removes lift, increases sink, and can stall the airplane; the demonstration shows why flap retraction gates matter.
Effectiveness of Controls: at slow airspeed, rapid small inputs often do very little. Smooth, positive inputs work better than twitchy corrections.
The demonstration is complete when all SCATSAFE elements are understood and the aircraft is recovered to a normal, trimmed energy state.
Expect the stick shaker to be on through portions of the maneuver.
The usual misses are poor clearing discipline, abrupt controls, weak trim, and altitude control that degrades while the student watches the effect instead of flying the aircraft.

events.overview: This sortie is about crosswind control first and recovery discipline second. You should be able to brief how the wind changes the takeoff, approach, and landing picture, then keep normal unusual-attitude recoveries clearly separated from OCF so a bad upset does not get worse.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Crosswind work is one continuous control problem from lineup through rollout. The big mistake is treating takeoff, final, and landing as separate moments instead of one uninterrupted wind-correction picture.

children.text: Before lineup, note wind direction and gusts from tower and the windsock so the first control input is anticipated instead of reactive.
Hold positive aileron into the wind once in position for takeoff. Use up to full deflection at the start of the roll, then relax aileron as speed builds to keep the wings level at liftoff.
Use rudder to stop weather-vaning and keep the nose on centerline. A left crosswind can add to the aircraft's normal left-yaw tendency, so expect to need even more right rudder.
Rotate firmly at 90 KIAS, or add half the gust factor up to 10 knots in gusty conditions, and let the aircraft fly off instead of forcing it into a skip.
Once safely airborne, level the wings, allow the aircraft to crab into the wind, and confirm the ball is centered.
Crab into the wind on downwind to hold the correct track and wingtip distance.

Overshooting winds increase groundspeed in the final turn and usually require slightly more bank with slightly lower power. Undershooting winds usually require slightly less bank with slightly higher power.
Start the final turn with about 30 degrees AOB. Do not exceed 45 degrees of bank; if more is required to make final, wave off.
After rollout on final, use aileron to hold extended centerline, rudder to align the aircraft with the runway, and extra power as required to overcome the drag from cross-controls.
In gusty conditions, add half the gust factor to final approach speed, up to a 10-knot increase.
Transition to the wing-low method on final and keep the upwind wing down through the flare. Do not level the wings prior to touchdown.
Use rudder to align the longitudinal axis with the runway and increase aileron into the wind as airspeed decreases and the controls become less effective.
Touch down on the upwind main first with zero side motion. A crab or drift at touchdown can start a swerve and runway departure.

On a full stop, keep feeding aileron into the wind during rollout, maintain directional control with rudder and brakes, and do not aggressively yank the aircraft back to centerline if touchdown started slightly off-center.
On a touch-and-go, hold the crosswind inputs on the deck, apply positive rotation at flying speed, then level the wings and let the aircraft crab into the wind once safely airborne.
Skipping on takeoff usually means the upwind wing started flying early because the aileron picture or rotation was wrong.
If proper crosswind control is not in before touchdown, or if an uncontrollable drift develops in the flare or after touchdown, wave off.
Do not let brake use or centerline fixation distract you from the real priority: keep the airplane aligned and the upwind wing under control.

items.text: Out-of-control flight starts when the aircraft is stalled and no longer responding like normal flight. The recovery only works if you recognize what phase you are in and stop trying to fly it like an unusual attitude.

children.text: Post-stall gyrations show up as uncommanded motion about one or more axes, erratic airspeed, high or stalled AOA, and controls that feel ineffective or reversed.
An incipient spin looks like oscillatory spin-like motion with stalled AOA, a fully deflected turn needle, and airspeed moving toward the steady-state value. Expect about two turns in this phase.
A steady-state spin stabilizes around 120-135 KIAS with the turn needle pegged in the spin direction, 18+ units AOA, and roughly 400-500 feet of altitude loss per turn.
Airspeed and nose attitude are poor stall cues here. Better cues are uncommanded pitch-up, nose drop, wing roll-off, or pitch bucking.

For post-stall gyrations and incipient spin, go PCL IDLE, physically confirm controls neutral, check altitude, and recover from the resulting unusual attitude once the stall breaks and the aircraft responds.
Be patient with neutral controls. Starting anti-spin guesses too early can make the departure worse.

If the aircraft is in a steady-state erect spin, use NATOPS erect-spin recovery logic: identify spin direction, apply full opposite rudder, move the stick forward of neutral, keep ailerons neutral, and hold the inputs until rotation stops before recovering from the resulting unusual attitude.
If gear or flaps are down during an unintentional spin, retract them immediately to protect against airspeed-limit damage.
A normal unusual-attitude recovery does not fix a stalled or departed aircraft. If the aircraft condition is in doubt, go directly to OCF recovery.
Physically neutral stick matters more than trimmed neutral.
If OCF continues into an unrecoverable rapid descent below 6000 feet AGL, eject.

items.text: Contact unusual attitudes are visual recoveries. The goal is to get back to controlled flight above 6000 feet AGL without creating a stall, accelerated stall, or OCF in the process.

children.text: Set PCL to MAX as required in low-airspeed situations.
Roll past 90 degrees AOB toward the nearest horizon and use back stick to bring the nose down to it.
Roll upright as the nose approaches the horizon. If the airspeed is very low, allow the nose to fall slightly below the horizon before rolling fully upright so the controls come alive again.
Once the aircraft is responding normally, roll wings level, raise the nose to level flight, check oil pressure, and set power as required.
Roll to the nearest horizon while simultaneously retarding PCL to IDLE.
Use speed brake as required and make a smooth pull to level flight while respecting the 316-KIAS limit and performing AGSM.
If AOA is below 18 units and airspeed is very low, you can advance power. If AOA is above 18 units or the aircraft is not responding normally, transition to OCF recovery.
Roll the shortest way to the horizon.
Use power as required.
As the nose approaches or slightly passes the horizon, check and report oil pressure, then adjust power to maintain level flight.
Never push the nose over with forward stick in a nose-high recovery. That creates zero or negative G and can deepen the problem.
Avoid stopping the roll at knife-edge. Rolling past 90 degrees and using positive G is the expeditious recovery method.
Stick shaker or buffet means you are near a stall. Reduce back pressure.
If the aircraft is stalled or in OCF, stop trying to fly a normal unusual-attitude recovery and go straight to OCF recovery.

events.overview: This sortie is the bridge from normal contact flying into engine and emergency-landing decision making. Be ready to brief the limits that matter, the PT6/PMU logic behind the indications you see, and the differences between an ELP, a PEL, and a forced landing when time and energy are running out.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Know the limits you are most likely to brief, violate, or use to decide whether the aircraft is still being flown normally. This is not a memorization contest for every number in NATOPS; it is about knowing the ones that change your go/no-go and landing decisions.

children.text: Maximum ramp weight is 6950 pounds. Maximum takeoff and landing weight are 6900 pounds. Maximum zero fuel weight is 5850 pounds.
Maximum baggage-compartment weight is 80 pounds.
Ground operation is limited to ambient temperatures from -23 C to +43 C.
Maximum touchdown rate is 600 FPM when the mains are serviced to 185 +/- 5 PSI, and 780 FPM when they are serviced to 225 +/- 5 PSI.
Those landing-rate numbers matter because a low-energy ELP or forced landing can tempt you into accepting a sink rate that damages the aircraft.
Do not open the canopy on the ground with surface winds above 40 knots.
Ejection-seat occupant limits are approximately 131.8 to 279.4 pounds including equipment and flight gear.

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full NATOPS-style engine brief. For this event, be able to connect the PT6A-68, PMU, and propeller system to the cues that change whether you continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

children.text: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine engine, so the gas-generator section can still be healthy while the propeller side is the part misbehaving.
The PMU normally schedules fuel, acceleration, deceleration, and propeller response. Weight-on-wheels logic gives you about 60-61% N1 on the ground and about 67% N1 in flight.
The reduction gearbox and propeller interface logic are why NP, torque, and thrust can change even when the gas-generator section has not completely failed.
Healthy N1 with abnormal NP or torque should make you think propeller or control logic before you call it a total engine failure.
Loss of oil pressure or hydraulic pressure together with rapidly decaying N1, torque, and ITT is a much stronger engine-failure picture.
If the PMU drops offline or is selected OFF, fuel scheduling becomes manual and the workload jumps immediately, especially during landing or restart decisions.
Do not casually lift the PCL cutoff gate in flight. Mishaps have happened from inadvertent shutdown attempts.
Once ST READY extinguishes, the automatic start protections are gone, so any PMU OFF or manual-fuel work demands tighter monitoring.
Starts with PMU OFF are not recommended, and any event that leaves you in manual mode should immediately change how cautious you are with throttle movement and landing rollout planning.

items.text: Engine malfunctions are easier to manage when you stop chasing a single annunciator and instead build a full picture from power, N1, torque, ITT, NP, oil pressure, and hydraulic pressure.

children.text: A flameout usually gives you rapid loss of power and airspeed, rapidly decaying N1, torque, and ITT, loss of oil and hydraulic pressure, and the propeller moving toward feather.
An engine seizure can look similar, but often drives oil and hydraulic pressure to zero more abruptly and may include a CHIP warning.

A rollback is an uncommanded power reduction, often from PMU scheduling problems. If the PMU stays online, fuel flow and N1 may simply be lower than expected; if it drops offline, you may get a step change in power.
Uncommanded propeller feather usually shows up as reduced NP, increased torque, more prop noise, less thrust, and sometimes vibration.
A good quick discriminator is whether N1 is still healthy while torque or NP are not. That points you toward prop-system logic rather than a full engine failure.
High-value red warnings for this event are PMU FAIL, FUEL PX, OIL PX, CHIP, CHK ENG, GEN BUS, and BATT BUS.
PMU STATUS in flight matters because it can leave you at flight idle on landing and change the rollout picture.
Do not memorize every amber or white advisory for this event. Focus on the engine indications that change whether you continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

items.text: The emergency landing pattern is the geometry you use for both a PEL and a forced landing. The profile is the same; the difference is whether power is still available and how you correct a low-energy state.

children.text: Interception is normally at high key, 3000 feet AGL, with 2500 feet AGL as the minimum high-key intercept.
Think of the profile in checkpoints: high key at 3000 feet AGL, low key at 1500 feet AGL, base key at 600-800 feet AGL, and final at 110 KIAS minimum.
Maintain 120 KIAS minimum until intercepting final. Do not trade airspeed away just to hit an altitude number.
Best glide clean is about 125 KIAS with roughly 1350-1500 FPM sink and about 2 nautical miles of glide for every 1000 feet lost.
With the gear down and clean otherwise, best glide is about 105 KIAS and glide ratio drops to about 1.6 nautical miles per 1000 feet lost.
Use winds, runway suitability, field elevation, and actual energy state to decide whether you can reach high key, low key, or need another option.

ORM 3-2-1 drives the low-altitude decision chain: do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual forced-landing scenario unless you are on profile, runway in sight, and in a position to maneuver safely to land.
At 300 feet AGL you make the final continue-or-eject decision, at 200 feet the gear should be confirmed down, and at 100 feet the aircraft should be on centerline.
If the profile is falling apart, do not delay the wave-off in training or the eject decision in the real event.
A high-energy state is fixed with methods like 360s, bow ties, S-turns, slips, or early drag, but every choice should still preserve a predictable arrival at high key.
The primary reference in the ELP is the runway. Crosscheck actual position and energy against the next checkpoint early enough to make a smooth correction.
Do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual forced-landing situation unless the runway is in sight, you are on profile, and you can still maneuver safely to land.
Allowing the aircraft to get slow to hit altitude checkpoints is dangerous; maintain 120 KIAS minimum until intercepting final and 110 KIAS minimum on final.
Treat ORM 3-2-1 and the final continue/eject gate as hard warning-and-caution discipline, not as flexible guidelines.

items.text: A PEL is for an engine problem where power still exists but failure may be imminent. The student trap is treating it like a routine recovery and burning up the engine's remaining time with slow procedures or excessive troubleshooting.

children.text: The memory aid is Turn, Climb/Accelerate, Clean, Check, BIP, Determine, Deliver, Reduce, Lower, Report.
Turn toward the nearest suitable field immediately. Then climb at 140 KIAS to DEGA or accelerate to build energy if a climb is not appropriate.
Clean the aircraft as soon as practical because extra drag kills climb and glide performance.
Check for secondary indications and use boost pump and ignition as required.
Do not blindly select boost pump or ignition on if an airstart would not be warranted after a failure, such as oil-system malfunction, chip light, fire light, or FOD.
Determine the runway before intercepting the profile and deliver the ISPI report early enough that everyone else understands your plan.
Reduce to 4-6% torque no sooner than DEGA.
Lower the gear no later than high key, fly 120 KIAS minimum on profile, lower flaps no sooner than low key, and use power immediately to fix a low-energy state.
Inside base key, use normal power corrections to ensure a safe and controlled landing instead of preserving some imaginary perfect emergency picture.
Time is the critical resource in many PELs. Do not turn an impending engine failure into an actual one by being slow.
On a PEL, never accept being below profile prior to the actual point on the ground. Power is available, so use it.
If a safe landing becomes unlikely, the answer is not to keep troubleshooting. Commit to the next safe option.

items.text: A forced landing is what happens when power is gone or insufficient for continued flight and the airplane has enough energy to reach a suitable hard-surface landing area. If that energy or runway picture is not there, the answer becomes eject, not hope.

children.text: The first memory items are Zoom/Glide 125 KIAS minimum, PCL OFF, intercept the ELP, and attempt an airstart only if warranted.
Do not attempt an airstart if the failure involves oil-system malfunction, chip light, fire light, or FOD.
If an airstart is not warranted, pull the firewall shutoff handle and commit to either the forced landing or ejection decision.
Use the nearest suitable hard-surface field of adequate length and align the aircraft with the landing direction as early as possible.
If you cannot reach high key, intercept the ELP at another point with the proper configuration and airspeed rather than stretching the glide into a bad setup.
At low key, use flaps only if energy supports it. If the airplane is not on profile approaching base key, eject in the real event or wave off in the simulated one.
Do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual engine-failure case unless you are on profile, runway in sight, and in a position to maneuver to land.
Maintain 110 KIAS minimum on final until the landing transition. Anticipate a longer flare with 4-6% torque simulating a feathered prop.
If touchdown will occur past the first one-third of the runway in a simulated event, wave off. In the actual event, do not delay the eject decision once safe landing is unlikely.
Air-starts are not recommended below 2000 feet AGL because the primary task there is either safe recovery or ejection.
A flamed-out engine at 125 KIAS typically shows 0% indicated N1, torque near zero, and may still show a small residual oil-pressure indication.
Do not dissipate energy casually in a real forced landing. Use the time you have to build the safest runway plan possible.

items.text: Aldis lamp signals matter when the radios are gone and the tower still has to control you. The student value here is not just the colors; it is knowing how to acknowledge them and how they change your immediate action.

children.text: On the ground: steady green means cleared to take off, flashing green means cleared to taxi, steady red means stop, flashing red means taxi clear of runway, flashing white means return to starting point, and alternating red/green means exercise extreme caution.

In flight: steady green means cleared to land, flashing green means return for landing, steady red means give way and continue circling, flashing red means do not land, and alternating red/green means exercise extreme caution.
A red pyrotechnic signal in flight means do not land and wave off immediately regardless of previous instructions.
Acknowledge in daytime with aileron or rudder movement on the ground and wing rocking in the air.
At night, acknowledge by flashing aircraft lights.

events.summary: NATOPS limits, PT6/PMU basics, and the ELP-to-PEL-to-forced-landing decision chain.

items.text: Start with the big picture, then walk the air path, then the fuel path, and only then talk about cockpit indications. That flow makes the brief sound like you understand the engine instead of reciting disconnected parts.

children.text: Purpose: convert fuel and air into shaft horsepower for the propeller while supplying the accessory and lubrication systems that keep the engine alive.
Architecture: free-turbine, reverse-flow engine with separate gas-generation and power sections.
Briefing payoff: once you understand where power is made and how the propeller is controlled, engine-failure indications make a lot more sense.

items.text: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine turboprop flat-rated to produce 1100 shaft horsepower. It is a reverse-flow design with two independent sections.

children.text: Gas-generation section: four-stage axial compressor, single-stage centrifugal compressor, combustion chamber, and single-stage compressor turbine.
Power section: two-stage axial-flow power turbine, exhaust case, and reduction gearbox.
The power turbine is not mechanically linked to the compressor. That is why the engine can still be producing gas-generator indications even when the propeller side is degrading.
The reduction gearbox takes turbine speed of roughly 30,000 RPM down to about 2000 RPM at the Hartzell four-blade constant-speed propeller.
The engine is cooled and lubricated by a dedicated oil system, and the engine data manager monitors the operating parameters that drive the EICAS messages you brief.
The accessory-drive section powers the engine-driven components that keep the engine, oil, and propeller-control systems functioning.

items.text: The air molecule brief is the easiest way to explain how the PT6 makes power: trace the air from the intake to the exhaust and explain what each section is doing to it.

children.text: Inlet air travels rearward through the intake duct and inertial separator, which helps throw debris and moisture out of the airstream.
The air then moves forward through the four-stage axial compressor and the single-stage centrifugal compressor. The diffuser slows that flow and converts velocity into static pressure.
Diffused air passes through straightening vanes before it mixes with atomized fuel in the combustion chamber.
The expanding gas first drives the single-stage compressor turbine, which is mechanically linked to the compressor and keeps the gas-generator cycle going.
That same gas then drives the separate two-stage power turbine, which turns the reduction gearbox through its own shaft.
Exhaust gases leave through the stacks and add a small amount of thrust, but the real output the pilot cares about is the shaft power being delivered to the propeller.

items.text: The fuel molecule brief should explain how the engine meters fuel rather than just saying fuel goes to the nozzles.

children.text: Fuel leaves the tanks and reaches the engine fuel pump and fuel-management unit, where it is metered based on PCL position and system inputs.
Metered fuel is sent through the flow divider to the fuel nozzles, where it is atomized into the compressed air inside the combustion chamber.
During start, the igniters light the mixture. Once the engine is running, combustion becomes self-sustaining.
The PMU and related control logic are why fuel scheduling, acceleration, deceleration, and propeller response feel coordinated in normal operations.

Mounted around the reduction gearbox are the chip detector, PIU, torque probe, and PMA, which is why a gearbox or propeller-control problem can change what the fuel and power picture looks like from the cockpit.
If you can explain how the FMU, PMU, and propeller-control pieces interact, you are much better prepared to talk through rollback, feather, or PMU-related malfunctions.

events.overview: This sortie is about understanding what the hydraulic system buys you before you go spin, OCF, and crosswind work. Be ready to brief the hydraulic system well enough to explain normal versus emergency services, then keep the spin, OCF, anti-spin, and crosswind boundaries straight once the aircraft departs normal flight.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full hydraulic walk-through. For this event, know what hydraulic power you are counting on in normal flight, what changes when the normal system is lost, and which indications change your gear, flap, or NWS decisions.

children.text: Normal hydraulic power runs the landing gear, TO/LDG flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering.
The engine-driven pump maintains roughly 3000 +/- 120 PSI from a 5-quart reservoir. That normal-system pressure is what you are relying on anytime you move gear, flaps, or speed brake.
Think normal versus emergency: the power package and selector manifold do the routine work, and the emergency accumulator gives you one backup shot if the main system is gone.
HYDR FL LO points you toward a fluid-quantity, leak, or normal-system problem and should make you stop assuming normal gear or flap operation is guaranteed.
EHYD PX LO after emergency use is expected. EHYD PX LO together with HYDR FL LO suggests a leak or hydraulic-fuse problem and a thinner backup margin.
Emergency gear extension leaves the inboard doors extended, and emergency flap extension uses the same flap selector but the flaps cannot be retracted once they are out.
Disengage NWS before sharp turns that require differential braking.
Do not take off with a known NWS problem; centering issues can create takeoff or landing control problems.
If the emergency accumulator has been discharged for maintenance, the related caution should be out before flight.

items.text: The spin is not a finesse maneuver. It is a deliberate stalled-yaw entry used to teach recognition, orientation, and disciplined recovery once the aircraft departs normal flight.

children.text: Trim the aircraft in slow cruise at 150 KIAS.
Minimum entry altitude is 13,500 feet AGL. Enter below 22,000 feet pressure altitude and recover before 10,000 feet pressure altitude.
The entry is built to begin with PCL going to IDLE before the nose comes up; do not build the pitch picture first and pull power late.
Perform the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist and clear the area thoroughly, including TCAS as appropriate.
Check wings level, retard PCL to IDLE, and smoothly raise the nose to about 30 degrees above the horizon.
At the stick shaker, lead the stall with slight rudder in the desired spin direction.
When the aircraft stalls and the nose pitches down, smoothly apply full rudder in the direction of spin and full back stick with ailerons neutral.
Call out altitude, AOA, airspeed, and turn-needle direction so the phase of the spin stays clear.
The maneuver is complete when the IP-directed recovery is finished, oil pressure is checked and reported normal, and the aircraft is back in controlled flight inside the working area.
Raising the nose before PCL is fully at IDLE.
Letting disorientation delay recognition or recovery.
Failing to neutralize controls as rotation stops or pulling too aggressively into a secondary stall.
Spins are flown clean. If gear or flaps are down in an unintentional spin, get them up immediately to avoid airspeed-limit damage.
Ailerons remain neutral throughout intentional spin training.
Silence the gear-warning horn before entry so it does not interfere with recognition calls.

items.text: OCF recovery procedures are for post-stall gyrations and incipient spins where the aircraft has departed normal flight but has not yet stabilized into a true steady-state spin.

children.text: Post-stall gyration shows up as uncommanded motion about one or more axes, erratic airspeed, high or stalled AOA, and controls that feel ineffective or wrong.
An incipient spin shows stalled AOA, a fully deflected turn needle, and airspeed changing toward the steady-state value. Expect about the first two turns here.
If you are not yet in a stabilized 120-135 KIAS, 18+ units AOA, steady-state picture, stay with OCF recovery rather than jumping to anti-spin inputs.
PCL - IDLE.
CONTROLS - NEUTRAL, physically not just trimmed neutral.
ALTITUDE - CHECK.
RECOVER FROM UNUSUAL ATTITUDE once the stall breaks and the aircraft begins responding normally.
If the aircraft is not recovering as expected, it is common for the elevator to still be slightly aft of neutral; feed in forward stick only enough to find true neutral.
Do not start inventing anti-spin inputs early just because the motion feels dramatic.
If the aircraft is in an unrecoverable descent below 6000 feet AGL, eject.

items.text: Anti-spin recovery procedures are for a true steady-state spin, not for every out-of-control motion. The key is recognizing when neutral-controls recovery is no longer the right answer.

children.text: A steady-state erect spin is identified by 18+ units AOA, airspeed stabilized around 120-135 KIAS, and the turn needle fully deflected in the direction of spin.
At that point the spin has stabilized enough that anti-spin controls, not neutral controls, are required.
Apply full rudder opposite the turn-needle direction.
Immediately follow with smooth, positive forward stick to a position forward of neutral.
Keep ailerons neutral and hold the controls until rotation stops.
Then neutralize the controls, level the wings by horizon reference, make a smooth pullout, check oil pressure, and add power as required.
Progressive and aggravated spins are not handled by random experimentation; if the motion has not stabilized into a true steady-state picture, default back to OCF recovery logic.

Intentional inverted departures and inverted spins are prohibited. If an inverted-spin picture develops, the recovery inputs differ from erect-spin recovery and the aircraft requires post-flight scrutiny.
Power-on or inverted departures/spins place very high loads on the engine and propeller system and may produce low oil pressure or CHIP indications.
A spiral can look like a spin, but anti-spin inputs will not stop a spiral and may worsen it.
Do not hold full aft stick turn after turn waiting for the airplane to save you. Once the spin is clearly steady-state, transition to the proper anti-spin inputs.
Forward stick well beyond neutral can create oil-pressure issues and engine damage, and anti-spin logic should never replace proper phase recognition.

items.text: This event expects you to apply crosswind technique repeatedly, not just once. The student value is showing that the crosswind picture survives takeoff, touch-and-go, and full-stop landing without drifting back into late or sloppy corrections.

children.text: Use up to full aileron into the wind at the start of the takeoff roll, relax it as speed builds, and use rudder to stop weather-vaning.
Rotate firmly at flying speed to avoid skipping, then level the wings and let the aircraft crab into the wind once safely airborne.
On downwind and in the final turn, adjust bank and power for overshooting or undershooting winds and do not exceed 45 degrees of bank to make final.
Use the wing-low method on final: aileron into the wind to stop drift, rudder to align the nose with the runway, and extra power as required to offset cross-control drag.
During gusty conditions, add half the gust factor to final approach speed, up to 10 knots.
Do not level the wings in the flare. Land on the upwind main first with zero side motion.
On full stops, keep increasing aileron into the wind as the aircraft slows and the controls lose effectiveness.
On touch-and-goes, hold the crosswind controls on the deck, use positive rotation, then level the wings and allow the aircraft to crab into the wind after liftoff.
If you cannot prevent overshooting final without exceeding 45 degrees of bank, or if drift/crab is not under control before touchdown, wave off.
Skipping on takeoff, landing in a crab, and letting the upwind wing rise on rollout all come from losing the wind-correction picture as the aircraft slows or lifts off.
Do not aggressively yank the aircraft back to centerline after an off-center touchdown. Keep the wing under control first.

events.summary: Hydraulic-system essentials, spin recognition, OCF versus anti-spin recovery, and repeated crosswind pattern application.

items.text: Start with purpose, then explain how normal hydraulic pressure is created and routed, then finish with what the emergency system does when the main system is gone. That sequence is much easier to brief than listing parts at random.

children.text: Purpose: provide hydraulic power for landing gear, flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering.
Normal-system flow: power package creates pressure, selector manifold routes it to the commanded service.
Emergency-system flow: accumulator pressure is saved for one-time emergency landing-gear and flap use.

items.text: The power package is the pressure-producing heart of the hydraulic system. It houses the reservoir, pump, and the components that regulate and protect system pressure.

children.text: The reservoir holds 5 quarts of hydraulic fluid, and the engine-driven pump maintains about 3000 +/- 120 PSI for the normal system.
A pressure reducer piston helps bring return pressure down, and the relief valve protects the system from overpressurization.
The pressure transmitter is what feeds the cockpit indication logic, and the filters are there to keep contamination from becoming a hydraulic problem.
The slide-valve assembly keeps the emergency system isolated during normal operations so the accumulator stays available for when you actually need it.
Think of 1800 PSI as the rough floor where the system still has enough pressure to do useful work, even though the normal target is much closer to 3000 PSI.

items.text: The selector manifold is the traffic cop. It takes pressure from the power package and sends it to the system you actually command from the cockpit.

children.text: Landing gear: the gear selector valve routes pressure to the main gear, nose gear, and inboard-door actuators. Three green lights mean down and locked; no lights mean up; a red light means transit or an associated gear-door condition.
Flaps: separate TO and LDG selector-valve paths let the flap actuator move the torque tube and flap system to the commanded setting.
Speed brake: hydraulic pressure extends it, and it auto-retracts with PCL to MAX, flap selection to LDG, or manual retract selection.
Nosewheel steering is hydraulically powered and gives about 12 degrees left or right of castor when engaged.
NWS is for ground steering only. If you need a sharper turn, disengage NWS before using differential braking so you are not fighting or damaging the steering system.
A speed brake that droops on the ramp is not automatically a malfunction; with pressure removed, the brake can settle because hydraulic pressure normally holds it up.

items.text: The emergency system is built around a helium-precharged accumulator that stores pressure for one-time emergency extension of the landing gear and flaps.

children.text: Pulling the emergency gear-extension handle releases accumulator pressure, isolates the main system, and ports pressure to the landing-gear and inboard-door actuators.
After emergency gear extension, the inboard doors remain extended. That is normal for the emergency configuration.
Emergency flap extension uses the same flap selector, but it is powered through the emergency path and the flaps cannot be retracted once extended.
A hydraulic fuse helps limit fluid loss into the emergency system if a leak develops.
An EHYD PX LO after emergency use is expected. EHYD PX LO together with HYDR FL LO is the combination that should make you think leak or fuse trouble instead of normal accumulator depletion.
If the emergency accumulator was discharged for maintenance, make sure the caution has cleared before flight so you do not launch with the backup already spent.

items.text: Most weak hydraulic briefs come from forgetting to tie indications back to what service you will actually lose next.

children.text: HYDR FL LO is a normal-system cue. EHYD PX LO is an emergency-system cue. Seeing both together means more than seeing either one alone.
Do not brief NWS as an isolated taxi feature; in this event it matters because a steering problem can become a takeoff, landing, or crosswind-control problem.
Be explicit that the emergency system is one-time use. Students often remember it exists but forget that you are spending stored pressure, not switching to a second normal system.
