events.overview: I6201 rehearses the complete transition from clearance to approach completion. Maintain procedure awareness through departure and course reversal, compute timing deliberately, use the VDP correctly, and treat the missed approach as a planned maneuver rather than a surprise.

sourceDocuments.summary: Source document tied to this event.
sourceDocuments.title: I6101 1542.166D

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Clearance and departure procedures begin with copying the clearance accurately, reading it back cleanly, and knowing whether the clearance includes an ODP, SID, radar vector, diverse departure, or visual climb over airport option.

children.text: For a normal instrument takeoff, set the climb attitude about 8 to 10 degrees nose high, trim, confirm a positive climb, retract gear and flaps on schedule, and accelerate toward 180 KIAS.
If obstacle clearance or a nonstandard gradient matters, brief the required climb before takeoff; the normal 180 KIAS climb profile is not a substitute for a published requirement.
Use best-rate performance when directed or required: approximately 140 KIAS and 15 degrees nose high.
For level-off, lead by about 10 percent of the vertical speed, reduce power, lower the nose, accelerate, and trim rather than chasing altitude after the fact.
Diverse departure assumptions only work when the airport has been assessed for that use and the aircraft can meet the climb performance requirement.
Before launch, identify the approach or recovery plan you would use for an emergency return and keep the missed-approach or climbout clearance separate from the published departure path.

items.text: A VOR procedure turn is a protected course reversal that gets the aircraft established inbound at the proper altitude before the final approach segment.

children.text: Before the fix, complete SNERT, slow to 150 KIAS about 5 NM prior, identify station passage, and run the 6 Ts.
Fly outbound for one minute, descend with about 15 percent torque as required, and level at procedure-turn altitude using a 33 percent lead.
Turn 45 degrees toward the protected barb side, time for one minute, twist inbound, then turn 180 degrees in the opposite direction to intercept final.
Use double-the-angle when the bearing pointer is within 5 degrees of the inbound course; otherwise use about a 45-degree intercept.
Established means the bearing pointer is within 5 degrees and the CDI is within one dot or centered.
Be BAC within 5 NM of the FAF, and stay within the published remain-within distance throughout the maneuver.

items.text: A non-depicted teardrop can be used as a procedure-turn variant when it keeps the aircraft on the protected side and inside the published remain-within distance.

children.text: At station passage, run the 6 Ts and turn outbound to about a 20-degree offset toward the barb or protected side.
Fly outbound for about two minutes at 150 KIAS, using roughly 15 percent torque for the descent as required.
Adjust outbound timing for wind and protected-airspace limits; the two-minute pattern is not permission to drift outside the remain-within distance.
Twist the inbound course at about one minute and thirty seconds, then turn inbound at two minutes.
Intercept with double-the-angle when close enough to the inbound course, or about a 45-degree intercept when larger corrections are required.
Be BAC within 5 NM of the FAF; if the intercept is not stabilizing, correct early rather than carrying the error to final.

items.text: FAF-to-MAP timing protects a non-precision approach when DME, GPS, or another distance reference is unavailable or becomes unreliable.

children.text: Use the timing table on the aerodrome sketch, convert approach airspeed to groundspeed with the forecast or observed wind, and interpolate when the exact groundspeed is not printed.
Start timing at the FAF, not after troubleshooting the descent, and keep the clock running as a backup even when another distance source is primary.
The event expectation is to explain how a headwind or tailwind changes groundspeed and therefore changes the time from FAF to MAP.
If DME fails after the FAF on a timed approach, use the clock to identify the MAP.
Do not descend early because the timing looks favorable; altitude, MDA, VDP, visual references, and safe-landing criteria still control the descent.

items.text: The VDP is the point on a non-precision approach from which a normal descent can be made from MDA to the runway touchdown zone.

children.text: Use the published VDP when available; if one is not published, a common planning estimate is HAT divided by 300.
For DME planning, subtract the computed VDP distance from runway DME to identify the approximate VDP DME.
If no VDP is published, treat that as a warning that obstacle clearance or procedure design may not support a normal descent from a simple calculated point.
Do not descend below MDA before the VDP just because the runway environment is in sight.
At the VDP, continue only if visual references and aircraft position support a safe descent to landing.
If safe landing criteria are not met by the MAP, execute the missed approach rather than forcing the descent late.

items.text: A missed approach is a disciplined climb and navigation procedure, not a last-second save; brief what triggers it, what path is protected, and what clearance is actually in effect.

children.text: Go missed at DA, DH, or the MAP when required visual references are not acquired, a safe landing cannot be made, ATC directs it, or course guidance becomes unusable.

Before the FAF, a full-scale CDI deflection normally calls for reintercepting and not descending; between FAF and MAP, climb as required, reestablish, proceed to the MAP, and execute the missed approach.
Do not execute the published missed early from MDA just because the field is not yet in sight; on a non-precision approach, the MAP still matters unless safety or ATC requires otherwise.
Use maximum allowable power, set approximately 10 to 15 degrees nose high, confirm two positive rates, retract the gear, and retract flaps above 110 KIAS.
Accelerate toward 180 KIAS with about 8 to 10 degrees nose high, then turn at standard rate to the assigned heading or published missed-approach course as appropriate.
Run DRAFT once climbing and controlled: destination, route, altitude, fuel, and transponder.
Separate an ATC-assigned climbout from the published missed approach. Fly the clearance you have, but know the published missed in case the clearance changes or communications fail.

The standard missed-approach obstacle gradient is 200 feet per NM unless a higher gradient is published; at 180 KIAS the T-6 normally has substantially more climb performance, but verify any published requirement.

events.overview: I6202 emphasizes procedure transitions and workload control. Build each approach before it begins, keep navigation orientation through arcs and vectors, manage holding or shuttle descent deliberately, and arrive at final configured with the missed approach already understood.

sourceDocuments.summary: Source document tied to this event.
sourceDocuments.title: I6102 1542.166D

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Arcing is used to position the aircraft inbound on an intermediate or final approach course by flying a constant DME from the NAVAID.

children.text: Expect arcing approaches to be identified by VOR/DME or TACAN in the approach margin; DME is required.
About 5 NM prior to the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS and have the arc direction, lead point, segment altitude, inbound course, and voice-report requirement ready.
At the IAF, use the 6 Ts, turn to place the bearing-pointer head on the 90-degree benchmark, comply with segment altitudes, and set the inbound course in the CDI.
Published lead radials marked LR-xxx are advisory and based on 200 KTAS with a half-standard-rate turn; at normal 150 KIAS approach speeds, compute the lead radial for a standard-rate turn.
For a radial-to-arc intercept, lead the arc by turn radius: 0.5 percent of groundspeed for standard-rate, or 1.0 percent of groundspeed for half-standard-rate.
For an arc-to-radial intercept, compute radials per NM as 60 divided by arc DME, then multiply by turn radius to find the no-wind lead radial.
If groundspeed is unavailable in time, KIAS may be used as a no-wind approximation, then adjusted for known wind.
On the arc, bearing-pointer head on the 90-degree benchmark holds DME in no wind; below the benchmark increases DME, and above it decreases DME.
If inside the arc, maintain heading or place the bearing-pointer head up to 15 degrees below the benchmark; if outside, place it up to 15 degrees above.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to BAC as required and continue the published low-altitude approach procedure.

items.text: RVFAC uses ATC radar vectors to place the aircraft on the final approach course by the most expeditious route consistent with traffic and terrain clearance.

children.text: Fly 200 KIAS on downwind, 150 KIAS on base, and 200 KIAS on an extended final or extended dog-leg until within 15 NM of the airport.
Tune and identify the NAVAID, verify the PFD source, set the final approach course in the CDI, and follow assigned headings and altitudes.
ATC uses MVA for terrain clearance while vectoring, but maintain your own situational awareness with available NAVAIDs and charts; query if the vector or altitude does not make sense.
Transition to BAC when within 5 NM of the FAF and the aircraft heading is within 90 degrees of the final approach course.
If no FAF is depicted, transition to BAC once established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach.
After approach clearance, maintain the last assigned heading and altitude until established on the approach, then lead the turn as the CDI centers.

items.text: A localizer approach uses the localizer component of the ILS for lateral guidance, but it is a non-precision approach flown to MDA and MAP.

children.text: The localizer intercept and D LIDS setup are the same discipline as ILS: DME hold if required, tune and identify localizer, set inbound course, select LOC, and use transition speed.
On an ILS or LOC approach where the glideslope is unavailable or not used, fly non-precision rules and minimums.
If CDI is full-scale before the FAF, reintercept; if not on scale by the FAF, do not descend below FAF altitude.
At the non-precision FAF, perform the 6 Ts and start timing as MAP backup if timing is available.
Set about 20 percent torque, trim for a 120 KIAS descent, and keep descent rate stabilized at no more than 1000 fpm.
About 100 feet prior to MDA, set roughly 42 percent torque and transition to level flight at or above MDA.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs between FAF and MAP, turn to reestablish and track while climbing to missed-approach altitude, then fly the missed at the MAP or as assigned.
Do not execute the missed just because MDA is reached; continue to the MAP unless safety, ATC, or loss of usable guidance requires otherwise.
Common errors are late D LIDS, flying through final, no backup timing, overcontrolling localizer corrections, using the wrong MDA, and continuing with full-scale CDI inside the FAF.

items.text: Holding keeps the aircraft inside protected airspace until ATC issues further clearance; the task is geometry, timing, correction, and communication all at once.

children.text: Start slowing within 3 minutes or 5 NM of the holding fix when clearance beyond the fix has not been received; normal T-6B holding airspeed is 150 KIAS.
A full uncharted holding clearance includes direction from fix, fix name, radial/course/bearing/route, leg length, turn direction, EFC, and delay information.
If the pattern is charted, hold as published unless ATC issues different instructions; if instructions are missing before an en route clearance limit, request them.
A standard pattern uses right turns; non-standard uses left turns. Inbound legs track the holding course, and outbound legs fly headings.
For standard entries, use parallel when the reciprocal lies between the heading index and 110 degrees left, teardrop when between the heading index and 70 degrees right, and direct otherwise.
For non-standard entries, reverse the entry-side logic. If the reciprocal is within 5 degrees of a boundary, either adjacent entry is acceptable.
At the end of the outbound leg, use tail-radial-turn to decide the inbound turn and establish on course promptly.
Use the no-wind orbit to measure wind: start timing when wings level or abeam, turn inbound toward the holding radial, then note crab angle and inbound time.
On correction orbits, triple the inbound drift correction outbound for no more than one minute, then use single drift if the outbound leg continues.
Adjust outbound timing by the inbound timing error; if inbound was 10 seconds short, add 10 seconds outbound.
Report established in holding with position, time, and altitude when required, and confirm EFC at least 5 minutes prior if it has not been confirmed.

items.text: A shuttle descent is an ATC-directed descent within holding that moves the aircraft to the next lower stack altitude while preserving protected-airspace control.

children.text: Shuttles are normally used after the lower aircraft in the stack has commenced the approach; vertical separation in the stack can be as little as 1000 feet.
Report leaving the current altitude for the assigned altitude, reduce power to about 15 percent torque, lower the nose to maintain 150 KIAS, and re-trim.
Lead the level-off about 50 feet prior, reset power near 33 percent torque, raise the nose to level flight, and re-trim.
Keep the holding correction alive during the descent; the altitude change does not pause timing, drift correction, or protected-airspace responsibility.
Common errors are fixating on altitude and losing the pattern, fixating on the pattern and missing level-off, or letting airspeed drift away from 150 KIAS.

events.overview: I3101 moves from basic radio navigation into full instrument approach sequencing. The event standard is to copy and fly the clearance, transition cleanly from takeoff to instruments, stay ahead of en route setup, and execute procedure-turn, teardrop, arcing, and missed-approach procedures without losing the aircraft.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Clearance and departure procedures connect the IFR clearance, the departure method, and the instrument takeoff scan into one plan before the aircraft moves.

children.text: Copy the clearance deliberately: aircraft identification, clearance limit, departure type, route, altitude, departure frequency, transponder code, and any additional restrictions or holding instructions.
Before takeoff, review terrain, hazards, climb gradients, and the assigned departure type; set NAVAIDs and displays so the first navigation task is ready before brake release.
Keep the most likely emergency return approach available. Departure setup should answer where you will point the aircraft if the climb does not go normally.
Fly a normal takeoff, use outside references and the attitude indicator at liftoff, then transition fully to the instrument scan as visual cues diminish.
Set about 8 to 10 degrees nose high, trim, verify the climb on the altimeter and VSI, then raise the gear and flaps.
Maintain the initial attitude until about 180 KIAS unless the departure or aircraft performance requires a different climb profile.
For best-rate climb, use about 140 KIAS and 15 degrees nose high.
Lead level-offs with roughly 10 percent of the climb rate; for example, start adjusting about 200 feet early during a 2000 FPM climb.
If below climb speed, reduce power as the pitch comes down. If above climb speed, maintain power long enough to accelerate, then stabilize and trim.
Know the departure families: ODP, SID, radar departure, diverse departure, and VCOA.
For a diverse departure, climb to 400 feet AGL before turning and plan on at least 200 feet per NM, which is about 600 FPM at 180 KIAS.

items.text: En route procedures are the discipline that keeps the aircraft ahead of the next clearance, fix, approach setup, and descent requirement.

children.text: Use the assigned airway, radial, DME, or point-to-point clearance as the controlling navigation task; FMS shortcuts do not replace the radio-navigation procedure being trained.

For point-to-point navigation, tune and identify the NAVAID, set the desired radial, visualize the present and desired radial/DME positions, then split the bearing-pointer and course-pointer heads for the initial no-wind heading.
Update the point-to-point solution as DME and bearing change. If DME will arrive first, split the needle to slow DME change; if the radial arrives first, track inbound or outbound to the fix.
Use the ABCDs early enough to matter: ATIS, brief the approach and minimums, cockpit setup, and descent checklist before the IAF.
Plan NAVAID changeover at the published changeover point, halfway between facilities if no point is shown, or about 10 NM before an intersection when required.
Keep fuel, weather, recovery options, and approach request timing in the scan instead of waiting for the terminal area to force the workload.

items.text: A procedure turn reverses course inside protected airspace so the aircraft can intercept the final approach course from the proper side and altitude.

children.text: Do not fly a procedure turn when SNERT applies: straight-in clearance, NoPT routing, established in aligned holding and cleared for the approach, radar vectors to final, or a timed approach.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS and prepare the six Ts.
At station passage, turn the shortest direction to parallel the outbound course. If that turn would exceed 90 degrees, use a 45-degree intercept.
Start 1 minute outbound when wings level or abeam, whichever occurs later; descend if required with about 15 percent torque at 150 KIAS.
Level at the procedure-turn altitude, normally adding power near 33 percent torque and re-trimming.
At 1 minute outbound, turn 45 degrees toward the protected side, start another 1-minute clock, and twist the inbound course.

At the end of the barb leg, turn 180 degrees opposite. If the bearing-pointer head is within 5 degrees of the inbound course, continue the turn with double-the-angle intercept; otherwise roll out on the barb heading for a 45-degree intercept.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and maintain altitude until slowing permits the descent.

items.text: A teardrop approach is another course-reversal option that uses an offset outbound leg toward the protected side before turning inbound.

children.text: A non-depicted teardrop may be used as a substitute for a depicted procedure turn when cleared for the approach; offset about 20 degrees from the final approach course toward the barb or protected side.
Remain within the published distance, typically 10 NM, and adjust the outbound leg for wind so the turn back inbound stays inside protected airspace.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS.
At station passage, turn toward the outbound teardrop course, start 2 minutes outbound when wings level or abeam, and descend if required with about 15 percent torque at 150 KIAS.
Level at the procedure-turn altitude, add power near 33 percent torque, and twist the inbound course at about 1.5 minutes outbound.
At 2 minutes outbound, turn in the depicted direction. Use double-the-angle if the bearing-pointer head is within 5 degrees of inbound; otherwise use a 45-degree intercept.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF and continue with the published approach.

items.text: Missed approach procedures protect the climb after an approach can no longer be continued visually, safely, or within course guidance.

children.text: Execute the missed approach at the MAP or DA/DH when the runway environment is not in sight, required visibility is not available, or the aircraft is not in position for a normal landing.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, attempt to re-intercept, do not descend, and notify ATC.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs between the FAF and MAP, climb toward the missed-approach altitude and notify ATC. Obstacle protection is only assured along published or assigned segments.
In training, distinguish the published missed approach from an assigned climbout; fly the clearance you were given unless safety requires otherwise.
At the MAP, set PCL MAX, pitch 10 to 15 degrees nose high, verify two positive rates, then raise the gear.
Above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps, accelerate toward 180 KIAS, and adjust toward an 8 to 10 degree nose-high climb attitude.
Start a standard-rate turn as required to the missed-approach course or assigned heading, then report missed approach with the reason.
Once climbing and navigating, pass DRAFT as required: destination, route, altitude, fuel, and time en route.
Standard obstacle-clearance planning uses 200 feet per NM; the T-6B normally exceeds that at about 180 KIAS and roughly 2000 FPM, but higher published gradients still require performance planning.

events.overview: I3102 builds the instrument approach workload around holding-pattern geometry. The event standard is to fly holding in lieu of a procedure turn, manage shuttle descents and intersection tasks without losing protected airspace, and connect oil-system indications to the correct PEL decision.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: HILO approaches use a published holding pattern in lieu of a procedure turn to reverse direction and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course.

children.text: The pattern is printed like holding, but it is treated like a course reversal. Only one turn in holding is authorized unless ATC clears additional turns.
A HILO approach always has a depicted FAF.
Case I permits descent to the holding altitude, then no lower until crossing the FAF.
Case II permits further descent once established inbound.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS and prepare for a normal holding entry.

At the IAF, use the six Ts: no timing requirement at station passage, turn using the proper entry, start outbound timing when wings level or abeam, transition if descent is required, twist the inbound course, and talk as required.
If descending, use about 15 percent torque and 150 KIAS, then level at the required altitude before the next descent point.
Use tail-radial-turn and, if needed, double-the-angle intercept to establish inbound before crossing the holding fix.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and continue with the published approach.

items.text: Holding is protected-airspace management: enter correctly, keep the inbound leg under control, and leave the pattern exactly as cleared.

children.text: Copy and read back the clearance, determine the holding side and turn direction, and slow to 150 KIAS within 3 minutes or 5 NM when required.
A standard pattern uses right turns; a non-standard pattern uses left turns.
Use the aircraft heading and the reciprocal of the holding course to choose direct, parallel, or teardrop entry.
If the reciprocal falls within 5 degrees of an entry boundary, either adjacent entry is acceptable.
Direct entry turns outbound in the pattern direction after fix passage.
Parallel entry flies outbound parallel to the inbound course, then turns opposite the pattern direction to intercept inbound.
Teardrop entry turns 30 degrees toward the holding side from the reciprocal of the holding course.
Use the six Ts at the fix and on each turn so timing, turns, configuration, CDI setting, and required reports stay in order.
Use tail-radial-turn to decide the inbound turn direction when tracking back toward the holding radial.
Triple the inbound drift correction on the outbound leg for up to 1 minute, then transition to single drift if the outbound leg continues.
Adjust outbound time by the inbound timing error: if inbound was 10 seconds short, add 10 seconds outbound; if it was long, subtract time.
Report position, time, and altitude when required, and confirm EFC at least 5 minutes prior if needed.

items.text: A shuttle descent is an ATC-directed descent inside holding that preserves the stack while moving the aircraft to a lower altitude.

children.text: Report leaving the current altitude for the assigned altitude.
Set about 15 percent torque, lower the nose to maintain 150 KIAS, and re-trim without letting the holding pattern unravel.
Lead the level-off by about 50 feet, add power near 33 percent torque, raise the nose to level flight, and re-trim.
The common trap is fixation: watching altitude so hard that the pattern drifts, or watching the pattern so hard that the level-off is missed.

items.text: Intersections are fixes that drive airway changes, timing reports, holding entries, approach transitions, missed approaches, and configuration or altitude tasks.

children.text: Use the primary NAVAID for the course being flown and the secondary NAVAID only as the crosscut used to identify the fix.
For VOR/DME intersections, track the primary course to the fix DME, note the time if required, then either continue outbound or start the standard-rate turn to the new course.
When turning to a new course, set up the next course within about 10 NM, maintain the wind-corrected heading until the turn lead, then intercept promptly if early or late.
For VOR-only intersections, estimate the fix time, tune the secondary NAVAID about 3 minutes prior, and watch the crosscut bearing-pointer tail.
If the tail is still more than 10 radials from the fix, retune the primary, wait briefly, and recheck.
When within 10 radials, hold heading until the tail rises to the crossing radial, then note time and continue or turn as cleared.
Late secondary setup, wrong turn lead, and trying to force the aircraft exactly over the fix when that is not required are the common errors.
For GPS fly-over waypoints, confirm the waypoint is next in sequence, cross it, then update course after the active leg changes.
For GPS fly-by waypoints, the system anticipates the turn; start the standard-rate turn when the CDI flashes and re-intercept promptly if the timing is off.

items.text: Oil system malfunctions are PEL-driving problems unless the indication is clearly limited to a brief amber caution with normal oil pressure.

children.text: Use this procedure for a red OIL PX warning, amber OIL PX caution, oil-pressure fluctuations, oil temperature out of limits, or visible oil leak.
If only the amber OIL PX caution illuminates, terminate maneuvering and check oil pressure. If oil pressure is normal, continued operation may be appropriate.
A momentary amber OIL PX during maneuvering may not indicate a malfunction, and simultaneous red and amber OIL PX with normal oil pressure indicates an SCU failure.
If an OIL PX warning occurs with oil pressure below 5 psi, the OIL TRX circuit breaker may be checked and reset if open, but troubleshooting must not delay aircraft control or the landing decision.

For red OIL PX, amber OIL PX lasting more than 5 seconds, oil-pressure fluctuations, or oil temperature out of limits, set PCL to the minimum necessary to intercept the ELP and avoid unnecessary PCL movement.
Execute a PEL. Higher power may aggravate the condition, so use only what the profile requires.
Normal steady-state oil pressure is 90 to 120 psi; oil pressure less than 90 psi at flight idle or above is indicative of a malfunction.
Normal flight oil temperature is 10 to 105 degrees C, with 106 to 110 degrees C limited to 10 minutes.

events.overview: I3103 develops precise approach setup while continuing to manage navigation and aircraft-system contingencies. Keep the clearance, course, configuration, and final-approach picture ahead of the aircraft, then apply the hydraulic emergency branch without abandoning instrument control.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: RVFAC uses ATC radar vectors to place the aircraft on the final approach course by the most expeditious route consistent with traffic and terrain clearance.

children.text: Fly 200 KIAS on downwind, 150 KIAS on base, and 200 KIAS on an extended final or extended dog-leg until within 15 NM of the airport.
Tune and identify the NAVAID, verify the PFD source, set the final approach course in the CDI, and follow assigned headings and altitudes.
ATC uses MVA for terrain clearance while vectoring, but maintain your own situational awareness with available NAVAIDs and charts; query if the vector or altitude does not make sense.
Transition to BAC when within 5 NM of the FAF and the aircraft heading is within 90 degrees of the final approach course.
If no FAF is depicted, transition to BAC once established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach.
After approach clearance, maintain the last assigned heading and altitude until established on the approach, then lead the turn as the CDI centers.

items.text: ILS provides localizer azimuth and glideslope vertical guidance; a LOC approach uses the localizer component for lateral guidance as a non-precision approach.

children.text: If the localizer is inoperative, the ILS is not authorized. If the glideslope is inoperative or not used, fly the LOC non-precision procedure and minimums.

The localizer signal is much more sensitive than VOR guidance. Set the published front course, confirm no flags or red Xs, receive the correct identifier, and make small heading corrections near the wind-corrected heading.
Use D LIDS before the final workload builds: DME hold if required, localizer tuned and identified, inbound course set, display source set to LOC, and speed appropriate for the transition.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF with no more than a 90-degree intercept, or when the glideslope comes alive at the published intercept altitude.
At glideslope intercept, set about 24% torque, descend on localizer and glideslope at 120 KIAS, and use power primarily for glideslope or descent-rate correction while pitch controls airspeed.
DA or DH is a decision point, not a level-off altitude. Continue only with the runway environment in sight and a safe landing possible; otherwise execute the missed approach.
Start backup timing at the non-precision FAF when timing is available, even during an ILS, so a glideslope failure can be handled without improvising.
At the LOC FAF, execute the 6 Ts, start backup timing if available, transition to descent, and use roughly 20% torque for a 120 KIAS descent not greater than 1000 FPM.
Begin arresting the descent about 100 feet before MDA, level at or above MDA, and continue tracking to the MAP.
The missed approach decision on a LOC is made at the MAP, not when the aircraft first levels at MDA.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, reintercept and do not descend below the FAF or glideslope-intercept altitude until the guidance is usable.
If more than one dot below glideslope, descend no lower than LOC MDA until the glideslope is reestablished or the aircraft reaches the non-precision MAP.
If more than two dots above glideslope, continue as a LOC-only non-precision approach instead of diving to recapture the glideslope.

If CDI becomes full-scale between the FAF and DA/DH or MAP, turn to reestablish and track the localizer while climbing to missed-approach altitude, then fly the published or assigned missed approach at the MAP.

items.text: Point-to-point navigation uses a VOR/DME or VORTAC to fly directly from present position to a radial/DME fix without waiting for radar vectors.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID.
Set the desired radial in the CDI; this helps build the picture even when it is not the heading you will fly.
Visualize the station at the center of the HSI compass card.
Plot the fix with the greater DME on the edge of the compass card and the smaller-DME fix proportionally closer to center.
Turn initially to a heading between the bearing-pointer head and the course-pointer head: split the heads.
Favor the bearing-pointer head when going to a smaller DME; favor the course-pointer head when going to a larger DME.
Use the pencil method to draw the present-position-to-desired-fix line, move that line to the center of the card, and read the updated no-wind heading.
Keep updating en route. If the line tilts right, turn right; if it tilts left, turn left.
As you near the fix, compare DME rate to radial-crossing rate.
If arriving at DME first, use the 90-degree benchmark to split the bearing pointer and desired radial; do not arc to the radial.
If arriving at the radial first, turn to track inbound or outbound as required toward the fix.
Common errors are delaying the initial turn, splitting the wrong heads, using the reciprocal radial, failing to update the pencil solution, and trying to arc to the fix.
HYD FL LO caution.
Hydraulic pressure below 1800 PSI.
Rapidly decreasing hydraulic pressure.
EHYD PX LO caution.
Landing gear, flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering should be considered unavailable.

items.text: If normal hydraulic pressure is lost:

children.text: Emergency landing gear and flap extension system should be considered unavailable.

items.text: Gear and flaps should generally be lowered early if hydraulic fluid loss is suspected.
If all hydraulic fluid is lost, a gear-up landing may become necessary.
Low hydraulic pressure may require emergency landing gear extension.

events.overview: I3104 centers on radar approaches and degraded-aircraft decision making. Translate controller instructions into stable corrections, understand the no-glideslope picture, and preserve instrument control while handling the IMC and propeller emergencies assigned to the event.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: PAR is a precision radar approach in which the final controller gives azimuth and glideslope corrections to guide the aircraft to DA/DH.

children.text: Expect surveillance radar vectors toward final, normally with standard-rate turns not exceeding 30 degrees AOB and prompt compliance with assigned headings and altitudes.
Complete landing checks, review minimums, lost-communication instructions, missed-approach or climbout instructions, and keep position orientation with available NAVAIDs.
PAR equipment provides precise runway centerline guidance, elevation guidance, and range; typical training limits are about 10 NM range, 20 degrees azimuth, and 7 degrees elevation.
When transferred to final controller, include gear status if required and be in before-approach configuration before glideslope intercept.
Begin descent only when told "on glideslope," not when told "approaching glidepath."
At glideslope intercept, use about 24 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and roughly 600 FPM. Pitch controls airspeed and power controls glideslope, with small prompt corrections.
At DA/DH, continue only if the runway environment is in sight and the landing is safe; do not level at DA/DH.

If communication is lost for more than 1 minute on vectors to final, more than 15 seconds on ASR or PAR without glideslope final, or more than 5 seconds on PAR final with glideslope, attempt secondary or tower frequency.
Proceed VFR if able, or execute the approved non-radar approach or published radar lost-communication procedure.
Miss immediately if directed by controller, tower, RDO, or wheels watch; if unsafe; or at DA/DH without required visual references.

items.text: Recommended altitudes are pilot-requested altitude gates on final that help stabilize a nonprecision radar approach to MDA.

children.text: They are based on the procedure descent gradient and are normally issued at each mile on final down to the last mile at or above MDA.
Use them as a rate-control aid, not permission to descend below published step-down restrictions or below MDA.
With recommended altitudes, adjust descent rate to meet each gate while keeping 120 KIAS and a stable configuration.
Without recommended altitudes, manage your own descent rate, level 100 feet prior to MDA, and maintain MDA until the MAP.

items.text: IMC emergency discussion starts with aircraft control, terrain clearance, ATC coordination, and crew coordination before checklist detail.

children.text: NATOPS procedures are the best available procedures, but they do not replace judgment when weather, terrain, multiple emergencies, or aircraft state change the problem.
Use the basic order: maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation, take proper action, and land as soon as conditions permit.
Inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or IMC abort requires a stable instrument scan before troubleshooting expands.

Maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit; squawk as required and tell ATC your intentions.
On an IFR clearance, coordinate deviations with ATC unless the emergency requires immediate action.
A declared emergency and radar vectors to a suitable recovery field may be the safest option; brief what you need from ATC before task saturation takes over.
The pilot at the controls executes critical action memory items and PIC-directed actions while preserving the scan.

items.text: Propeller malfunctions include uncommanded power change, failure to produce expected power, and uncommanded propeller feathering; the branch point is whether enough usable power remains for a PEL.

children.text: Engine rollback may show decreasing power or thrust, decreasing fuel flow and N1 with PMU on, or a step change in power with PMU off.
Uncommanded propeller feathering may show rapid NP decrease, torque increase, increased propeller noise, thrust loss, vibration, and degraded glide performance.
Prop-sleeve touchdown may cause NP fluctuations, torque increase, thrust decrease, vibration, and possible CHIP indication.
Set PCL to mid range, physically halfway between IDLE and MAX, then set the PMU switch OFF.
If NP is stable below 40 percent, pull the PROP SYS circuit breaker. Stable means below 40 percent with no upward change for 3 seconds at constant airspeed and torque.
Expect the propeller to unfeather in roughly 15 to 20 seconds if the procedure is effective.
Use PCL as required after the initial actions, monitoring torque, ITT, NP, and rate of descent.
If sufficient power is available, execute a PEL.

If power is insufficient, consider leaving the engine operating at mid-range PCL only when uncommanded feather is suspected and engine limits remain acceptable; otherwise transition toward engine shutdown, forced landing, or ejection as directed by the checklist and aircraft state.

With the PROP SYS circuit breaker pulled and PMU OFF, the feather dump solenoid is unpowered; the propeller feathers more slowly as oil pressure decreases, and glide performance may be considerably reduced.

If VSI remains greater than 1500 FPM at 125 KIAS with gear, flaps, and speed brake retracted and only 4 to 6 percent torque, increase torque as needed up to limits. If unable to reduce descent rate, set PCL OFF.

events.overview: I3105 combines night instrument workload with two approaches that demand strong orientation. Prepare the cockpit and airport sketch, calculate fuel before launch, maintain protected maneuvering through the arc and circle, and recognize when a fuel-system problem changes the recovery plan.

sourceDocuments.title: I3104 1542.166D

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Night cockpit setup is about preserving the scan, protecting night adaptation, and making every needed chart, light, and control usable before workload rises.

children.text: Set interior lighting early enough to read instruments and charts without washing out dark adaptation or making the display picture harder to interpret.
Know where utility, map, and kneeboard lighting are before the approach sequence; do not discover the lighting plan during a frequency change or missed approach.
Dim bright displays gradually and keep the standby instruments and backup lighting in the scan.
At night, a cockpit lighting, display, radio, or electrical problem can become a recovery-timing problem faster than it would in daylight.
Use exterior lighting with airfield courtesy and local procedures, especially around ground crews, other aircraft, and low-visibility taxi conditions.
If field orientation becomes uncertain, stop or stabilize the aircraft and re-sort the picture instead of continuing while unsure.

items.text: Arcing approaches use DME to move around a facility until a lead radial or turn point places the aircraft on the final approach course.

children.text: Confirm DME is required by the approach title or equipment notes, such as VOR/DME or TACAN.
At the IAF, turn to place the bearing pointer on the 90-degree benchmark, comply with segment altitudes, and set the inbound course in the CDI.
Use radial-to-arc and arc-to-radial intercept techniques rather than chasing the needle after the turn point has passed.
For radial-to-arc intercepts, standard-rate lead DME is about 0.5 percent of groundspeed; half-standard-rate lead DME is about 1 percent of groundspeed.
For arc-to-radial intercepts, estimate radials per NM as 60 divided by arc DME, then multiply by turn radius to find the lead radial.
Published lead radials are normally based on 200 KTAS and half-standard-rate turns; at 150 KIAS, compute a standard-rate lead and adjust for wind.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and continue inbound on the published approach.

items.text: A circling maneuver is a visual maneuver from an instrument approach, but it still lives inside protected circling airspace and published or assigned restrictions.

children.text: Before beginning, plan how the circle will work based on wind, runway alignment, terrain, towers, obstacles, and airport environment.
After breaking out, identify the intended runway and remain at or above circling altitude until continuously in a position to descend to landing at a normal rate using normal maneuvers.
Use normal visual checkpoints when possible, but expect 180, 90, and final spacing to look different because circling altitude may be higher or lower than a normal pattern.
Review circling restrictions on the approach plate, AP/1, IFR Supplement, and NOTAMs; restrictions such as 'Circling NA' in a sector are controlling.
Published circling minimums provide at least 300 feet of obstacle clearance when the aircraft remains inside the protected circling area.

Newer inverse-C circling minima use both approach category and circling MDA to set the protected radius; for Category C, the radius ranges from 2.7 NM at 1000 feet MSL or less to 3.3 NM at 9001 feet MSL and above.

Unless instructed otherwise, maneuver by the shortest path to base or downwind. Passing over the airport or other runways is not prohibited, but traffic, wind, and controller instructions still matter.
If visual reference is lost while circling, fly the missed approach for that procedure unless ATC has assigned an alternate missed approach.
Begin with an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway, then continue the turn until established on the prescribed missed-approach course.
At a non-towered field, consider overflying to observe wind, traffic, runway condition, and pattern direction before committing to the circle.

items.text: Flight planning is the PIC's proof that the route, weather, fuel, airfields, procedures, and risk picture support the intended operation.

children.text: CNAF requires the PIC to be familiar with available weather reports and forecasts, NOTAMs, TFRs, fuel requirements, terminal instrument procedures, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, and anticipated traffic delays.
The PIC and mission commander, when one is designated, must conduct a risk assessment before flight.
Plan the route around preferred IFR routes, SIDs, STARs, published airways, restricted-area avoidance, terrain, weather, and fuel, not just the shortest line between airports.
DoD and joint civil-military airfields are generally authorized, but PPR may be required when they are not home, local training, alternate, or emergency-divert fields.
Civilian airfields must support mission value, training value, or government interest; before planning one, verify local procedures, runway length and load-bearing capability, services, and security.
Closed-tower operations require the proper command authorization; closed airfields are takeoff/landing prohibited except for emergencies.

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full tank, probe, and pump walk-through. For this event, know what fuel-system cues matter in flight and which ones change whether you keep maneuvering, knock off aerobatics, or start working an abnormal recovery.

children.text: The collector tank is what keeps the engine fed in unusual attitudes, and the flip-flop valve is what gives you limited inverted fuel instead of a magic unlimited supply.
Automatic fuel balancing should quietly handle normal imbalances. When it does not, your job is to recognize whether you have a simple imbalance, a probe problem, or a real feed issue.
Minimum aerobatic fuel is 150 pounds per side, and max imbalance is 50 pounds. Those are event-useful numbers because they change what you can safely keep doing.
FUEL PX means motive-flow pressure is low and should drive an immediate cross-check of boost-pump status, fuel flow, and engine behavior.
FP FAIL means the quantity-probe logic has failed and automatic balancing is gone, but the independent L/R FUEL LO lights are still trustworthy.
If boost-pump operation or low-pressure warnings show up during inverted flight or aerobatics, stop the maneuvering and treat it as a maintenance-significant fuel-system cue.
Do not manually balance fuel with FP FAIL active because the quantity picture may be wrong and you can make the imbalance worse.
Fuel flow at or above 800 PPH is not a normal number to ignore; it can be the first sign of a malfunction that becomes an engine problem.
Treat repeated auto-balance resets as a clue that the system is not really healthy, not just as a way to keep the caution light quiet.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: SID/STAR procedures are published ATC routes with clearance consequences; brief the chart as an executable clearance, not just a name in the flight plan.

children.text: A SID provides obstruction clearance and transition from the terminal area to en route structure.
Before takeoff, review the full SID, surrounding terrain, hazards, climb gradient requirements, transition, and lost-communication or emergency-return consequences.
Set NAVAIDs, displays, and FMS procedure as required before departure; if using the FMS, the SID must be retrieved from the database and checked against the clearance.
Keep the primary recovery approach available in case the SID turns into an emergency return.
A STAR is an ATC-coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and transitions the aircraft from en route structure toward terminal instrument procedures.
You must have the approved chart to accept a STAR, and RNAV STARs require appropriate FMS equipment and database support.
Published speed restrictions are mandatory unless ATC modifies them; published altitude restrictions become vertically authorized only with the appropriate clearance.
"Expect" altitudes and speeds are planning information only unless ATC specifically issues them as part of a further clearance.
"Cleared the arrival" normally means fly the lateral route and published speeds while maintaining the last assigned altitude until ATC authorizes descent.
"Descend via" authorizes lateral and vertical navigation on the arrival to comply with published altitude and speed restrictions, but not below the published bottom altitude.
When checking in on a new frequency while descending via, include "descending via" so the next controller knows the vertical clearance.
MEAs are not STAR restrictions, but the aircraft is still expected to remain above required en route minimum altitudes.

items.text: Obstacle Departure Procedures provide obstacle clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure when obstacles require something more specific than a diverse departure.

children.text: ODPs are labeled with "OBSTACLE" in the title on DoD/FAA charts.
They are developed when obstacles penetrate the departure obstacle-clearance surface and may be textual, graphical, or RNAV.
There is normally one ODP per runway, designed to provide the least restrictive obstacle-clearance route.
ODPs are not usually assigned by ATC unless needed for separation; the pilot must determine whether one exists and whether it should be flown.
Plan for higher-than-standard climb gradients, initial headings away from the intended course, special altitude restrictions, and close-in obstacles.
Check whether aircraft performance can meet the required gradient under expected conditions, including any emergency or degraded-performance plan.
If using an ODP, file or tell ATC clearly enough that the first controller understands the intended departure path.

items.text: The Trouble T symbol tells you non-standard takeoff minimums, obstacle information, or special departure procedures may apply.

children.text: The symbol appears on IAP, DP, ODP, or SID charts and points you to the takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information for that airport.
The details are grouped by airport in the front section of the approach-plate or TPP booklet, usually alphabetically.
Trouble T is an obstacle-clearance alert; Navy takeoff weather minimums are related planning data but come from CNAF/OPNAV rules.
Read the actual text before departure. The symbol alone does not tell you the climb gradient, runway-specific restriction, or required route.
Some departures may still be legal with standard minimums if the aircraft meets a specific climb or routing requirement.
Convert any climb gradient in feet per NM into a required climb rate using groundspeed in NM per minute times the required feet per NM.

items.text: Obtaining an IFR clearance from an uncontrolled airport is a preflight planning item, not a radio scramble at the hold-short line.

children.text: Common options include telephone clearance through FSS or ATC, published radio frequencies, RCO, UNICOM relay, direct ATC phone number, GCO, or a VFR departure to pick up IFR in the air when weather and rules allow.
A GCO is a remote ground-to-ground link used from the ground; four microphone clicks normally connects to ATC and six to AFSS when configured that way.
Plan the method before startup and have the backup method ready if the first contact path is saturated or unavailable.
If ATC issues a clearance void time, be airborne before the void time or contact ATC with intentions.
ATC also issues a notification time, no more than 30 minutes after the void time; failure to contact by that time can trigger overdue-aircraft action.
Once the void time passes, the IFR slot is released. Do not depart IFR on an expired clearance.
If departing VFR to pick up IFR, maintain VFR until the IFR clearance is received and accepted.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: GPS procedures begin with database and display discipline: the FMS can reduce workload only when the active waypoint, CDI source, and bearing-pointer picture are correct.

children.text: For direct-to navigation, load the desired waypoint, make it active, select FMS as the PFD source, and use the FMS bearing pointer to orient before tracking the CDI.
For GPS intersections, confirm the next waypoint is loaded on the LEGS page before the aircraft reaches the fix.
Approaching a waypoint, the NAV page cue changes from magenta to white over a magenta background, and along-track distance counts down toward 0.0 when crossing directly over the waypoint.
A fly-over waypoint is annotated with /O and must be crossed before turning; after passage, the pointer sequences to the next waypoint.
A fly-by waypoint gives turn anticipation. When the CDI deviation bar flashes, begin a standard-rate turn and intercept or roll out on the new course.
For timing or reporting at a fly-by waypoint, note the time when wings are level and the aircraft is on course or established on an intercept.

items.text: GPS approaches require correct loading, TAA altitude discipline, approach-mode verification, and a deliberate missed-approach sequence.

children.text: Use LDDHA: load the approach with the correct transition, direct to the IAWP or build the vector-to-final leg as cleared, display FMS, verify any hold or HILO, and confirm APR mode.
A Terminal Arrival Area transitions aircraft from the RNAV en route structure to the terminal area while providing obstacle clearance.
Being cleared direct to an IAF or IF/IAF without an approach clearance does not authorize descent to the lower TAA altitude.
Once cleared for the approach, descend only as authorized by the depicted TAA sector, feeder route, ATC clearance, and published restrictions.
Slow to 150 KIAS within 5 NM of the IAWP when not on radar vectors, then transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAWP.
Expect HSI scale-change advisory about 3 NM before the FAWP and verify APR annunciation about 2 NM before the FAWP.
At the FAWP, use the six Ts and descend with about 15 to 20 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and no more than 1000 FPM to LNAV MDA.
The T-6B is certified for RNAV (GPS) approaches to LNAV MDA minimums; do not use VNAV, LNAV/VNAV, or LPV-style vertical minimums.
Level at MDA and continue to the MAWP. If the runway environment is not in sight or landing is unsafe at the MAWP, execute the missed approach.
The FMS will not automatically sequence the missed approach at the MAWP; select MISS APR and execute when the missed approach is required.
If APR mode is not active by 2 NM from the FAWP or GPS integrity is lost before the FAWP, use a backup approach if authorized; otherwise continue at FAWP altitude to the MAWP and go missed.
If GPS integrity is lost inside the FAWP, transition to a backup if authorized, climb to missed-approach altitude, track to the MAWP, execute the missed, and tell ATC as soon as practical.

items.text: A HILO is a holding pattern in lieu of a procedure turn; it is both the course reversal and the protected holding structure for the approach.

children.text: Fly a normal holding entry, run the 6 Ts at the fix, and remember the tail-radial-turn logic while establishing in the depicted pattern.
Unless ATC clears otherwise, expect one turn in holding before continuing inbound on the approach.
The HILO fix is normally the FAF, so the aircraft must be configured, at altitude, on course, and ready to time or descend as the final segment begins.
Use the published depiction to determine whether descent is authorized while outbound or only after established inbound.
If the procedure has a holding altitude and a lower FAF crossing altitude, do not descend below the holding altitude until the procedure authorizes it.
Be BAC within 5 NM of the FAF and avoid treating the HILO like an unpublished shortcut to final.

children.text: A published IAP, DP, or STAR must be retrieved by name from a current navigation database; do not manually build an IFR procedure waypoint by waypoint.

items.text: GPS holding uses the same holding logic as radio holding, but waypoint passage and abeam cues come from FMS sequencing and along-track distance.

children.text: Confirm the holding waypoint, inbound course, turn direction, leg length or timing, altitude, and EFC before the fix.
When holding at a GPS waypoint, abeam occurs when along-track distance reaches its minimum and begins increasing.
If abeam cannot be determined, start outbound timing when wings are level after the outbound turn.
Use normal holding corrections: track inbound, apply outbound wind correction, and keep speed, altitude, EFC, and fuel in the scan.

items.text: GPS flight modes change CDI sensitivity and required navigation performance, so mode awareness is part of the instrument scan.

children.text: ENR mode uses 2 NM full-scale deflection, or 1 NM per dot.
TERM mode uses 1 NM full-scale deflection, or 0.5 NM per dot.
APR mode uses 0.3 NM full-scale deflection, or 0.15 NM per dot, and displays APR plus the green NPA annunciator.
Departure starts in TERM and normally changes to ENR either more than 33 NM from the origin or above 16,000 feet AGL from origin elevation.
ENR changes to TERM when within 30 NM of the destination and below 15,000 feet AGL from destination elevation.
TERM changes to APR about 2 NM before the FAWP when a valid GPS approach is loaded and integrity is available at the current position, FAWP, and MAP.
APR returns to TERM once MISS APR is selected, with HSI scale returning to 1 NM full scale and RNP returning to 1.0 NM.
At the MAP, the bearing pointer flips and distance-to-go increases, but guidance remains along extended final until MISS APR is manually initiated.

items.text: RVFAC for RNAV approaches uses radar vectors to establish the aircraft on an RNAV final approach course while the FMS is configured for the correct leg and approach mode.

children.text: Load the RNAV approach from the current database with the correct runway and transition or vectors-to-final setup.

Maintain ATC-assigned heading and altitude until established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach or otherwise cleared lower.
Keep the chart ahead of the FMS: the published procedure, not the magenta line alone, controls altitude, course, and missed-approach requirements.
Use RVFAC speed discipline from the radio-instrument pattern: 200 KIAS on downwind or extended final outside about 15 NM, and 150 KIAS on base unless directed otherwise.

Verify the HSI scale-change cue near 3 NM from the FAWP and APR annunciation near 2 NM from the FAWP.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A no-gyro approach is available under radar control when the directional gyro or stabilized compass information is inoperative or unreliable.

children.text: Tell ATC the heading system is unreliable and request a no-gyro PAR, ASR, PAR without glideslope, or no-gyro vectors to a visual approach if conditions support it.
Comply with normal PAR or ASR configuration, minimums, lost-communication, and missed-approach procedures; no-gyro only changes how turns are commanded.
ATC may also initiate no-gyro vectors if they observe incorrect directional responses.
Before final, make all turns at standard rate unless the controller directs otherwise, and start the turn immediately when told "turn left" or "turn right."
Stop the turn immediately when told "stop turn."
On final, use half-standard-rate turns unless the controller directs another rate.
Acknowledge instructions unless ATC states no further acknowledgements are required.

The common errors are slow turn compliance, using the wrong turn rate, arriving on final late to before-approach configuration, and confusing missed-approach, climbout, and lost-communication instructions.

items.text: A BFI approach is the control plan when the PFD or primary attitude/air-data picture is unusable because of ADC, IRU, IAC, or display failures.

children.text: Transition to the BFI first, then stabilize straight-and-level flight before troubleshooting expands.
Use coordinated rudder and aileron to level the wings, set a known pitch attitude, and crosscheck airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, and performance.
Complete the applicable NATOPS emergency procedure only after the aircraft is under control.
The BFI does not present turn information like the PFD; use attitude, heading trend, and the 10 percent or 20 percent bank-start rules for half-standard-rate or standard-rate turns.
The sideslip indicator is on top of the roll pointer and moves with it, which looks different from the PFD.
The altimeter uses 20-foot increments, the heading display shows only a partial scale, and VSI is a digital readout with up or down trend.
Use small corrections. The BFI workload trap is overcontrolling because the display looks unfamiliar.
A BFI recovery may pair naturally with no-gyro vectors or a radar approach because ATC can reduce heading-reference workload while the pilot preserves attitude and performance.
If communications, transponder, or remaining avionics are degraded too, declare the emergency and ask for the simplest recovery that preserves terrain clearance and workload margin.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A high-altitude approach transitions the aircraft from high-altitude structure to the final approach course by combining a penetration descent with an instrument approach.

children.text: Complete the Descent Checklist before terminal entry and review the chart for printed penetration instructions, altitude restrictions, DME restrictions, and the final approach transition.

At the IAF, execute the 6 Ts. Time only when required, turn as published or in the shortest direction to parallel the penetration course, transition into the descent, twist the appropriate course, and talk when a report is required.
Use the published high-altitude chart, not memory of a local example, to decide whether the penetration is teardrop, arcing, or straight-in.
Fly 200-250 KIAS during the penetration and set power and speed brake as required for about 2000-4000 FPM until approaching the level-off.
About 1000 feet before level-off, reduce the descent rate to 500-1500 FPM so the aircraft does not arrive low, fast, or task-saturated.
Level segments of the penetration may be flown at normal cruise, then transition to low-altitude approach procedures once established inbound and configured to before-approach condition.
T-6B high-altitude charts use Category C minimums; do not look for Category B minimums on those charts.
For a teardrop penetration, begin the penetration turn at one-half the initial altitude or the published penetration turn, as applicable, and use 30 degrees AOB.
During the last half of the teardrop turn, if the bearing pointer is not within 5 degrees of the inbound course, stop the turn with a 45-degree intercept.
If the bearing pointer is within 5 degrees of the inbound course, continue the turn and roll out with a double-the-angle intercept.
For an arcing penetration, use about 1 percent of groundspeed for lead computations when intercepting an arc or a radial from an arc, and do not exceed 30 degrees AOB.

items.text: Non-radar communications replace radar monitoring with pilot position, altitude, and time reports that let ATC maintain IFR separation.

children.text: In both radar and non-radar environments, report vacating an assigned altitude, VFR-on-top altitude changes, inability to climb or descend at least 500 FPM, missed approach, and a true-airspeed change of 5 percent or 10 knots from the filed value.

Also report reaching or leaving a holding fix unless the military training/radar exception applies, any loss of IFR navigation or communications capability, safety-of-flight information, and unforecast or hazardous weather.
When reporting equipment loss, include the aircraft identification, equipment affected, and the effect on IFR capability.
In a non-radar environment, also report leaving the FAF inbound on a non-precision approach or leaving the outer marker or substitute fix inbound on a precision approach.
Send a corrected estimate any time a previously submitted ETA is more than 3 minutes in error.
On initial non-radar contact, include present position, altitude, and the estimate for the next reporting point; in radar service, altitude and terminal information are normally the focus.
Report over compulsory reporting points shown by solid triangles, and over every point used to define direct-route legs when operating non-radar.
Use a courtesy call before a long report, then give the PTAPTP sequence: current position, time, altitude; next position and ETA; next succeeding position.
When ATC advises radar contact, discontinue normal position reports; resume them if radar contact is lost or radar service is terminated.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Treat avionics failures as an aircraft-control problem first, then a checklist and systems-management problem.

children.text: For electronic display failures, confirm indications in both cockpits if occupied, crosscheck alternate data sources, and reference the BFI or other backup instruments as required.

Use the applicable NATOPS procedure for the actual failure. In these procedures, "reset" means resetting a circuit breaker that is already open; assess severity and equipment lost before opening or resetting any CB.
If the failure affects IFR navigation, communications, altitude reporting, or aircraft monitoring, tell ATC what equipment is affected and how IFR capability is degraded.
Dual IAC failure can remove the HUD, UFCP, and MFD displays in both cockpits; single IAC failure may show erratic or lost MFDs and cockpit synchronization errors.
Reference the BFI as required, place NORM/REPEAT switches to NORM in both cockpits, and check/reset IAC circuit breakers if open.
Do not select REPEAT in a cockpit with working MFDs when IAC synchronization errors are present, because that can cost usable display information in both cockpits.

With IAC XTALK, expect REPEAT functionality and shared settings such as baro, heading bugs, minimums, mag/true selection, bingo, clock, and G reset to operate independently; confirm altimeter settings in each cockpit.

IRS failure removes attitude or heading on the HUD/MFD; use the BFI, place the aircraft in straight-and-level unaccelerated flight, check/reset the IRS CB if open, monitor alignment, and plan to land as soon as practical.
MFD-only failure may be handled with REPEAT in the failed cockpit and MFD CB checks; MFD failure with other avionics failures points to the FWD/AFT AVI buses and requires BFI crosscheck.
UFCP failure removes cockpit access to functions such as FMS execute, mag/true heading toggle, HUD speed-source toggle, and UFCP radio tuning.
BFI display failure is its own emergency: stabilize straight and level, check the STBY INST and AFT STBY CBs as applicable, and land as soon as practical if the display does not return.
EDM failure can remove direct monitoring of engine, fuel, electrical, hydraulic, and pressurization data; if engine instruments do not return on EICAS, land as soon as practical.
ADC failure makes primary airspeed, altitude, and VSI unreliable or unavailable; reference the BFI and AOA as necessary, and expect TAD, aural gear warning, and transponder Mode C effects.
Loss of ICS/audio may require the affected cockpit auxiliary cord, AUDIO CB check/reset if open, and EMR/NRM selection; EMR gives unamplified VHF audio and no UHF audio.
ADS-B or transponder failures are coordination events with ATC. If the aircraft is transmitting erroneous data, setting the transponder to standby removes Mode C, Mode S, TCAS, and ADS-B functions.
AOA computer failure is most recognizable by loss of HUD AOA and gear-down indexer information; check/reset the AOA CB if open and land as soon as practical.

items.text: Obstacle Departure Procedures provide obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure when a simple diverse departure is not enough.

children.text: ODPs are a type of departure procedure and are labeled with "OBSTACLE" in the title on DoD/FAA charts.
The Trouble T symbol points to nonstandard takeoff minimums, obstacle information, or specific climbout requirements that must be read before departure.
Complex or RNAV ODPs may be graphical; textual ODPs are normally found with takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information in the front section of the chart booklet.
Research the departure before leaving the planning space, including terrain, hazards, climb gradients, required headings, and any special routing.
ODPs are not normally assigned by ATC unless required for separation, so the pilot must determine whether one exists and how it affects the departure plan.
If using an ODP, file or tell ATC clearly enough that the first controller understands the intended departure path.
Have the immediate-return approach ready, because an avionics or aircraft emergency after takeoff can collide with the same terrain and obstacle problem the ODP was built to solve.
Convert a published climb gradient to cockpit climb rate with: required FPM equals groundspeed in NM per minute times required feet per NM.
A diverse departure normally assumes climb to 400 feet AGL before turning and at least 200 feet per NM until reaching the minimum IFR altitude, unless the procedure says otherwise.
If aircraft performance, weather, or emergency planning cannot support the required climb or route, solve that before takeoff rather than accepting an unsafe IFR departure.

items.text: An ILS full procedure turn is a protected-airspace course reversal used to align the aircraft with the localizer final approach course before flying the precision approach.

children.text: Do not fly the procedure turn when SNERT applies: straight-in clearance, NoPT routing, established in holding aligned with the course and cleared for the approach, radar vectors to final, or a timed approach.
Tune and identify the localizer, select LOC as the PFD source when appropriate, and brief both the ILS and localizer-only plan in case the glideslope becomes unavailable.
Remember localizer sensitivity: CDI indications are much tighter than VOR, about 1.25 degrees per dot and 2.5 degrees full-scale.

items.text: When and how to set it up:

children.text: About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS.

At station passage, execute the 6 Ts: turn the shortest direction to parallel the outbound course, start one minute outbound when wings level or abeam, descend if required at about 15% torque and 150 KIAS, set the outbound CDI course, and report when required.
If the outbound course is more than 90 degrees from the inbound course to the IAF, use an intercept heading not greater than 45 degrees.
Level at procedure-turn altitude with about 33% torque, re-trim, and maintain that altitude until established inbound.
At the end of outbound timing, turn 45 degrees toward the protected side shown by the barb, start a one-minute clock when wings level, and twist the inbound course.
At the end of the barb leg, turn 180 degrees opposite the first turn.
If the bearing pointer is not within 5 degrees of the inbound course approaching the barb heading, stop the turn on the barb heading and intercept.
If the bearing pointer is within 5 degrees of the inbound course, continue the turn and roll out with a double-the-angle intercept.
Stay within the published remain-within distance, normally 10 NM unless the chart says otherwise.
The aircraft is established on course when the bearing pointer is within five radials of the inbound course and, with the CDI set correctly, the course deviation bar is between one dot and centered.
Once established inbound and within 5 NM of the FAF when DME is available, configure to before-approach condition.
Maintain altitude until reaching 120 KIAS, then descend as required: slow down, then go down.
Continue with normal low-altitude final approach, glideslope intercept, missed-approach, and required communication procedures.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: En route fuel management uses the planned Estimated Fuel Remaining for each leg as a benchmark against the Actual Fuel Remaining in the aircraft.

children.text: Verify the actual fuel load before flight; a normal T-6B single-point refuel planning load is 1100 pounds, but the gauges are the aircraft truth source.
Build EFR during planning by subtracting start, taxi, takeoff fuel and then each leg's planned fuel from the remaining fuel line above it.
At the end of each leg, compare AFR to EFR. AFR greater than or equal to EFR means the plan is still supported; AFR less than EFR requires immediate investigation.
Make the fuel comparison part of the OPS Check so it happens before the aircraft is already boxed into a low-fuel decision.
Common reasons for AFR shortfall are less fuel onboard at takeoff than planned, higher climb or cruise fuel flow, slower groundspeed, flight-log math error, or a fuel leak.
The earlier the cause is identified, the more useful the options are: adjust power or routing, request priority handling, divert, or transition to a fuel-conservation profile as appropriate.
If fuel endurance becomes the controlling factor, use NATOPS max-endurance guidance rather than guessing at a low-burn technique.
The DRAFT report organizes a divert request: Destination, Route, Altitude, Fuel remaining in hours plus minutes, and Time en route to the alternate.
The workbook builds that data from the flight log so the divert call can be read instead of improvised under pressure.
For DD Form 1801 endurance, use the planned profile: time from takeoff to destination fix plus fuel remaining at that fix converted to hours and minutes.

items.text: A feeder fix is the fix that begins a feeder route from en route structure toward an IAF or other approach-entry point.

children.text: Feeder fixes are often shown with thin arrows rather than the thick NoPT track used for a straight-in entry.
A feeder fix that is not labeled NoPT or IAF is not itself the approach entry; it is the start of the published route to the IAF.
Use the chart language and symbology to decide whether you are cleared onto a feeder route, direct to an IAF, or onto a NoPT transition.
If cleared for the approach while tracking inbound from a feeder fix, descend only to the higher of the feeder-route altitude or the IAF crossing altitude.
At the IAF, execute the published approach procedures for that entry instead of carrying feeder-route habits into the terminal segment.
The feeder fix solves route transition; it does not automatically cancel altitude assignments or authorize a procedure turn unless the approach clearance and chart support it.

items.text: Feeder routes connect en route structure to an IAF, IF, or other published approach segment and become part of the approach clearance when assigned or accepted.

children.text: Follow the published course and altitude along the feeder route to the IAF or IF.
If cleared direct or vectored to join an approach, maintain the last assigned ATC altitude until established on a published segment and cleared for the approach or cleared lower.
Once established on the published segment, descend no lower than the minimum altitude published for that segment.
At least one feeder route may exist, but multiple feeder routes or transitions can feed the same approach; choose the one that matches the clearance.
Do not treat a feeder route as an informal shortcut. It carries charted course, altitude, and entry consequences.
When the chart uses NoPT on a thick track, the no-procedure-turn entry is explicit; when that label is absent, confirm whether the route only feeds an IAF.

items.text: CDI reverse sensing is a localizer setup error: the needle appears to command the opposite correction when the CDI course is set to the wrong side of the localizer.

children.text: For normal ILS or LOC approaches, set the front course depicted for the final approach course.
For LOC BC approaches, identify and set the true front course, which is the reciprocal of the depicted back-course final approach course.
In the T-6B, selecting the correct front course prevents reverse sensing whether flying a back course or outbound on a front course.
If the back course itself is set into the CDI on a LOC BC, expect reverse sensing.
Tune, identify, and monitor the localizer as soon as practical during the transition, then set PFD source to LOC when ready for localizer tracking.
Course and glideslope indications are reliable only when warning flags or red Xs are absent, the localizer identifier is received, and the aircraft is within usable range.
Expect localizer sensitivity to increase near the transmitter; inside the FAF, use small heading corrections near the wind-corrected heading instead of chasing the needle.
For a LOC BC final, disregard glideslope indications and fly the non-precision profile to the published MDA and MAP.

If full-scale CDI deflection occurs between the FAF and MAP, turn to reestablish and track the localizer while climbing to the missed-approach altitude, unless a published maximum altitude restricts the climb before the MAP.

Common errors are setting the back course in the CDI, flying through final, overcorrecting, continuing with full-scale deflection inside the FAF, and executing the missed at MDA instead of at the MAP.
