events.overview: I4101 is the first aircraft event in the radio-instrument sequence. The event standard is to turn CRM into cockpit behavior, enter and correct holding without losing SA, and fly a VOR final segment on speed, on course, and above MDA until the approach permits descent.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: CRM is the use of defined behavioral skills on every flight to reduce crew-preventable errors, improve coordination, and manage risk.

children.text: The seven CRM skills are decision making, assertiveness, mission analysis, communication, leadership, adaptability/flexibility, and situational awareness.

Decision making is not just choosing an option; it includes assessing the situation, verifying information, identifying solutions, anticipating consequences, communicating the decision, and evaluating the result.
Assertiveness is professional participation. Maintain a safety-relevant position until the facts show another option is better.
Communication must transfer and acknowledge the right information at the right time: aircraft control, altitude restrictions, approach clearance, missed-approach plan, fuel, and task saturation.
Threat and Error Management treats threats, errors, and undesired aircraft states as a continuous loop: identify threats, resist or trap errors, and recover from aircraft states that reduce margins.
CRM skills are the tools; TEM is the framework for using those tools before, during, and after an instrument task.
In this event, likely threats include radio congestion, clearance ambiguity, high cockpit workload entering holding, approach setup errors, weather changes, and task fixation near MDA or MAP.
Procedural compliance is a CRM habit. Use briefed flows, checklists, and positive verbal transfer instead of assuming the other pilot or the automation has it handled.
Brief who owns aircraft control, radios, FMS/UFCP work, charts, checklist calls, and approach backup duties before the workload starts.

Transfer aircraft or subsystem control with positive verbal communication over the ICS. If ICS is unavailable, use the NATOPS backup: the pilot requesting control shakes the stick, and the pilot relinquishing control raises both hands.
Avoid sandbag syndrome: the student still owns active monitoring, callouts, and challenge even when the instructor is capable of fixing the situation.
Use the event SSRs as CRM tasks too: front/rear cockpit differences and the vertigo demonstration need briefed responsibilities, not improvised cockpit choreography.

items.text: Holding keeps the aircraft inside protected airspace around a fix until ATC issues further clearance.

children.text: Start slowing within 3 minutes or 5 NM of a clearance limit if further clearance has not been received.
The normal T-6B holding airspeed is 150 KIAS. Published maximums are 200 KIAS through 6000 feet MSL, 230 KIAS from 6001 to 14,000 feet, and 265 KIAS above 14,000 feet, with chart or field exceptions.
A full uncharted holding clearance includes direction from the fix, holding fix, radial/course/bearing/airway/route, leg length if distance is used, direction of turns if nonstandard, and EFC.
If no pattern is charted and no holding instructions are issued, ask ATC before reaching the clearance limit.
EFC is not clearance to leave holding or start an approach unless lost-communications rules apply.
Standard holding uses right turns; nonstandard holding uses left turns.
Determine entry by comparing aircraft heading to the reciprocal of the holding course. Use direct, parallel, or teardrop entry as appropriate for the pattern direction.
If the reciprocal of the holding course is within 5 degrees of an entry boundary, either adjacent entry is acceptable.
During teardrop entries with DME or ATD legs of 4 NM or more, turn to parallel the holding course after 4 NM to avoid excessive displacement.
Use the 6 Ts at the fix and through the pattern: time, turn, time, transition, twist, talk.
Make holding turns at standard rate, not more than 30 degrees AOB.
Fly headings outbound and track the holding course inbound.
Use Tail-Radial-Turn at the end of the outbound leg to decide the direction of the inbound turn toward the holding radial.
Use a no-wind orbit to identify wind direction and timing error, then apply correction orbits.
Triple the inbound crab on the outbound leg for no more than one minute, then continue any remaining outbound time with single-drift correction.
Adjust outbound time by the inbound timing error: if the inbound leg was short, add time outbound; if it was long, subtract time outbound.
Report entering holding with PTA: position, time, altitude or flight level, unless the radar-training exception applies.
Confirm EFC at least 5 minutes before the EFC time.
Report leaving holding when required; altitude and time are not normally part of the leaving-holding report.

If cleared for the approach while in a published hold, listen for tense. Present-tense clearance may allow immediate turn toward the IAF; future-tense clearance requires waiting for the stated condition.
Keep fuel, EFC, altitude, and next clearance in the scan. In stacked holding, altitude control is as important as lateral geometry.

items.text: A VOR non-precision final segment should be flown on speed, on course, and to a controlled level-off at or before MDA so the aircraft is set up for landing or missed approach.

children.text: Arrive at the FAF configured to before-approach condition.

At the FAF, execute the 6 Ts: start timing if required, turn shortest direction to parallel or intercept the final approach course, transition to descent, twist the FAC into the CDI if needed, and talk when a report is required.
Use about 20% torque for a 120 KIAS descent to the next segment altitude or MDA, adjusting pitch for airspeed and power for descent rate.
Keep the descent stabilized and not more than 1000 FPM.
Begin arresting descent about 100 feet before MDA.
Level at MDA at or before the published or derived VDP, maintain about 120 KIAS, and continue to the MAP.
Do not descend below MDA just because the runway environment is in sight; wait until reaching the VDP and ensure a safe landing can be made.
If no VDP is published, a derived VDP may be computed as HAT divided by 300 for a roughly 3-degree descent path, but absence of a published VDP may indicate obstacle-clearance concerns.
Use radar-altimeter bugging as a backup low-altitude cue when appropriate; it is not the primary method for identifying DA/DH or MDA.
VOR approaches may identify the MAP by timing, DME, DME backed up with timing, or station passage; brief the primary and backup method before the FAF.
If the field is in sight and a safe landing can be made, maneuver to land using the briefed visual segment.
At the MAP, if the field is not in sight or a safe landing cannot be made, execute the missed approach.
Common errors are excessive corrections near the VOR, failing to back up DME with timing, descending below MDA, and late MAP recognition.

events.overview: I4102 moves the radio-instrument flight sequence from VOR work into localizer precision and non-precision recoveries, radar vectors to final, and weather limits that can change the recovery plan. The event standard is to set D LIDS early, correct localizer and glideslope errors before they grow, preserve terrain awareness on vectors, and exit icing at the first indication.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: ILS provides localizer azimuth and glideslope vertical guidance; a LOC approach uses the localizer component for lateral guidance as a non-precision approach.

children.text: If the localizer is inoperative, the ILS is not authorized. If the glideslope is inoperative or not used, fly the LOC non-precision procedure and minimums.

The localizer signal is much more sensitive than VOR guidance. Set the published front course, confirm no flags or red Xs, receive the correct identifier, and make small heading corrections near the wind-corrected heading.
Use D LIDS before the final workload builds: DME hold if required, localizer tuned and identified, inbound course set, display source set to LOC, and speed appropriate for the transition.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF with no more than a 90-degree intercept, or when the glideslope comes alive at the published intercept altitude.
At glideslope intercept, set about 24% torque, descend on localizer and glideslope at 120 KIAS, and use power primarily for glideslope or descent-rate correction while pitch controls airspeed.
DA or DH is a decision point, not a level-off altitude. Continue only with the runway environment in sight and a safe landing possible; otherwise execute the missed approach.
Start backup timing at the non-precision FAF when timing is available, even during an ILS, so a glideslope failure can be handled without improvising.
At the LOC FAF, execute the 6 Ts, start backup timing if available, transition to descent, and use roughly 20% torque for a 120 KIAS descent not greater than 1000 FPM.
Begin arresting the descent about 100 feet before MDA, level at or above MDA, and continue tracking to the MAP.
The missed approach decision on a LOC is made at the MAP, not when the aircraft first levels at MDA.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, reintercept and do not descend below the FAF or glideslope-intercept altitude until the guidance is usable.
If more than one dot below glideslope, descend no lower than LOC MDA until the glideslope is reestablished or the aircraft reaches the non-precision MAP.
If more than two dots above glideslope, continue as a LOC-only non-precision approach instead of diving to recapture the glideslope.

If CDI becomes full-scale between the FAF and DA/DH or MAP, turn to reestablish and track the localizer while climbing to missed-approach altitude, then fly the published or assigned missed approach at the MAP.

items.text: RVFAC uses ATC radar vectors to place the aircraft on final approach course without flying the full published transition.

children.text: Approach control owns obstacle clearance through its minimum vectoring altitude while vectoring, but the pilot still maintains terrain and position awareness with the chart, NAVAIDs, and assigned altitudes.
Do not blindly follow vectors into uncertainty. If the vector, altitude, clearance, or terrain picture does not make sense, query ATC early.
Because there are no published segment minimums until joining a published approach segment, keep the last assigned altitude until established and cleared lower or cleared for the approach.

Set up the approach while on vectors: tune and identify the NAVAID, confirm the correct PFD source, set the final approach course, brief the final segment, and monitor how the vector geometry is developing.
Normal vector speeds are 200 KIAS on downwind, 150 KIAS on base, and 200 KIAS on extended final or dogleg until within 15 NM of the airport unless directed otherwise.
When cleared for the approach, maintain the last assigned heading and altitude until established on the final approach course or until ATC issues a lower altitude.
Lead the final turn as the CDI centers, then transition into the published low-altitude approach procedure.
Configure to before-approach condition within 5 NM of the FAF and with no more than a 90-degree intercept.
If the approach has no FAF, transition to before-approach condition once established on final approach course and cleared for the approach.
Common errors are late NAV-source changes, flying through final, losing terrain SA, and waiting until the final turn to build the approach picture.

items.text: The T-6B is approved only for transit through a limited band of light rime icing; prolonged or sustained flight in known icing conditions is prohibited.

children.text: Expect possible icing any time the aircraft is in visible moisture with OAT at or below 5 degrees C.
The first visible indication may be ice near the forward canopy bow or windshield base, and the rear cockpit may not detect accumulation as early as the front cockpit.
Rime ice is usually rough, milky or opaque, and forms when supercooled droplets freeze rapidly on impact.
At the first indication of icing, exit by climbing, descending, or changing direction instead of waiting to see whether accumulation worsens.
Verify PROBES ANTI-ICE ON, temperature controller MANUAL, DEFOG ON, and EVAP BLOWER HI, then manage temperature to avoid a DUCT TEMP caution.
Once clear of icing conditions, expect accumulated ice to melt or sublimate over several minutes, but continue to evaluate aircraft performance and visibility.
After an icing encounter, aerobatics are prohibited until ice has melted or sublimated.
With ice still present, limit maneuvering to 30 degrees of bank and 0 to 2 G up to stall warning.
If landing with ice accumulation, increase approach speed by 10 KIAS and ensure either cockpit has enough forward visibility to land safely.
Plan around freezing levels, visible moisture, and thunderstorm/icing forecasts before flight, and report hazardous weather such as icing to ATC or FSS.

events.overview: I4103 combines radar-approach precision with degraded-instrument and physiological decision making. Translate controller calls into smooth corrections, maintain the no-gyro picture, and recognize when crew symptoms or OBOGS indications require immediate oxygen, communication, and recovery action.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: PAR is a precision radar approach: the final controller gives azimuth and glideslope corrections to guide the aircraft to DA/DH.

children.text: Expect surveillance radar vectors toward final, then a handoff to the final controller once the aircraft is within precision-radar coverage.
Precision radar approach limits are about 10 NM range, 20 degrees azimuth, and 7 degrees elevation.
Review minimums, lost-communication instructions, missed approach or climbout instructions, and keep position orientation with available NAVAIDs during the vector sequence.
Single-pilot T-6B minimums may raise very low published PAR minimums; do not brief below the applicable 200-foot HAT and 1/2 SM or 2400 RVR floor.
Fly 200 KIAS on downwind and 150 KIAS on base; if held on an extended final or dogleg, maintain 200 KIAS until within about 15 NM unless directed otherwise.
Transition to before-approach configuration and complete landing checks before glideslope intercept.
The initial call to final controller should include gear status and any locally required altitude or heading status.
Do not begin descending on the 'approaching glidepath' advisory. Begin descent only when told the aircraft is on glidepath.
At glideslope intercept, use about 24% torque, 120 KIAS, and roughly 600 FPM, then make small prompt corrections.
Use pitch primarily for airspeed and power primarily for glideslope or descent-rate control; avoid large PCL movements.
At DA/DH, continue only with the runway environment in sight and a safe landing possible; otherwise execute the missed approach or assigned climbout.
Execute a missed approach if directed by controller, tower, runway duty officer, or wheels watch, or whenever a safe landing cannot be made.
Lost communications are defined as more than 1 minute on vectors to final, more than 15 seconds on ASR or PAR without glideslope final, or more than 5 seconds on PAR final with glideslope.
If lost comm occurs, attempt secondary or tower frequency, proceed VFR if able, or execute the approved non-radar approach or published radar lost-communication procedure.
Keep missed approach, climbout, and lost-communication instructions separate; they solve different problems.

items.text: ASR is a non-precision radar approach using airport surveillance radar for course and range guidance; PAR W/O GS is also non-precision, but uses precision-radar azimuth and range on final.

children.text: Because no glideslope is provided or used, the pilot owns the descent profile, MDA level-off, and MAP decision.
PAR W/O GS may publish a lower MDA than ASR because its course and range information are more precise, but it is still non-precision.
The controller will advise the MAP location, range updates, and descent to MDA or step-down fixes.
If circling is planned, provide the aircraft category when needed so ATC issues or confirms the correct circling MDA.
Promptly comply with vectors and altitudes, maintain SA, and acknowledge all transmissions until instructed otherwise.
Use 200 KIAS on downwind and 150 KIAS on base; on extended final or dogleg, remain at 200 KIAS until within about 15 NM unless directed otherwise.
Transition to before-approach configuration and complete landing checks on final or dogleg within 15 NM.
With recommended altitudes, set about 24% torque, establish 120 KIAS, and adjust descent to meet the mile-by-mile altitude gates.
Without recommended altitudes, set about 20% torque, trim for 120 KIAS, and maintain a stabilized descent not greater than 1000 FPM.
Recommended altitudes are a pilot-requested stabilization aid; they do not authorize descent below step-down fixes or below MDA.
Begin level-off about 100 feet before MDA, maintain MDA and assigned heading to the MAP, and go missed at the MAP if the runway environment is not in sight or landing is unsafe.
Do not drop to MDA early just to get level. Heavy rain and low altitude can increase ground clutter and contribute to loss of radar contact.
If told 'radar contact lost' and the runway environment is not in sight, execute the missed approach or assigned climbout.

items.text: A no-gyro approach is available under radar control when the directional gyro or stabilized compass information is inoperative or unreliable.

children.text: Tell ATC the heading system is unreliable and request a no-gyro PAR, ASR, PAR without glideslope, or no-gyro vectors to a visual approach if conditions support it.
Comply with normal PAR or ASR configuration, minimums, lost-communication, and missed-approach procedures; no-gyro only changes how turns are commanded.
ATC may also initiate no-gyro vectors if they observe incorrect directional responses.
Before final, make all turns at standard rate unless the controller directs otherwise, and start the turn immediately when told "turn left" or "turn right."
Stop the turn immediately when told "stop turn."
On final, use half-standard-rate turns unless the controller directs another rate.
Acknowledge instructions unless ATC states no further acknowledgements are required.

The common errors are slow turn compliance, using the wrong turn rate, arriving on final late to before-approach configuration, and confusing missed-approach, climbout, and lost-communication instructions.

items.text: A BFI approach is the control plan when the PFD or primary attitude/air-data picture is unusable because of ADC, IRU, IAC, or display failures.

children.text: Transition to the BFI first, then stabilize straight-and-level flight before troubleshooting expands.
Use coordinated rudder and aileron to level the wings, set a known pitch attitude, and crosscheck airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, and performance.
Complete the applicable NATOPS emergency procedure only after the aircraft is under control.
The BFI does not present turn information like the PFD; use attitude, heading trend, and the 10 percent or 20 percent bank-start rules for half-standard-rate or standard-rate turns.
The sideslip indicator is on top of the roll pointer and moves with it, which looks different from the PFD.
The altimeter uses 20-foot increments, the heading display shows only a partial scale, and VSI is a digital readout with up or down trend.
Use small corrections. The BFI workload trap is overcontrolling because the display looks unfamiliar.
A BFI recovery may pair naturally with no-gyro vectors or a radar approach because ATC can reduce heading-reference workload while the pilot preserves attitude and performance.
If communications, transponder, or remaining avionics are degraded too, declare the emergency and ask for the simplest recovery that preserves terrain clearance and workload margin.

items.text: Hypoxia and hyperventilation can feel similar early, so the safe cockpit answer is to protect oxygen first, then normalize breathing once the oxygen source is secure.

children.text: Hypoxia is oxygen deficiency in body tissues; early signs can include poor judgment, euphoria, fatigue, tunnel vision, dizziness, or headache.
Advanced hypoxia can progress to cyanosis, confusion, loss of coordination, unconsciousness, and incapacitation.
Susceptibility increases with factors such as fatigue, dehydration, illness, alcohol, medication, smoking, carbon monoxide exposure, temperature stress, and exertion.
Hyperventilation is abnormally rapid or deep breathing that lowers carbon dioxide.
Symptoms can include lightheadedness, tingling, drowsiness, muscle spasms, a feeling of suffocation, and in severe cases unconsciousness.
When breathing oxygen under increased pressure, breathe slightly slower and shallower than normal to avoid inducing hyperventilation.
If unsure which one you have, treat it like hypoxia first: secure oxygen, verify flow, descend as required, tell the other cockpit, then consciously slow and normalize breathing.
Do not let symptom analysis pull both pilots heads-down; keep one pilot flying and scanning.

items.text: An OBOGS malfunction is a crew-survival problem before it is a system-analysis problem. Keep flying, get a secure oxygen source, descend when required, and use the checklist.

children.text: An OBOGS FAIL warning can indicate low bleed-air pressure, low oxygen concentration, or an internal failure detected by the system.
OBOGS TEMP indicates a heat-exchanger failure and is treated as an OBOGS failure.
Physiological symptoms or zeolite-dust indications can occur without a warning light; coughing, respiratory irritation, or white dust in the mask still demand immediate action.
Engine failure, total electrical failure, main battery depletion, or battery failure removes OBOGS support.
Check both cockpits: supply ON, concentration MAX, pressure EMERGENCY, flow indication, hose/CRU-60/P connection, and mask seal.
If symptoms are recognized, immediately execute the OBOGS Failure/Overtemp/Physiological Symptoms procedure instead of troubleshooting first.
Emergency oxygen provides about 10 minutes; above 10,000 feet cockpit altitude, pulling the green ring is required before depletion risk becomes incapacitating.
Initiate descent below 10,000 feet MSL, secure OBOGS supply OFF as directed, and land as soon as practical.

events.overview: I4104 tests whether the student can keep an instrument flight safe when weather, communications, energy, or aircraft condition degrades. Prepare the source-backed escape and communications procedures, calculate a usable descent rate, define the stabilized gate, and commit early to a missed approach when the picture is not acceptable.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Thunderstorms and extreme turbulence should be avoided because they can produce flameout, structural damage, hail, lightning, and violent updrafts or downdrafts.

children.text: Use forecasts, radar, ATC, and route changes to avoid thunderstorms; do not accept IMC in an area where thunderstorms are known to be present unless there is no safer alternative.

If penetration becomes unavoidable, set PROBES ANTI-ICE ON, tighten the lap strap, lock the shoulder harness reel, stow loose items, and set instrument lighting high before lightning starts destroying night adaptation.
Plan the shortest practical path through the activity and avoid unnecessary turns inside the storm.
Recommended penetration airspeed is 180 KIAS; do not exceed turbulent-air penetration speed of 207 KIAS.
Trim for level flight at the penetration speed, then control by attitude reference. Do not chase rapid indicated-airspeed swings.
Use smooth, moderate aileron and elevator inputs, maintain the power setting that supports the desired speed and altitude, and avoid large or abrupt attitude changes.
Allow altitude to vary in severe vertical gusts. Sacrifice altitude before sacrificing attitude control.

items.text: Treat 'any emergency procedure' as a cumulative oral spot check: the answer needs the cue, immediate action, checklist backup, N/W/C that changes the plan, and the recovery branch.

children.text: Start with aircraft control, crew oxygen and survival, terrain clearance, and ATC coordination before diving into low-priority troubleshooting.
Use NATOPS memory items when required, then back them up with the checklist as time and aircraft state permit.
Explain the branch point: continue, divert, PEL, forced landing, or eject, and what cue would move you to the next branch.
In IMC, brief the first safe altitude, who flies, who talks, what you need from ATC, and how the selected approach or vectors protect workload.

items.text: A high-altitude approach transitions the aircraft from high-altitude structure to the final approach course by combining a penetration descent with an instrument approach.

children.text: Complete the Descent Checklist before terminal entry and review the chart for printed penetration instructions, altitude restrictions, DME restrictions, and the final approach transition.

At the IAF, execute the 6 Ts. Time only when required, turn as published or in the shortest direction to parallel the penetration course, transition into the descent, twist the appropriate course, and talk when a report is required.
Use the published high-altitude chart, not memory of a local example, to decide whether the penetration is teardrop, arcing, or straight-in.
Fly 200-250 KIAS during the penetration and set power and speed brake as required for about 2000-4000 FPM until approaching the level-off.
About 1000 feet before level-off, reduce the descent rate to 500-1500 FPM so the aircraft does not arrive low, fast, or task-saturated.
Level segments of the penetration may be flown at normal cruise, then transition to low-altitude approach procedures once established inbound and configured to before-approach condition.
T-6B high-altitude charts use Category C minimums; do not look for Category B minimums on those charts.
For a teardrop penetration, begin the penetration turn at one-half the initial altitude or the published penetration turn, as applicable, and use 30 degrees AOB.
During the last half of the teardrop turn, if the bearing pointer is not within 5 degrees of the inbound course, stop the turn with a 45-degree intercept.
If the bearing pointer is within 5 degrees of the inbound course, continue the turn and roll out with a double-the-angle intercept.
For an arcing penetration, use about 1 percent of groundspeed for lead computations when intercepting an arc or a radial from an arc, and do not exceed 30 degrees AOB.

items.text: Non-radar communications replace radar monitoring with pilot position, altitude, and time reports that let ATC maintain IFR separation.

children.text: In both radar and non-radar environments, report vacating an assigned altitude, VFR-on-top altitude changes, inability to climb or descend at least 500 FPM, missed approach, and a true-airspeed change of 5 percent or 10 knots from the filed value.

Also report reaching or leaving a holding fix unless the military training/radar exception applies, any loss of IFR navigation or communications capability, safety-of-flight information, and unforecast or hazardous weather.
When reporting equipment loss, include the aircraft identification, equipment affected, and the effect on IFR capability.
In a non-radar environment, also report leaving the FAF inbound on a non-precision approach or leaving the outer marker or substitute fix inbound on a precision approach.
Send a corrected estimate any time a previously submitted ETA is more than 3 minutes in error.
On initial non-radar contact, include present position, altitude, and the estimate for the next reporting point; in radar service, altitude and terminal information are normally the focus.
Report over compulsory reporting points shown by solid triangles, and over every point used to define direct-route legs when operating non-radar.
Use a courtesy call before a long report, then give the PTAPTP sequence: current position, time, altitude; next position and ETA; next succeeding position.
When ATC advises radar contact, discontinue normal position reports; resume them if radar contact is lost or radar service is terminated.

items.text: A stabilized approach has the aircraft on the correct lateral and vertical path, in the intended configuration, at the planned airspeed and descent rate, with only small corrections required.
Brief the gate and limits from the current FAA Instrument Procedures Handbook, FTI, and local guidance; if the approach is not stable by the required point, execute the missed approach or wave-off.

sections.title: Stabilized Approach Criteria (FAA Instrument Procedures Handbook)

items.text: Convert the published descent gradient and actual groundspeed into a target vertical speed before beginning descent; for a nominal 3-degree path, groundspeed multiplied by about five gives a useful feet-per-minute cross-check.
Recompute when groundspeed changes, compare the result with altitude-to-go and distance-to-go, and correct early rather than chasing the glidepath close to minimums.
Stabilized Approach Criteria (FAA Instrument Procedures Handbook)

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Clearance and departure procedures connect the IFR clearance, takeoff minimums, departure method, and initial instrument scan before the aircraft moves.

children.text: File early enough to prevent a clearance delay; the local notes use at least 30 minutes before ETD, or 4 hours when operating above FL230.

Copy the clearance in the CRAFT flow plus local additions: aircraft identification, clearance limit, departure type, route, altitude, departure frequency, beacon code, and any holding, delay, or restriction.
At towered fields, expect clearance delivery or ground to issue the clearance; at non-towered fields, expect a phone or remote-frequency clearance with a void time.
On initial departure contact, know whether you are in radar or non-radar service. Radar contact normally changes what ATC expects; non-radar work may require position, altitude, and estimate reports.
Fly a normal takeoff, use outside references and the attitude indicator at liftoff, then transition fully to instruments as visual cues reduce.
Set about 8 to 10 degrees nose high, trim, verify climb on the altimeter and VSI, then raise gear and flaps.
Maintain the initial climb attitude until about 180 KIAS unless the departure or climb-gradient requirement demands a different profile.
For best-rate climb, use about 140 KIAS and 15 degrees nose high.
Lead level-offs with about 10% of vertical speed; for example, begin about 200 feet early during a 2000 FPM climb.
Brief the assigned departure type: ODP, SID, radar departure, diverse departure, or VCOA.
ODPs provide obstacle clearance and are labeled OBSTACLE in the FLIP approach book; SIDs are ATC procedures printed graphically for pilot use and transition the aircraft toward en route structure.
Radar departures use ATC vectors when no DP is published, when assigned, or when requested.
Diverse departures require climbing to 400 feet AGL before the first turn and maintaining at least 200 feet per NM until reaching the minimum IFR altitude; at 180 KIAS, that is about 600 FPM.
A VCOA keeps the pilot in VFR conditions over the airport until reaching a published altitude before proceeding outbound IFR.
Before takeoff, review terrain, hazards, climb gradients, the first altitude/heading restriction, and the emergency-return approach.
Set required NAVAIDs, courses, displays, and FMS procedure data before takeoff; if the FMS is used, verify the loaded procedure matches the clearance.

Confirm current CNAF/local takeoff minimums for the departure. The training notes use at least 300-foot ceiling and 1 SM for non-precision support, and at least 200-foot ceiling and 1/2 SM or 2400 RVR for precision support.

items.text: Stereo routes, or canned flight plans, are pre-coordinated local IFR routes published in the current IFG or local SOP to reduce clearance length and routine ATC coordination.

children.text: Treat the route code as shorthand, not as the clearance itself. Decode the route, altitude, departure, NAVAIDs/fixes, expected handoffs, and recovery implication before accepting it.
File or request the coded route through the local process, such as Base Ops or the controlling facility, and verify the current code in the current IFG.
Coded departures may include runway-dependent heading, altitude, frequency, and transponder expectations. Fly the clearance issued today, not a memorized example from an old guide.
If departing a field away from home base, confirm whether a return-route code is valid and how it should be filed or requested from that field.
Before takeoff, brief how lost comm, divert, and weather decisions change if you are on a local coded flight plan.
If ATC amends the route or altitude, the actual clearance replaces the route-code expectation.
The common error is knowing the route name but not the first heading, first altitude, NAVAID sequence, or lost-comm trigger.

items.text: Airway navigation keeps IFR aircraft on the protected route structure: along the airway centerline on ATS routes, or along the direct course between the fixes or NAVAIDs defining the route.

children.text: Victor airways and T routes are low-altitude routes from 1200 feet AGL up to, but not including, FL180; Jet routes and Q routes are high-altitude routes from FL180 through FL450.
Federal airways are normally 4 NM either side of centerline, for 8 NM total width, with 1000 feet of obstacle clearance in non-mountainous areas and 2000 feet in mountainous areas.
Past 51 DME from a station, the protected area expands by about 2 NM on each side for each additional 13 NM.
Lead turns as required to stay inside protected airspace. Flyover waypoints are exceptions and are depicted with the flyover symbol.
MEA is the lowest altitude that assures obstacle clearance and navigation signal coverage for the segment.
MOCA is the lowest altitude with obstacle clearance and NAVAID reception within 22 NM of the facility.
MAA limits altitude to prevent conflicting NAVAID reception; MRA is the minimum altitude for reliable VOR reception at an intersection; MCA is the minimum altitude required when crossing a fix.
OROCA gives off-route obstacle clearance in a chart grid, but it is not a substitute for being on the cleared route.
For over-the-station intercepts, run the 6 Ts at station passage: time, turn, time, transition, twist/intercept, and talk.
Turn the shortest direction to parallel or intercept the outbound course. If the course change is more than 90 degrees, use up to a 45-degree intercept.
For VOR/DME intersections, track the primary course to the fix, use DME for fix identification, lead any required turn, and note time if needed.
For VOR-only intersections, tune the secondary NAVAID about 3 minutes before ETA, monitor within about 10 radials, identify the fix, then return to the primary navigation task.
Filled compulsory-reporting symbols require position reports when not in radar contact or when ATC requires them.

items.text: Lost-communication discussion has two layers: the local IFG procedure for the departure/recovery environment and the FIH/FAR route-altitude-clearance-limit logic for IFR flight.

children.text: Squawk 7600, keep flying the airplane, and try to reestablish contact on assigned, secondary, tower, FSS, guard, or NAVAID voice frequencies as appropriate.
Local lost-comm procedures may specify exact headings, altitudes, timers, aids, approaches, or tower light-signal flows. Brief those from the current IFG before launch instead of relying on memory.
For radar approaches, lost comm timing remains: more than 1 minute on vectors to final, more than 15 seconds on ASR or PAR W/O GS final, or more than 5 seconds on PAR final with glideslope.
Do not confuse lost-communication instructions, missed-approach instructions, and climbout instructions. They may all be issued during radar approach work, but they answer different problems.
If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable at a safe, suitable field.
If VFR cannot be maintained, apply the route priority: assigned, vectored, expected, filed.
Apply the altitude priority for each route segment: highest of last assigned altitude, minimum IFR altitude, or altitude ATC advised to expect.
If the clearance limit is a fix from which an approach begins, start descent and approach as close as possible to EFC, or ETA if no EFC was received.
If the clearance limit is not an approach fix, leave it at EFC, or on arrival if no EFC, proceed to a fix from which an approach begins, and start descent/approach as close as possible to ETA.

For local IFR lost comm after takeoff or on a coded flight plan, expect the IFG to tell you how long to remain on the last assigned heading or route, what altitude to maintain or climb to, and what aid or approach to use.
For local VFR lost comm, maintain VMC, squawk 7600, make blind calls if able, observe tower light or ALDIS signals, and avoid entering a controlled pattern until the traffic flow is understood.
The student standard is not to recite one base's numbers from memory; it is to brief the current local lost-comm page, then connect it to the FIH/FAR decision tree.

events.overview: I4202 is the FMS arrival event: build and verify the route, load procedures from the current database, manage discontinuities and crew edits, then fly the RNAV arrival or approach with chart discipline instead of blind magenta-line trust. The event standard is to make the FMS support the clearance while the chart, ATC clearance, and aircraft state remain the controlling references.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: An FMS flight plan is one active route containing an origin airport, destination airport, and at least one waypoint; two routes may be loaded, but only one can be active.

children.text: Create or recall the route on the ROUTE page, review and edit the waypoint sequence on the LEGS page, and add SID, STAR, and approach procedures from the DEP/ARR page.

Use the current navigation database for procedures. A SID, STAR, approach, or transition should be retrieved by procedure name and verified against the chart, not hand-built as a loose list of waypoints.
The flight number on MFD ROUTE page 1 is the Flight ID transmitted to ATC through Mode S.
Local habit may reserve RTE 1 for the primary route and RTE 2 for the filed alternate, but the aircraft truth is that only the active route drives navigation.
During edits, expect a flashing green EXEC cue on PFD/NAV and an inverse cyan MOD cue on the LEGS page.
Press EXEC on the UFCP to make the modification active, or ERASE before execution to discard the pending modification.
Only one cockpit can edit the flight plan at a time. If the other cockpit tries to edit before EXEC, the FMS can show ENTRY CONFLICT.
The active TO waypoint and active leg are highlighted magenta; inactive-route waypoint names are cyan. Use color as a cue, then verify the actual leg data.
Review the LEGS page before EXEC for waypoint order, course, distance, altitude/speed advisory data, and procedure leg type.
Route discontinuities are inserted when the FMS cannot build a continuous path, such as after some direct-to, procedure, or route insertions.
Close discontinuities only after verifying the chart and clearance support the connection. A clean magenta line is not proof that the route is legal.
Any waypoint may be made the current TO waypoint by moving it to the TO position, but doing so removes intervening waypoints and can bypass restrictions.
FMS turn anticipation can roll in or out up to about 4 degrees per second and up to 30 degrees AOB, but the pilot is still responsible for airspace, restrictions, and clearance compliance.
For SID selection, choose the runway, SID, and transition from DEP/ARR, then review the first legs and restrictions before EXEC.
For STAR selection, choose the destination arrival and transition, review all legs and restrictions, close only valid discontinuities, then execute.
For approach selection, choose the approach and transition from DEP/ARR, verify the initial, final, and missed-approach legs, then execute.
For holding, use the HOLD page or the /H scratchpad method on the desired fix, then verify direction, leg length or timing, and the clearance that authorizes the hold.

items.text: FMS arrivals use the FMS to transition from en route structure to a STAR, TAA, RNAV approach, or vector-to-final setup while the chart and clearance remain controlling.

children.text: A STAR clearance authorizes the published lateral route and any assigned restrictions, but published expect altitudes or speeds are planning information until ATC assigns or clears them.
A TAA transitions aircraft from RNAV en route structure into protected terminal airspace and provides at least 1000 feet of obstacle clearance within the depicted sector.
Being cleared direct to an IAF or IF/IAF without an approach clearance does not authorize descent to the lower TAA altitude.
Once cleared for the approach and inside the applicable TAA sector, descend no lower than the depicted minimum altitude for that sector unless ATC assigns something more restrictive.
The T-6B is certified to fly RNAV (GPS) approaches to LNAV MDA minimums only; do not use LNAV/VNAV, VNAV, or LPV minimums.
GPS stand-alone approaches require the procedure to be loaded from the current database; underlying ground-based NAVAIDs are not required, but may be monitored when available.
GPS overlay of non-precision procedures is limited to authorized overlays retrievable from the current database. Localizer, LDA, and SDF procedures are not authorized as GPS overlays.
For any RNAV DP, STAR, or approach, the loaded FMS procedure must match the charted procedure and clearance.
Use LDDHA: Load the GPS approach, Direct to the IAWP, Display source to FMS, Hold/HILO or missed approach set correctly, and Approach mode verified.
If radar-vectored to final, make the FAWP the active leg and extend the inbound final approach course as required, then comply with vectoring instructions until cleared for the approach.
Slow to 150 KIAS within 5 NM of the IAWP when flying the full published entry.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAWP.
Expect the HSI scale-change cue near 3 NM from the FAWP and verify APR annunciation near 2 NM from the FAWP.
At the FAWP, execute the 6 Ts as applicable, then descend using about 20% torque, 120 KIAS, and a stabilized rate not greater than 1000 FPM.
Level at MDA and fly to the MAWP; do not let the FMS lead you into an early descent below MDA.
If the runway environment is not in sight or landing is unsafe at the MAWP, execute the missed approach.
The FMS will not automatically sequence the missed approach at the MAWP; once stabilized in the climb and clean, select MISS APR and EXEC as required to sequence the published missed.
If GPS integrity is lost before the FAWP, transition to an authorized backup approach if available.
If no backup is available before the FAWP, continue on course to the FAWP, maintain the FAWP altitude to the MAWP, then execute the missed approach.

If GPS integrity is lost inside the FAWP, treat it as serious: transition to an authorized backup if available, climb to missed-approach altitude, continue tracking to the MAWP, and inform ATC as soon as practical.
Common errors are loading the wrong approach or transition, misusing TAA/feeder altitudes, late BAC, missing APR mode, and using the wrong minimums.

events.overview: I4203 ties degraded-heading recovery, emergency field selection, and fuel accountability into one decision loop. The event standard is to use ATC to reduce heading workload when needed, keep a suitable recovery field in mind before the emergency, and compare planned fuel to actual fuel early enough that fuel never becomes a surprise.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A no-gyro approach is available under radar control when directional gyro or stabilized compass information is inoperative, inaccurate, or no longer trusted.

children.text: Tell ATC the heading system is unreliable and request a no-gyro PAR, ASR, PAR W/O GS, or vectors to a visual approach if VMC supports it.
Comply with the normal PAR, ASR, or PAR W/O GS procedure; no-gyro only changes how ATC commands turns.
Configuration, minimums, lost-communication, missed-approach, and climbout discipline still come from the underlying approach.
ATC may initiate no-gyro vectors if the controller sees incorrect directional responses or suspects the pilot has lost directional awareness.
Before final, start the turn immediately when told 'turn left' or 'turn right' and use standard rate, not more than 30 degrees AOB, unless directed otherwise.
Stop the turn immediately when told 'stop turn.'
On final, use half-standard-rate turns unless the controller directs another rate.
Acknowledge instructions until ATC says no further acknowledgements are required.
Common errors are slow compliance, wrong turn rate, late before-approach configuration, poor DA/MDA transition, and mixing up missed approach, climbout, and lost-communication instructions.

items.text: Emergency field selection is a continuous habit: every OPS Check should update the nearest suitable recovery option based on fuel, engine/system state, weather, terrain, lighting, and airspace.

children.text: Preflight chart study should identify diverts along the route, not just at the destination. Note runway length, orientation, elevation, lighting, surface, approaches, and communications.
Local SOPs may set specific runway-size, surface, lighting, solo, or night requirements. Verify current local standards instead of relying on memory.
Use the FMS NRST page, charts, NAVAIDs, ATC, and visual references together; no single tool decides suitability by itself.
For a precautionary emergency landing, communicate if able without delaying the emergency procedure. The useful call is who you are, where you are, and what you need.
If an engine fails at night at or above 2000 feet AGL and a lighted runway is not immediately available, ejection is highly recommended if restart is not attempted or is unsuccessful.
If an engine fails below 2000 feet AGL, attempting a restart is not recommended; if a lighted runway is not immediately available, first priority is setting up to eject.

In a low-level engine malfunction, climb to cope. Airfields within an arc circumscribed by the wingtips may be reachable with an immediate turn and climb, but a suitable field much beyond about 3 NM is unlikely from low level.
A zoom from about 240 knots groundspeed can gain roughly 1300 feet; consider whether that altitude buys restart, field selection, or ejection margin.
Route abort triggers include insufficient fuel, aircraft malfunction, bird hazard, and weather.
In VMC, maintain terrain clearance and VFR altitude rules if possible, set the appropriate transponder code, maintain VMC, and coordinate with the controlling agency.
An abort into IMC is an emergency: climb immediately to at least ERAA, squawk 7700, contact ATC, and do not let route-finding distract from aircraft control.
If communications cannot be established at an unfamiliar field, observe traffic, runway markings, segmented circle, wind indicators, and pattern direction from a safe altitude if time permits.

items.text: Fuel management compares the fuel plan to the aircraft reality before a low-fuel decision is forced. The basic cockpit comparison is Estimated Fuel Remaining versus Actual Fuel Remaining.

children.text: During planning, calculate EFR by verifying actual fuel load, subtracting start/taxi/takeoff fuel, then subtracting each leg's estimated fuel burn.
At the end of each leg, compare AFR to EFR. AFR greater than or equal to EFR supports the plan; AFR less than EFR requires immediate investigation.
Likely causes include less fuel onboard at takeoff, higher climb or cruise fuel flow, slower groundspeed, math or flight-log error, unplanned routing, or fuel leak.
Make the comparison part of the OPS Check so the decision happens while there are still route, altitude, divert, and ATC options.
CNAF fuel planning requires sufficient usable fuel for meteorological factors and mission requirements.

If no alternate is required, plan fuel from takeoff to destination plus a 10% reserve. If an alternate is required, plan takeoff to the destination approach fix, then to the alternate, plus a 10% reserve.
The planned reserve after final landing may not be less than 20 minutes of flight; for turbine fixed-wing aircraft, compute that at maximum endurance at 10,000 feet.
The workbook uses the T-6B NATOPS/PCL maximum-endurance value of 333 PPH at 10,000 feet on a standard day, yielding about 111 pounds for 20 minutes and a rounded planning reserve of 115 pounds.
Local training minimums may be higher than the regulatory planning reserve; confirm current squadron/CNATRA minimum fuel and emergency fuel numbers before relying on them.
When fuel endurance becomes the controlling factor, use NATOPS maximum-endurance data instead of inventing a low-burn technique.
Maximum endurance AOA is 8.8 units; maximum range AOA is 4.4 units.
Recommended clean holding speed is 125 to 150 KIAS, but no slower than maximum endurance speed of 125 KIAS.
Use DRAFT for a divert request: destination, route, altitude, fuel remaining in hours plus minutes, and time en route.

Minimum fuel tells ATC no undue delay can be accepted; it is not itself an emergency. If traffic priority is needed to ensure a safe landing, declare emergency fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: CNAF takeoff minimums start with instrument-rating authority and emergency-return capability, not with the weather you hope to have after departure.

children.text: A special instrument rating has no takeoff ceiling or visibility minimums; the departure depends on pilot judgment and flight urgency.
Only an aircraft commander with a special instrument rating, and on the flight controls, may depart below the applicable minimums.
For normal student planning, brief the standard instrument-rating rules unless current orders or the aircraft commander direct otherwise.
If the available emergency-return approach is non-precision, takeoff requires the published minimums for that approach, but not less than a 300-foot ceiling and 1 SM visibility.
If a compatible precision approach is available and usable for the landing runway, takeoff may use those precision minimums when they are lower than 300/1.
The precision-supported floor is still 200-foot ceiling and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
Before using a number, verify the landing runway, available approach, NOTAMs, installed and operable equipment, Trouble T data, and departure procedure.

items.text: Approach minimums answer two separate questions: may the approach be started, and may the aircraft continue below MDA or DH.

children.text: Use approved DoD FLIP or equivalent published procedures. For straight-in approaches, RVR governs when available; for circling approaches, prevailing visibility governs.
The pilot is responsible for determining that weather and visibility are adequate for the approach and landing.
A single-piloted aircraft shall not commence an instrument approach if the reported weather is below the published minimums for the type of approach being conducted.
Once commenced, the pilot may continue to the approved published landing minimums, but the fixed-wing single-pilot absolute floor is 200-foot ceiling or HAT and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
Do not descend below MDA or continue below DH unless the runway environment is in sight and a safe landing can be made.
On a precision approach, execute the missed approach at DH if the runway environment is not in sight or a safe landing cannot be made.
On a non-precision approach, execute the missed approach at the MAP if visual reference is not established or the landing cannot be accomplished.

If visual reference is lost while circling, fly the published missed approach; begin with a climbing turn toward the landing runway, then maneuver the shortest direction to join the missed-approach course.

During radar approaches, expect missed-approach or climbout instructions if safe limits are exceeded, aircraft position or identification is in doubt, radar contact is lost, radar malfunction is suspected, or tower-observed conditions make approach completion unsafe.
The missed approach remains available at pilot discretion at any time; do not wait for the controller if the aircraft is unstable, unqualified to continue, or not in a safe landing position.

items.text: Alternate filing minimums convert the destination forecast into a required alternate plan during the period 1 hour before ETA until 1 hour after ETA.

children.text: File using the actual weather at departure, existing and forecast weather along the route, and the destination and alternate forecasts for ETA plus or minus 1 hour.
If destination weather is forecast below 3000-foot ceiling and 3 SM visibility, an alternate is required.
If the destination is forecast from 0-0 up to, but not including, published minimums, the alternate must be forecast at 3000-3 or better.

If the destination is forecast from published minimums up to, but not including, 3000-3, the alternate must be at least published minimums plus 300-1 for a non-precision approach, or plus 200-1/2 for a precision approach.
If destination weather is forecast 3000-3 or better, CNAF does not require an alternate for that reason, though local training rules or fuel planning may still require one.
When an alternate is required, it must have a published approach compatible with installed and operable navigation equipment.
If the destination lacks that kind of approach, or if the alternate forecast is below 3000-3, the alternate approach must also be flyable without two-way radio communication.
For single-piloted aircraft, or any aircraft with only one operable UHF/VHF transceiver, PAR or ASR minimums may not be used as the basis for selecting an alternate.

For T-6B planning, do not base a required alternate on a GPS-only approach or GPS substitution for an out-of-service NAVAID; the required alternate needs an available approach that does not require GPS.
The workbook flow is practical: check destination and alternate weather, NOTAMs, approach availability, NAVAID compatibility, airfield status, and fuel before deciding the alternate is viable.
Record the decision on the flight-planning matrix so the plan survives reroutes, holding, missed approaches, or a lost-communications branch.
If proceeding to the alternate in flight, format the request with DRAFT: destination, route, altitude, fuel remaining, and time en route.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Flight planning is the PIC's proof that the route, weather, fuel, airfields, procedures, and risk picture support the intended operation.

children.text: CNAF requires the PIC to be familiar with available weather reports and forecasts, NOTAMs, TFRs, fuel requirements, terminal instrument procedures, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, and anticipated traffic delays.
The PIC and mission commander, when one is designated, must conduct a risk assessment before flight.
Plan the route around preferred IFR routes, SIDs, STARs, published airways, restricted-area avoidance, terrain, weather, and fuel, not just the shortest line between airports.
DoD and joint civil-military airfields are generally authorized, but PPR may be required when they are not home, local training, alternate, or emergency-divert fields.
Civilian airfields must support mission value, training value, or government interest; before planning one, verify local procedures, runway length and load-bearing capability, services, and security.
Closed-tower operations require the proper command authorization; closed airfields are takeoff/landing prohibited except for emergencies.

items.text: The jet log turns a route into flyable numbers: headings, distances, groundspeeds, ETEs, fuel burns, EFRs, and the DRAFT data needed if the plan changes.

children.text: Create a new leg at each NAVAID, for course changes greater than 6 degrees, at each compulsory reporting point, and at both ends of a direct leg.
The first leg is STTO: use 1 minute and 50 pounds unless extended ground time or local conditions require more.
Use climb data, cruise data, winds, route distance, and split-leg entries when the aircraft reaches cruise altitude during a leg.
Round distance and time to the nearest whole number; round any fuel fraction over a 5-pound increment up to the next 5 pounds.
Verify actual fuel load, subtract STTO, subtract each leg's planned burn, and carry EFR forward checkpoint by checkpoint.
At the destination, convert fuel remaining to hours plus minutes using cruise fuel flow, then carry that into the alternate line and DRAFT report.
The fuel plan includes climb/route to destination, route to alternate, planned approaches, reserve, start/taxi, total required, total fuel aboard, and spare fuel.
The workbook uses 50 pounds per planned approach, 50 pounds for normal start/taxi, and 115 pounds as the T-6B planning reserve for CNAF's 20-minute maximum-endurance requirement.

items.text: The DD-1801 is the formal DoD flight plan; for IFR, it tells ATC what route, equipment, altitude, timing, and alternates the aircraft is requesting.

children.text: CNAF requires the PIC or formation leader to submit a flight plan unless a daily flight schedule is authorized in lieu of the form.
The workbook recommends filing IFR at least 30 minutes before ETD to avoid clearance delay; IFR operations above FL230 should be filed at least 4 hours before ETD when practicable.
Use DD-1801 for domestic or international DoD flight planning, and follow current FLIP General Planning block instructions rather than memorized old examples.
Item 7 aircraft identification must match the Mode S Flight ID; mismatches can prevent correlation with the stored flight plan.
Item 8 declares IFR/VFR and type of flight; U.S. domestic ATC systems do not accept a flight plan that begins VFR and later changes to IFR.
Item 9 identifies the aircraft type and wake category; T-6B planning uses the published type designator from current planning guidance.
Item 10 and Item 18 describe equipment, surveillance, PBN, and remarks. For T-6B PBN, verify the current template and do not claim WAAS navigation capability from ADS-B-only WAAS.
Item 13 uses departure airport and UTC off-block time.
Item 15 carries true airspeed, cruising level, and route. File SIDs, airways, DCT legs, change points, and STARs in the order the aircraft will fly them.
Item 16 includes destination, total EET, and up to two alternate airports.
Item 18 clarifies details such as date of flight, registration, operating agency, delay, destination or alternate names when ZZZZ is used, and plain-language remarks.

items.text: The DD-175-1 is the military flight weather brief; it feeds the go/no-go decision, the jet log, TOLD, alternate selection, and en route weather plan.

children.text: For any intended route forecast to include IMC, obtain a flight-route weather brief from a DoD-qualified forecaster or approved forecasting service.
The primary ashore method is FWB; if FWB is unavailable, approved support may come from NAFC, FSS, Air Force Weather, Marine Corps services, or an approved commercial service.
When filing a DD-175 or DD-1801, request a DD-175-1 from a DoD-qualified forecaster; request it at least 1 hour before the proposed brief time when possible.
The brief void time may not exceed the weather-briefed time by more than 3 hours, and may not exceed ETD by more than 30 minutes.
If the brief is outside that window, get an extension or rebrief before takeoff.
All times are Zulu; heights are AGL or MSL as annotated; winds and temperatures support both weather judgment and the jet-log/TOLD calculations.
Part I covers takeoff data: departure, runway temperature, dewpoint, pressure/density altitude, surface and climb winds, local watches or warnings, RSC/RCR, and takeoff-alternate remarks.
Part II covers en route and mission data such as flight-level winds, clouds, obscurations, freezing levels, thunderstorms, turbulence, icing, and precipitation.
Part III covers destination and alternate forecasts; visibility and ceilings are the controlling values for approach minimums and alternate requirements.
Part IV and V preserve comments, hazards, PMSV/PIREP notes, briefing number, briefer identity, void time, and rebrief/extension record.

items.text: CNAF takeoff and approach minimums are the weather gates that keep an IFR departure, approach commencement, and approach continuation legal and sensible.

children.text: For a standard instrument rating, non-precision-supported takeoff requires the published minimums for the available approach, but not less than 300-foot ceiling and 1 SM visibility.
If a compatible precision approach is available and usable for the landing runway, takeoff may use those precision minimums, but never below 200-foot ceiling and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
Before using either number, verify the runway in use, emergency-return approach, NOTAMs, installed equipment, Trouble T data, and departure procedure.
A single-piloted aircraft shall not commence an approach if reported weather is below published minimums for the type of approach being flown.
The fixed-wing single-pilot absolute floor is 200-foot ceiling or HAT and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
Do not descend below MDA or continue below DH unless the runway environment is in sight and a safe landing can be made.
Execute the missed approach at DH for a precision approach or at the MAP for a non-precision approach when visual reference or safe landing position is not there.

sections.title: CNAF M-3710.7 Takeoff and Approach Minimums

items.text: Alternate filing minimums decide whether a destination forecast is enough by itself or whether a usable backup field must be filed and fueled.

children.text: File using actual departure weather, route weather, and destination/alternate forecasts for 1 hour before ETA until 1 hour after ETA.
If destination weather is forecast below 3000-foot ceiling and 3 SM visibility, an alternate is required.
If destination weather is forecast from 0-0 up to but not including published minimums, the alternate must be forecast 3000-3 or better.

If destination weather is forecast from published minimums up to but not including 3000-3, the alternate must meet published minimums plus 300-1 for a non-precision approach or plus 200-1/2 for a precision approach.
A required alternate must have a published approach compatible with installed and operable navigation equipment.
If the destination lacks that kind of approach, or if the alternate forecast is below 3000-3, the alternate approach must be flyable without two-way radio communication.
Do not use PAR or ASR minimums as the basis for a single-piloted alternate, or when the aircraft has only one operable UHF/VHF transceiver.
For T-6B planning, the required alternate needs an available approach that does not require GPS; do not rely on GPS substitution for an out-of-service NAVAID.

items.text: FSS is a weather, flight-plan, NOTAM, inflight advisory, emergency, and search-and-rescue support path; use it for flight-service work, not as a substitute for ATC clearance discipline.

children.text: Flight Service Specialists are FAA-certified pilot weather briefers. They may translate and interpret available forecasts and reports, but they do not create original forecasts.
FSS briefings may be standard, abbreviated, outlook, or inflight; ask for the kind of brief you actually need.
Common access methods include 1-800-WX-BRIEF, 1800wxbrief.com, published discrete frequencies, and common inflight frequencies such as 122.2 VHF or 255.4 UHF.
When DAIP is unavailable, FSS can support NOTAM review, but request special notices or domestic/international notices explicitly if you need them.
At nonmilitary installations, closing the flight plan is the PIC's responsibility and must be done with flight service or another proper agency.
Canceling an IFR clearance is not the same as closing the flight plan; make sure the landing report is delivered.

If no communication link exists before departure, CNAF permits filing by phone or, when legal, by radio after takeoff, but never use that path to justify unauthorized IMC flight in controlled airspace.

items.text: Strange field operations start when the aircraft is away from normal support and the PIC must make sure the aircraft is inspected, serviced, secured, and ready for the next launch.

children.text: If mission requirements dictate an overnight stay and ground support equipment or personnel are not available, NATOPS makes the PIC responsible for postflight and preflight inspections.
Postflight starts with parking brake set, interior checked, gust lock engaged, and ejection-seat/CFS safety pins installed in both cockpits.

The exterior check looks for leaks, flap and speed-brake condition, gear and door condition, tire damage, brake-wear indicators, loose panels, covers, restraints, chocks, tie-downs, and static grounding as required.
Check oil with the dipstick 15 to 20 minutes after shutdown for the most accurate result.
Oil must be serviced within 30 minutes of shutdown; normal level is between ADD and MAX HOT, and oil at or below ADD must be serviced to MAX HOT.
Use the dipstick, not the sight glass, for the correct oil-level indication.
Secure the aircraft before leaving: canopy locked, external CFS doors closed and locked, baggage door latched and locked, avionics doors latched, and sun shields installed as required.
The wing and tail tie-down points are sufficient in normal conditions; secure the nose gear as well when windy or extreme conditions are anticipated.
If high winds are expected and time permits, move the aircraft to a hangar; NATOPS warns that winds above 80 knots can cause structural damage.
Before planning a strange field, confirm fuel, servicing, security, parking, hangar or tie-down support, and who can move the aircraft if the parking brake must be released for towing.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: En route weather is a continuous reassessment problem: use each source for what it is good at, then decide whether the route, approach, or alternate still makes sense.

children.text: ARTCCs broadcast AWWs, Convective SIGMETs, SIGMETs, AIRMETs, urgent PIREPs, and CWA alerts once on all non-emergency frequencies when the hazard area is within 150 NM of their airspace.
Those broadcasts alert you that hazardous weather information exists; contact FSS or another appropriate source for the details.

FSS can provide en route advisories by radio, commonly on 122.2 VHF, 255.4 UHF, or published discrete frequencies. FSS briefers interpret available forecasts and reports, but do not create original forecasts.
PMSV, radio call 'METRO,' can pass weather information, update or extend DD-175-1 data, and receive significant or hazardous PIREPs.

ATIS usually provides airport name, code letter, UTC time, winds, visibility, obstructions, weather, sky condition, temperature, dew point, altimeter, density-altitude advisory when applicable, approach, and runway in use.
ATIS service volume is normally 20 to 60 NM from the site and up to 25,000 feet AGL.
ASOS/AWOS provides minute-by-minute automated surface observations; discrete-frequency reception is normally engineered to about 25 NM and 10,000 feet AGL.
UNICOM may provide wind, recommended runway, weather, and airport advisory information at public-use airports without tower or FSS.
ATC radar can help with precipitation avoidance, but controllers describe only what their equipment supports: light, moderate, heavy, extreme, or intensity unknown.
ARTCC WARP weather can lag actual conditions by up to about 6 minutes, and ATC radar does not detect turbulence.
Treat thunderstorms as turbulence threats even if the displayed precipitation intensity seems manageable; operations within 20 NM of thunderstorms require great caution.

Report hazardous weather, thunderstorms or lightning, turbulence, icing, wind shear, cloud bases/tops/layers, visibility, precipitation, strong winds, and unexpected conditions by PIREP. Follow up with METRO when practical.

items.text: A divert to the alternate should sound like a prepared clearance request, not a scramble after the missed approach.

children.text: Fly the missed approach or assigned climbout first, then tell ATC your intentions once the aircraft is climbing, configured, and under control.
Use DRAFT for the clearance request: destination, route, altitude, fuel remaining, and time en route.
The route uses the same rules as the DD-1801 route section; do not invent a shorthand route that ATC cannot clear.
Altitude should comply with hemispheric or assigned altitude rules, terrain, MEA/MOCA/OROCA, weather, and ATC clearance.
Fuel in DRAFT is endurance in hours plus minutes until flameout, normally based on cruise fuel flow, not pounds remaining.
Time is ETE to the alternate in hours plus minutes, built from the jet log or an updated in-flight calculation.
Before committing, update weather, confirm approach availability and minimums, compare actual fuel to the fuel plan, and keep another field or emergency branch in mind.

items.text: A change of flight plan while airborne formalizes a new destination, route, altitude, or timing picture so ATC and flight service can protect and track the aircraft.

children.text: Use the change-of-flight-plan format on the inside back cover of the IFR Enroute Supplement.

Be ready with type of flight plan, aircraft identification, type aircraft or TD code, estimated true airspeed, original destination when applicable, departure point, present position and time, new route and altitude or flight level, new destination when applicable, ETE or ETA, fuel endurance, required alternate, and the station where the original flight plan was filed.
Once ATC issues an amended clearance, the amended route, altitude, and clearance limit replace the previous expectation.

Mandatory IFR reports still apply: leaving an assigned altitude, unable to climb or descend at least 500 FPM, missed approach, cruising TAS changes of 5 percent or 10 knots, required holding reports, navigation or communication capability loss, safety-of-flight information, and unforecast or hazardous weather.
If the request is long, use a courtesy call first so the controller is ready to copy.
Do not let the paperwork format delay basic aircraft control, terrain clearance, fuel awareness, or emergency declaration when priority handling is needed.

sections.title: Change of Flight Plan While Airborne

items.text: The IFR Supplement is both a planning source and an in-flight reference for airports, facilities, communications, NAVAIDs, and theater procedures.

children.text: Check the cover effective dates, then update the publication with NOTAMs and AP/1 information during planning.
The inside front cover contains special notices for new requirements or major FLIP changes.
The inside back cover contains FAA formats for position reports, change of flight plan, and filing flight plans in flight; the outside back cover contains ICAO formats.
Section A is the codebook: sample entries, legend, and abbreviations used to decode facility listings.
Section B is the airport and facility directory, including city/airport cross references, airport listings, ATC centers, FICs, communication stations, and radio navigation aids.

Section C contains theater flight data and procedures such as ADIZ procedures, cruising altitudes, no-NOTAM preventive maintenance, FACSFAC procedures, laser hazards, mandatory frequency airspace, and CTAF information.
For actual planning, use it to confirm field hours, time conversion, runway dimensions, barriers, services, PPR, PMSV, communications, NAVAID data, and unusual field restrictions.

items.text: A circling maneuver is a visual maneuver from an instrument approach, but it still lives inside protected circling airspace and published or assigned restrictions.

children.text: Before beginning, plan how the circle will work based on wind, runway alignment, terrain, towers, obstacles, and airport environment.
After breaking out, identify the intended runway and remain at or above circling altitude until continuously in a position to descend to landing at a normal rate using normal maneuvers.
Use normal visual checkpoints when possible, but expect 180, 90, and final spacing to look different because circling altitude may be higher or lower than a normal pattern.
Review circling restrictions on the approach plate, AP/1, IFR Supplement, and NOTAMs; restrictions such as 'Circling NA' in a sector are controlling.
Published circling minimums provide at least 300 feet of obstacle clearance when the aircraft remains inside the protected circling area.

Newer inverse-C circling minima use both approach category and circling MDA to set the protected radius; for Category C, the radius ranges from 2.7 NM at 1000 feet MSL or less to 3.3 NM at 9001 feet MSL and above.

Unless instructed otherwise, maneuver by the shortest path to base or downwind. Passing over the airport or other runways is not prohibited, but traffic, wind, and controller instructions still matter.
If visual reference is lost while circling, fly the missed approach for that procedure unless ATC has assigned an alternate missed approach.
Begin with an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway, then continue the turn until established on the prescribed missed-approach course.
At a non-towered field, consider overflying to observe wind, traffic, runway condition, and pattern direction before committing to the circle.

items.text: VDP is the point on a non-precision straight-in final where a normal descent from MDA can begin to the runway, provided the required visual references and safe landing position exist.

children.text: If a VDP is published, it appears in the profile view and should be used as the normal descent gate.
Do not descend below MDA before the VDP just because the runway environment is in sight.
Level at MDA at or before the published or derived VDP, then continue to the MAP if the runway environment or safe landing position is not available.
If the runway environment first appears at the MAP, a normal descent may not be possible; a longer landing must be acceptable or a missed approach is the better decision.
If no VDP is depicted, compute a derived point by dividing HAT by the desired descent gradient.
For an approximate 3-degree path, use 300 feet per NM: HAT / 300 = VDP distance in NM from the runway end.
If DME is available at the runway end, subtract or add the VDP distance as appropriate to derive the VDP DME.
Absence of a published VDP may indicate obstruction-clearance penetration on final. A computed VDP can be useful, but it is not permission to ignore obstacles or published notes.
