events.overview: I4303 makes the cross-country plan survive route changes and abnormal events. The event standard is to know which airspace rules apply, keep a usable recovery field and fuel plan updated, and fly high-altitude approach energy from the published chart instead of memory.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Airspace classification tells you which rule set controls the route, who provides separation, what clearance or communication is required, and how much flexibility you have if the plan changes.

children.text: Controlled airspace includes Class A, B, C, D, and E; ATC service is provided to IFR and VFR flights according to the class.
Class G is uncontrolled airspace: the portion that has not been designated Class A, B, C, D, or E.
When overlapping airspace applies, use the more restrictive rule set; do not let a sectional color or local habit override the actual airspace designation.
IFR operations in controlled airspace require an IFR flight plan and an appropriate ATC clearance.
Class A is generally 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600, and operations are IFR unless otherwise authorized.
Class B requires an ATC clearance; Class C and D require the appropriate ATC communication/clearance for the operation; Class E may be controlled without a tower or surface-area feel.
For a divert or route change, ask what clearance, equipment, communication, and weather minimums are needed before pointing the airplane at the new airspace.
Prohibited and restricted areas are regulatory special-use airspace; warning areas, MOAs, alert areas, and controlled firing areas are nonregulatory special-use airspace.

If an IFR route would enter active joint-use restricted airspace, ATC either clears the aircraft through when released to FAA control or issues a clearance that avoids it unless the flight has authorization.
MOA activity changes frequently, so use current charts, controlling-agency status, FSS/ATC, and day-of notices before treating the airspace as available.

items.text: Emergency field selection is a continuous cross-country habit: every OPS Check should update the nearest suitable recovery option before the aircraft needs it.

children.text: During route study and in flight, screen fields for runway length and width, surface, lighting, approaches, weather, winds, elevation, terrain, services, security, NOTAMs, and airspace.
Local SOPs may set specific runway-size, night, wet-runway, or solo requirements; verify the current local standard instead of baking one local number into the brief.

Use the FMS NRST page, IFR Supplement, charts, NAVAIDs, ATC, and visual references together. The NRST page can limit airport results by runway length and surface, but suitability still requires pilot judgment.
Initial reaction to a low-altitude malfunction is to trade excess airspeed for altitude when able; altitude buys terrain clearance, glide range, restart time, and ejection margin.
For engine failure, zoom/glide at 125 KIAS minimum and turn immediately toward a suitable landing surface if one is available.
Do not delay the decision to eject below 2000 feet AGL; an airstart is not recommended below 2000 feet AGL because primary attention should be to eject or safely recover the aircraft.
At night, if engine failure occurs at or above 2000 feet AGL and a lighted runway is not immediately available, ejection is highly recommended if restart is not attempted or is unsuccessful.

For a PEL, land-as-soon-as-practical, or land-as-soon-as-possible situation, use ATC vectors and the NRST/IFR Supplement picture to get pointed at a field while preserving aircraft control and energy.
For route aborts, keep the chart, FMS, NAVAIDs, and ATC in the loop; do not let field selection become a heads-down search while the aircraft drifts away from safe altitude or clearance.
If total disorientation, inadvertent IMC, or malfunction occurs on a route, climb to the planned ERAA, notify the controlling agency, and decide whether to continue, divert, or recover.

items.text: A high-altitude approach transitions from high-altitude structure to the final approach course by combining a penetration descent with an instrument approach.

children.text: High-altitude approaches support efficient fuel consumption, higher true airspeed, and delaying low-altitude weather exposure until closer to the destination.
The approach may use a teardrop, arcing, or straight-in penetration. Once the aircraft is configured to before-approach condition, the low-altitude final-approach procedures are the same.
Use the published chart for penetration course, turn direction, altitude restrictions, DME restrictions, and any profile-view notes; do not fly a local example from memory.
Inbound to the IAF, complete the Descent Checklist.
At the IAF, execute the 6 Ts: time when required, turn to parallel the penetration course, transition into the penetration, twist the CDI course, and talk when a report is required.
If the outbound course is more than 90 degrees from the inbound course to the IAF, turn with an intercept heading not to exceed 45 degrees.
Initiate the penetration by reducing power as required for about 2000-4000 FPM, fly 200-250 KIAS, and use speed brake as required.
Manage energy to meet every course, altitude, and DME restriction; about 1000 feet before level-off, reduce descent rate to 500-1500 FPM.
Level segments of the penetration may be flown at normal cruise.

For a teardrop penetration, begin at one-half the initial altitude or the published penetration turn, use 30 degrees AOB, then use bearing-pointer position during the last half of the turn to choose a 45-degree or double-angle intercept.
For an arcing penetration, use about 1 percent of groundspeed for lead computations when full standard rate is not practical, and do not exceed 30 degrees AOB.
High-altitude approach charts do not publish Category B landing minimums; T-6Bs use Category C minimums on those charts.

items.text: CNAF minimum fuel planning starts with enough usable fuel for meteorological factors and mission requirements, then adds the required reserve logic.

children.text: If no alternate is required, plan fuel from takeoff to destination plus a 10% reserve of planned fuel requirements.
If an alternate is required, plan fuel from takeoff to the approach fix serving the destination, then to the alternate, plus a 10% reserve.
In no case may the planned reserve after final landing at the destination or required alternate be less than 20 minutes of flight.
For turbine fixed-wing aircraft, compute that 20-minute reserve using maximum-endurance operation at 10,000 feet; model-specific minimum fuel reserve requirements come from NATOPS.
The workbook uses the T-6B NATOPS/PCL maximum-endurance fuel flow of 333 PPH at 10,000 feet on a standard day.
Twenty minutes at 333 PPH is about 111 pounds, rounded to 115 pounds using the workbook planning rule.
Local training minimums or SOP reserves may be higher; confirm current local fuel gates before treating a reserve number as sufficient for release.
If ATC routing, altitude, weather, or delay will make planned reserves inadequate, inform ATC and alter destination as required.
Minimum fuel is an advisory that no undue delay can be accepted; it is not an emergency and should not be expected to produce special handling.
If traffic priority is needed to ensure a safe landing, declare an emergency and report fuel remaining in minutes.
Report both minimum fuel advisories and emergency fuel state each time control is transferred to a new controller.

items.text: Fuel management turns the jet log into an in-flight decision tool by comparing planned fuel remaining to actual fuel remaining before the divert options disappear.

children.text: Build Estimated Fuel Remaining during planning from actual fuel load, start/taxi/takeoff fuel, route fuel, approach fuel, alternate fuel, and reserve.
At the end of each leg and during OPS Checks, compare Actual Fuel Remaining to EFR.
AFR greater than or equal to EFR supports the plan; AFR less than EFR requires immediate investigation.
Likely causes include less fuel onboard at takeoff than planned, higher fuel flow, slower groundspeed, unplanned routing, math or flight-log error, or a fuel leak.
When endurance becomes the controlling factor, use NATOPS maximum-endurance guidance rather than inventing a low-burn technique.
T-6B maximum-endurance AOA is 8.8 units; maximum-range AOA is 4.4 units.
Recommended clean holding speed is 125-150 KIAS, but not slower than maximum-endurance speed of 125 KIAS.
Use published PCL/NATOPS data for time, distance, and fuel performance instead of relying on a single cockpit rule of thumb.
If the fuel picture starts moving the wrong way, act while choices remain: adjust altitude or routing, reduce unnecessary delay, request priority if needed, or divert.
Keep DRAFT data ready for a divert request: destination, route, altitude, fuel remaining in hours plus minutes, and time en route.
Do not wait for the planned alternate to become the only option; fuel management is meant to create time, not explain why it ran out.

events.overview: I4304 closes the I43 block by tying lost-communication predictability, published departure and arrival procedures, obstacle-clearance planning, and cumulative EP discipline into one cross-country brief. The event standard is to make the next safe action obvious even if radios, weather, or aircraft status stop matching the plan.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Lost communications is a predictability problem first: keep flying, make the aircraft easy for ATC to protect, and use emergency authority if the published rule no longer produces the safest outcome.

children.text: No single rule covers every lost-communications situation; the PIC remains the final authority and may deviate from Part 91 as required by an in-flight emergency.
Unless emergency authority is being used, ATC will protect for the assumption that the aircraft is complying with 14 CFR 91.185.
Squawk 7600 on Mode A/3, but remember the aircraft may not be in radar coverage.
If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
This VFR rule also applies in Class A airspace.
Land as soon as practicable does not mean land immediately at an unsuitable or unauthorized airport; use judgment to reach a safe, suitable landing option.
For route, use AVE-F: assigned route, vectored direct to the fix/route/airway in the vector clearance, expected route, then filed route.
For altitude, use AME for each route segment: the highest of assigned altitude, minimum IFR altitude, or expected altitude.
Make altitude changes required by MEA, MCA, MRA, and any valid expected-further-clearance altitude at the specified time or fix.
If cleared to a fix from which an approach begins, begin descent or approach as close as possible to the EFC time, or ETA if no EFC was received.

If the clearance limit is not an approach fix, leave it at EFC time, or on arrival if no EFC was received, then proceed to a fix from which an approach begins and time the descent or approach as close as possible to ETA.
Monitor NAVAID voice if available and attempt contact on the last assigned frequency, FSS, New York Radio or San Francisco Radio, and 121.5 MHz as able.
If contact is made through FSS or radio relay, give position, altitude, last assigned frequency, and request further clearance from the controlling facility.
During radar approaches, lost-communication timing may be no more than 1 minute on vectors to final, 15 seconds on ASR or PAR without glideslope final, and 5 seconds on PAR final.

If radar-approach communications are lost, attempt secondary or tower frequency, proceed VFR if possible, or execute the approved non-radar approach or specific lost-communication procedure for that radar approach.

items.text: SID/STAR procedures are published ATC routes with clearance consequences; brief the chart as an executable clearance, not just a name in the flight plan.

children.text: A SID provides obstruction clearance and transition from the terminal area to en route structure.
Before takeoff, review the full SID, surrounding terrain, hazards, climb gradient requirements, transition, and lost-communication or emergency-return consequences.
Set NAVAIDs, displays, and FMS procedure as required before departure; if using the FMS, the SID must be retrieved from the database and checked against the clearance.
Keep the primary recovery approach available in case the SID turns into an emergency return.
A STAR is an ATC-coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and transitions the aircraft from en route structure toward terminal instrument procedures.
You must have the approved chart to accept a STAR, and RNAV STARs require appropriate FMS equipment and database support.
Published speed restrictions are mandatory unless ATC modifies them; published altitude restrictions become vertically authorized only with the appropriate clearance.
"Expect" altitudes and speeds are planning information only unless ATC specifically issues them as part of a further clearance.
"Cleared the arrival" normally means fly the lateral route and published speeds while maintaining the last assigned altitude until ATC authorizes descent.
"Descend via" authorizes lateral and vertical navigation on the arrival to comply with published altitude and speed restrictions, but not below the published bottom altitude.
When checking in on a new frequency while descending via, include "descending via" so the next controller knows the vertical clearance.
MEAs are not STAR restrictions, but the aircraft is still expected to remain above required en route minimum altitudes.

items.text: Any emergency procedure should be briefed as a decision process: recognize the cue, keep the aircraft controlled, execute memory items when required, back up with the checklist, and choose the correct recovery branch.

children.text: Start with aviate, navigate, communicate. An EP answer that skips aircraft control, terrain/airspace, or weather is incomplete even if the checklist words are memorized.
State the cue, the immediate action or memory item if one exists, the checklist backup, and the warning/caution/note that changes the decision.
Tie the procedure to the event environment: departure obstacle clearance, lost communications, high-altitude recovery, fuel state, weather, and nearest suitable field.
For each EP, decide whether the branch is continue, land as soon as practical, land as soon as possible, PEL, forced landing, or eject.
If the procedure affects IFR capability, tell ATC what failed, what capability remains, and what clearance or recovery support is needed.

Use N/W/Cs to protect against the common traps: delaying ejection below limits, resetting or pulling the wrong circuit breaker, troubleshooting while low or task saturated, or continuing into weather with degraded equipment.
Do not invent an exhaustive EP list for the brief; be ready to apply the method to whichever NATOPS EP the instructor selects.

items.text: Obstacle Departure Procedures provide obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure when obstacles require more than a basic diverse departure.

children.text: ODPs are a type of departure procedure and are labeled with "OBSTACLE" in the title on DoD/FAA charts.
Textual ODPs are normally found with takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information in the front section of the chart booklet; complex and RNAV ODPs may be graphical.
ODPs are not normally assigned by ATC unless needed for separation, so the pilot must determine whether one exists and how it affects the departure.
Research the departure before leaving the planning space: terrain, hazards, close-in obstacles, climb gradients, required headings, and special routing.
If using an ODP, file or tell ATC clearly enough that the first controller understands the intended departure path.
If ATC assigns another departure procedure, radar vector, or clearance that changes the plan, confirm obstacle clearance and performance before accepting it.
Keep the immediate-return approach ready because an emergency after takeoff can combine aircraft control, obstacle clearance, and weather minimums in the same moment.
A diverse departure normally requires climbing to 400 feet AGL before turning and at least 200 feet per NM until reaching the minimum IFR altitude, unless a procedure says otherwise.
Convert a published climb gradient to cockpit climb rate with: required FPM equals groundspeed in NM per minute times required feet per NM.
At 180 KIAS, groundspeed is about 3 NM per minute; a 200 feet-per-NM gradient is therefore about 600 FPM.
If performance, weather, loading, or emergency planning cannot support the required climb or route, solve that before takeoff.

items.text: The Trouble T symbol is the chart cue that nonstandard takeoff minimums, obstacle information, or special departure requirements may apply.

children.text: The symbol can appear on IAP, DP, ODP, or SID charts and points to the takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information for that airport.
The controlling details are in the front section of the approach-plate or TPP booklet, normally grouped alphabetically by airport.
The symbol alone does not tell you the runway-specific restriction, obstacle note, climb gradient, or required route; read the text before departure.
Some departures may still allow standard takeoff minimums only if the aircraft meets a specific climb or routing requirement.
Trouble T is an obstacle-clearance alert; Navy takeoff weather minimums are related planning data but come from CNAF rules.
When Trouble T, ODP, and CNAF weather minimums all apply, brief them separately: obstacle route and climb, departure weather legality, and emergency-return plan.

events.overview: I4490 is the instrument check-flight preparation event. The standard is to show examiner-ready judgment: the flight plan is complete, current data is checked, lost-communications and weather-minimum decisions are defensible, and prior instrument procedures can be explained without leaning on local gouge.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Lost communications should be briefed as a predictable plan that ATC can protect, with PIC emergency authority available when the rule does not fit the actual safety problem.

children.text: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
Land as soon as practicable does not mean land immediately at an unsuitable field, and the VFR branch also applies if the failure occurs in Class A.
Squawk 7600 and attempt recontact on the last assigned frequency, FSS, New York Radio or San Francisco Radio, 121.5 MHz, and NAVAID voice as able.
For IFR route, use AVE-F: assigned, vectored direct to the specified fix/route/airway, expected, then filed.
For IFR altitude, use AME for each segment: highest of assigned altitude, minimum IFR altitude, or expected altitude.
Make MEA, MCA, MRA, and valid EFC-altitude changes at the appropriate segment, time, or fix; do not apply an expected altitude before it becomes usable.
If the clearance limit is a fix from which an approach begins, begin descent or approach as close as possible to the EFC time, or ETA if no EFC was received.
If the clearance limit is not an approach fix, leave it at EFC time, or on arrival if no EFC was received, then proceed to a fix from which an approach begins.

For radar approaches, brief the specific lost-communication interval and backup plan: secondary or tower frequency, VFR if possible, approved non-radar approach, or the radar approach's published lost-communication procedure.

items.text: CNAF minimums are the check-flight weather gates: can the aircraft legally depart, may the approach be commenced, and may it continue below MDA or DH.

children.text: For a standard instrument rating, a non-precision-supported takeoff requires the published minimums for the available approach, but not less than a 300-foot ceiling and 1 SM visibility.
If a compatible precision approach is available and usable for the landing runway, takeoff may use those precision minimums, but never below 200-foot ceiling and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
A special instrument rating has no takeoff ceiling or visibility minimums, but only an aircraft commander with that rating, on the flight controls, may depart below the applicable minimums.
Use approved DoD FLIP or equivalent procedures. For straight-in approaches, RVR governs when available; for circling, prevailing visibility governs.
A single-piloted aircraft shall not commence an instrument approach if reported weather is below published minimums for the type of approach being conducted.
The fixed-wing single-pilot absolute floor is 200-foot ceiling or HAT and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
Do not descend below MDA or continue below DH unless the runway environment is in sight and a safe landing can be made.
On a precision approach, execute the missed approach at DH if the runway environment is not in sight or a safe landing cannot be made.
On a non-precision approach, execute the missed at the MAP if visual reference is not established or the landing cannot be accomplished.
If visual reference is lost while circling, start with a climbing turn toward the landing runway, then maneuver the shortest direction to join the published missed-approach course.

items.text: The check flight requires a completed DD-1801, DD-1801-C stopover plan, and jet log that agree with each other and with the weather, NOTAM, fuel, alternate, and delay plan.

children.text: CNAF preflight planning requires familiarity with weather reports and forecasts, NOTAMs, TFRs, fuel requirements, terminal procedures, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, anticipated traffic delays, and risk.
The DD-1801 is the formal IFR flight-plan request; the jet log is the cockpit math that proves headings, distances, ETEs, fuel burns, EFRs, alternate fuel, and DRAFT data.
Build the route and fuel story from the same assumptions: fuel aboard, start/taxi/takeoff fuel, climb and cruise profile, approach fuel, alternate fuel, reserve, and spare fuel.
Use DD-1801 for the initial leg and DD-1801-C for subsequent legs in a stopover flight plan.
The DD-1801-C uses the same completion guidance as DD-1801, can support three additional legs, and carries new fuel endurance and persons on board in Block 19 for each leg.
Use Block 18 on the DD-1801-C only when information changes from the initial DD-1801.
For an en route holding delay, use DLE/ with the significant point on the route followed by the delay length in four-digit hours and minutes.
For a terminal delay, show the practice instrument approach delay in the route structure so ATC can see the intended terminal work.
For this event, the first leg should include the en route holding delay and the second leg should include the terminal delay; the jet log must carry the fuel and timing consequences of both.

sections.title: Flight Planning, DD-1801, and Jet Log

items.text: NOTAMs are time-critical aeronautical information that can change whether the planned route, procedure, airport, NAVAID, airspace, or GPS plan is usable.

children.text: For DoD operations, use DAIP when available; if DAIP is unavailable, get a NOTAM briefing through FSS by phone or other approved means.
Check departure, destination, alternate, route, ARTCCs along the route, TFRs, special-use airspace activity, and any GPS/RAIM issue that affects the planned procedures.
If a location is not covered by the U.S. NOTAM system, use FSS or direct airport contact as needed.
NOTAM(D) can cover airport, taxiway, lighting, and facility status that may not change approach criteria but still affects execution.
FDC NOTAMs are regulatory and may amend instrument procedures, published charts, or advertise TFRs.
Pointer NOTAMs point to another NOTAM; SAA NOTAMs activate special-activity airspace; military NOTAMs cover military NAVAIDs and airports in the NAS.
Domestic and International Notices are not included in a standard FSS briefing unless requested, so ask for them if they have not already been reviewed.
CNAF makes FLIP procedures, special notices, instructions, and NOTAMs mandatory for naval aircraft pilots.
A check-flight NOTAM answer should end with a cockpit effect: procedure unavailable, alternate invalid, NAVAID unusable, airspace unavailable, timing changed, or no factor.

items.text: En route weather is not a one-time preflight snapshot; it is the in-flight update loop that protects the route, destination, alternate, and fuel plan.

children.text: Use PMSV/METRO, FSS, ARTCC weather advisories, ATIS, ASOS/AWSS, AWOS, UNICOM/AUNICOM, ATC weather avoidance assistance, and PIREPs as the route develops.
ARTCC may broadcast the availability of severe weather forecast alerts, convective SIGMETs, SIGMETs, AIRMETs, urgent PIREPs, and CWA information affecting their area.
FSS specialists may brief and interpret available reports and forecasts, but they are not original forecasters.
PMSV/METRO can update weather information, help with DD-175-1 updates, and receive PIREPs for rapid dissemination.
Compare each update against approach minimums, alternate requirements, fuel-to-alternate, severe weather watches, SIGMETs, icing, thunderstorms, turbulence, and route delays.
If the DD-175-1 void time, weather briefed time, route, or delay plan no longer supports the flight, update the plan before the check flight becomes a fuel or legality problem.
Use ATC weather avoidance assistance for precipitation information, but remember ATC radar does not detect turbulence and NEXRAD-based products can be delayed.
Give PIREPs for hazardous weather and useful cloud, visibility, icing, turbulence, wind shear, or precipitation observations.

items.text: Any emergency procedure in a check-flight event is a cumulative oral evaluation of judgment, not just a memory-item recital.

children.text: State the cue, maintain aircraft control, execute required immediate action, back it up with the checklist, and identify the N/W/C that changes the branch.
Tie the procedure to the phase of flight: departure obstacle clearance, en route weather, lost communications, fuel state, approach minimums, alternate selection, or recovery-field suitability.
Finish with the branch: continue, land as soon as practical, land as soon as possible, PEL, forced landing, or eject.
If the emergency affects IFR capability, tell ATC what failed, what capability remains, and what clearance or vectors are needed.
Do not invent an exhaustive EP list for the event. Be prepared to apply the same method to whichever NATOPS EP the instructor selects.

Common check-flight misses are treating a warning as a note, troubleshooting below the useful altitude band, delaying ejection past a limit, or forgetting that a systems failure can invalidate the IFR plan.

items.text: Any previously discussed item means the check flight can reach back across the instrument syllabus; prepare prior events as linked procedures rather than isolated flash facts.

children.text: For each prior item, know the purpose, setup, clearance meaning, numbers or gates, execution flow, common error, missed or lost-communication branch, and source.

High-value review lanes are scan and basic instrument maneuvers, holding, course intercepts, PAR/ASR/no-gyro, ILS/LOC, GPS/RNAV/TAA, SID/STAR, ODP/Trouble T, fuel management, DD-1801/jet log, NOTAMs, and weather.
If a question is local or scenario-specific, answer from the current chart, IFG, ATC clearance, or local procedure for that day; do not rely on stale route names or memorized frequencies.
A strong check-flight answer ends in a cockpit action: what you would set, brief, request, fly, verify, or discontinue.

events.overview: N3101 introduces day visual navigation as a planned route-management problem: prepare a readable chart, fly with dead reckoning and pilotage, correct timing and course early, and keep divert, airspace, HUD, and VFR field-entry decisions ahead of the aircraft.

sourceDocuments.summary: Source document tied to this event.
sourceDocuments.title: N3101 1542.166D

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: VFR chart preparation turns the route into a cockpit tool: current sectional, clean markings, known checkpoint sequence, planned timing, and continuation-fuel gates that support an abort or continue decision.

children.text: Bring current sectionals, dividers, a navigation plotter, pencil, black ballpoint pen, highlighters, and a template for circles, squares, and arrows.
Pick the final checkpoint as the target and assign the Time on Target. Select prominent checkpoints from start to target, normally spaced about 3 to 25 minutes apart.
Avoid congested airspace, OLFs, controlled fields, and alert areas to the maximum practical extent during checkpoint and route selection.
Circle checkpoints about nickel-size, connect them with straight course lines, and stop lines at the circle edge so chart detail stays readable.
Measure true course with the plotter, apply average isogonic variation, and compute magnetic course using TC minus easterly variation or TC plus westerly variation.
Measure checkpoint center-to-center distance, round to the nearest 0.5 NM, and record the leg data on the jet log.
Plan visual-navigation timing at 210 KGS, or 3.5 NM per minute, and place 1-minute tick marks perpendicular to the course line.
Compute continuation fuel backwards from the destination or final checkpoint so each checkpoint has a minimum fuel required to continue.

items.text: Emergency field selection is continuous route monitoring: know the closest suitable divert, update it during ops checks, and make the abort decision while fuel, altitude, and field reachability still leave options.

children.text: During preflight chart study, mark suitable emergency fields near each route segment and note runway length, orientation, elevation, lighting, and any obvious pattern or airspace issue.
In flight, perform ops checks about every 15 to 20 minutes and update the closest divert each time.

For a low-level engine malfunction, the Navigation FTI rule of thumb is that recovery is unlikely unless a suitable field is within about 3 NM; fields inside the wingtip arc may be reachable with an immediate turn and climb.
A zoom from 240 KGS gains about 1300 feet; use that altitude to improve options, but do not let troubleshooting delay the required emergency branch.
Plan an MSA for each leg as 500 feet above the highest obstacle within 10 NM of route centerline, rounded up to the next 100 feet.
Plan an ERAA for the route as 1000 feet, or 2000 feet in mountainous terrain, above the highest obstacle within 10 NM of route centerline, rounded to the nearest 100 feet.
For total disorientation, inadvertent IMC, or aircraft malfunction, climb immediately to at least ERAA. In IMC, squawk 7700, contact ATC, and get an IFR clearance.

items.text: Airspace classification is a chart-reading and communication requirement: identify the airspace before you get there, know what entry permission or communication is required, and do not assume flight following satisfies the pilot's responsibility.

children.text: Class B requires an explicit ATC clearance and is depicted with solid blue boundaries; Class C requires two-way communication and is depicted with solid magenta boundaries.
Class D requires two-way communication with the tower and is depicted with dashed blue boundaries; when the tower is closed, the surface area may revert as published.
Class E is controlled airspace not Class A through D and is shown by charted surface, 700-foot, or 1200-foot transition markings. Class G is uncontrolled airspace outside controlled boundaries.
TRSA service is not a separate airspace class, but CNATRA aircraft treat TRSA participation as mandatory where applicable.
Prohibited areas are no-entry without authorization; restricted areas require controlling-agency permission when active; warning areas mark similar hazards offshore.
Alert areas and MOAs require heightened lookout and status awareness; contact Flight Service or the published scheduling/controlling agency when the route may be affected.

Below 10,000 feet MSL, plan around the 250 KIAS speed limit unless a specific exception applies; below Class B shelves or within 4 NM of a Class C/D primary airport at or below 2500 feet AGL, expect 200 KIAS limits.

items.text: VFR field entry and departure are about arriving predictable: get weather, make the right call early enough, meet the airspace communication requirement, and enter the pattern without surprising local traffic.

children.text: Before entering Class B, C, or D airspace, the pilot must ensure the required clearance or two-way radio communication exists, even when receiving radar advisories.
For towered VFR arrivals, get ATIS or airport information first, then call with callsign, position, altitude, intentions, and the current information code.
For uncontrolled fields, monitor and self-announce on CTAF from about 10 NM to landing; include who you are, where you are, altitude as useful, runway or pattern intention, and the airport name.
If using FSS or UNICOM airport advisory service, remember the information is advisory; visual lookout and pattern deconfliction remain pilot responsibilities.
For VFR departure, tell tower or ground you are departing VFR, give destination or direction of flight as required, and comply with any heading, altitude, frequency, or transponder instruction.
At civilian fields, confirm how the VFR flight plan will be activated and closed; do not assume a tower automatically performs the same function as a military field.
At non-towered fields, monitor and broadcast from start or taxi until clear of the area, and use the published traffic pattern unless safety, weather, or published procedures require otherwise.

items.text: The HUD is a navigation aid, not a reason to stop looking outside: use it to cross-check flight path, heading, altitude, bank, navigation cues, and system validity while still flying the VNAV scan.

children.text: The forward HUD and right-MFD HUD repeater display aircraft flight, navigation, and tactical data. Master modes are NAV, A/A, and A/G.
HUD cues include flash for time-critical or field-of-view-limited information and a limit cross when a symbol has exceeded the HUD field of view.
The HUD does not show colors or OFF flags; invalid data may disappear or be replaced with an X.

The waterline pitch reference, flight path marker, climb-dive marker, and climb-dive ladder help interpret aircraft control and flight path, but they do not replace outside references on a VFR navigation route.
In NAV master mode, use heading scale, selected heading, active waypoint or course cues, bank scale, and sideslip indicator as cross-checks against the chart and ground.
Use the HUD for trend awareness, then confirm with clock-chart-ground. A clean HUD picture is not proof you are on the right visual checkpoint.

items.text: Route management is the VNAV control loop: stabilize on altitude and airspeed, navigate by dead reckoning and pilotage, identify checkpoints early, and update timing, fuel, and divert choices as the route develops.

children.text: Before leaving run-up, have charts, jet log, and publications open and accessible. Departure climbout is not the time to unfold charts or hunt for route data.
Stabilize on altitude and airspeed before the first checkpoint, trim the aircraft, and maintain a continuous VFR scan plus engine-instrument cross-check.
Use dead reckoning for time, speed, and heading prediction, and pilotage to confirm position with visual ground references.
Apply clock-chart-ground: check time, find the expected chart feature, then identify it outside. Look 2 to 5 minutes ahead and positively identify each checkpoint by about 1 minute out.
At each checkpoint, execute the 6 Ts: Time, Turn, Time, Transition, Twist, Talk.

Write ATA on the jet log, turn to the new heading, restart timing as required, adjust altitude for VFR cruising rules, set the heading bug to the next leg, and give an ops check if required or desired.
If the checkpoint does not appear as expected, avoid wandering. Continue a deliberate plan, verify position with at least two references, and climb to MSA if temporarily disoriented.

items.text: Standard time corrections adjust groundspeed or distance to protect ETA and TOT. Make the correction early, but do not spend fuel aggressively when continuation fuel is becoming the limiting factor.

children.text: Off-course maneuvering changes distance flown. If 1 minute early on a route with suitable geometry, delay a turn by 30 seconds, parallel about 2 NM off course at 210 KGS, and turn abeam to lose about 1 minute.
For the proportional method, change groundspeed 1 knot for every second early or late and hold it for the number of minutes equal to groundspeed in NM per minute. At 210 KGS, that is about 4 minutes.
For the 10 percent method, 10 percent of 210 KGS is 21 knots; holding that increase or decrease for 10 minutes gains or loses 1 minute, or about 6 seconds per minute held.
Do not correct timing blindly. First confirm whether the error came from airspeed, heading, wind, a course correction, or an identification mistake.
If fuel is close to continuation fuel, accepting a small timing error may be smarter than increasing power enough to force an early route abort.

items.text: Standard course corrections begin with position certainty: know where you are, know where the course is, then choose the smallest correction that gets you back on line without creating an avoidable timing error.

children.text: First, aim for a prominent feature in the distance that lies on course, then recheck heading and update the next on-course feature as you approach.
Second, use funneling features between about 10 and 2 o'clock, such as roads, ridgelines, valleys, or rivers that converge toward the checkpoint.
Before turning, confirm position with at least two references. A correction made from an uncertain position usually increases the error.
If no useful visual feature is available, use Standard Closing Angle: 60 divided by groundspeed in NM per minute.
At 210 KGS, the Navigation FTI standard is 15 degrees. Apply the SCA for 1 minute per mile off course, or double the angle for half the time when leg length demands it.
After regaining course, diagnose the cause: heading drift, wind different from forecast, checkpoint misidentification, poor power control, or faulty planning.

events.overview: N3102 moves visual navigation into the night environment. The standard is to keep the route, timing, lighting picture, local night restrictions, and emergency branches ahead of the aircraft while using the sim profile to practice mission management rather than GPS-following.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Night VNAV timing and course corrections use the same math as day VNAV, but the margin is thinner: keep the route at or above the night VNAV floor, identify checkpoints earlier, and correct before darkness turns small uncertainty into disorientation.

children.text: Nighttime visual-navigation routes shall not be flown lower than 2000 feet AGL.
Use 210 KGS, or 3.5 NM per minute, as the standard planning baseline unless the event or instructor directs otherwise.
Look farther ahead than you think you need to. At night, checkpoint confirmation often depends on lighting pattern, relative position, and timing rather than a crisp daylight shape.
Keep continuation fuel and route-abort options visible in the scan; aggressive speed increases can solve timing while creating a fuel problem.
For timing, use the same three methods: off-course maneuvering, proportional groundspeed change, and the 10 percent method.
For proportional corrections, change groundspeed 1 knot for every second early or late and hold it for the number of minutes equal to groundspeed in NM per minute; at 210 KGS, use about 4 minutes.
For the 10 percent method, 21 knots for 10 minutes gains or loses about 1 minute; each minute held is about a 6-second correction.
For course, first aim for an on-course feature, then use funneling features. If neither works, use SCA: at 210 KGS, apply 15 degrees for 1 minute per mile off course, or 30 degrees for half the time.

sections.title: Night VNAV Timing and Course Corrections

items.text: Night VFR chart interpretation uses the same sectional, but not the same sight picture. Mark the chart for readability and pre-brief which features will still be useful after sunset.

children.text: Use bold, dark route lines and larger print for magnetic courses, timing, and fuel data so the chart can be read under cockpit lighting without destroying night adaptation.
Expect lighted roads, towns, towers, airports, and coastlines to be more useful than unlit terrain detail. Some good daytime checkpoints become poor night checkpoints.
Preselect backup cues around each checkpoint: expected light pattern, nearby roads or towns, airfield beacon, runway orientation, and limiting features that tell you when you have gone too far.
Use MEF, MSA, and ERAA deliberately. If night position awareness degrades, climb before the route becomes a terrain-clearance problem.

The scenario emphasizes mission management, in-flight planning, in-flight computations, communication with ATC, and general VFR procedures. Do not treat own-ship or breadcrumbs as the primary navigation answer.
A complete night VNAV plan includes the plotted route, jet log, flight plan, DD-175-1 weather brief, NOTAMs, and BASH conditions.

items.text: Airfield and runway lighting tells you where the pavement is, what end you are looking at, and whether the taxi route is safe to enter. Brief the lighting before the field becomes the only outside reference.

children.text: Runway edge lights are white along the edges; on instrument runways they turn yellow in the last 2000 feet or the last half of the runway, whichever is less.
Runway threshold lights show green toward the approach and red toward departing aircraft.
REILs are flashing white lights on each side of the runway threshold.
Runway centerline lights on precision instrument runways are white until the last 3000 feet, then alternate red and white until the last 1000 feet, then all red.
Touchdown zone lights are two rows of white lights in the touchdown zone, normally the first 3000 feet.
Taxiway edge lights are blue; taxiway centerline lights are green.
Clearance bar lights are three steady yellow lights at holding points.
Stop bar lights are red across a taxiway and must not be crossed unless ATC clears the aircraft and the lights are off.
Approach lighting systems, including sequenced flashers, help align the aircraft with the runway environment before the runway lights dominate the sight picture.
Use VASI or PAPI trend correctly: 2 white and 2 red on a four-light PAPI indicates on glidepath; more white is high and more red is low.

items.text: Local night VNAV SOP is the night go/no-go filter: confirm current local rules for weather, runway suitability, lighting, flight-plan activation, and cockpit setup before treating the route as executable.

children.text: Night VNAV is not flown below 2000 feet AGL, and the scenario starts at a planned altitude before applying VFR semicircular rules.
Students should arrive with the assigned night VNAV route plotted on the VFR sectional and a completed jet log.
Flight planning for the event includes a completed flight plan, DD-175-1 weather brief, NOTAM review, and BASH conditions.
At night, taxi lights must be used whenever the aircraft is in motion.
Do not operate within a SIGMET at night unless the aircraft is equipped with operable radar capable of detecting and avoiding isolated thunderstorms.
For wet or night operations at fields at or below 3500 feet MSL, use the local runway suitability gate of at least 5000 feet by 100 feet.
For fields above 3500 feet MSL, use the local gate of at least 6000 feet by 100 feet.
Confirm current local procedures, runway data, lighting status, and route restrictions on the day of the event; the scenario route and frequencies are training setup, not a permanent source.

items.text: Any applicable night emergency procedure is a branch decision under reduced outside cues: keep aircraft control, climb or turn only with a known purpose, identify whether a lighted runway is immediately available, and coordinate early.

children.text: For night engine failure at or above 2000 feet AGL, comply with NATOPS. If a restart is not attempted or is unsuccessful and a lighted runway is not immediately available, ejection is highly recommended.
For night engine failure below 2000 feet AGL, attempting a restart is not recommended. If a lighted runway is not immediately available, the first priority is getting set up to eject.
Airspeed can be exchanged for altitude; use that option to improve survival choices without delaying the required branch.
If the emergency becomes a route abort in IMC, climb immediately to at least ERAA, squawk 7700, contact ATC, and obtain an IFR clearance.
For temporary disorientation, climb to MSA until positive position is regained. For total disorientation, inadvertent IMC, or aircraft malfunction, climb to ERAA.
For a night PEL, prioritize a lighted runway, field orientation, and communication that does not delay emergency procedures.
If no radio contact is available at a field, use observed traffic, runway and lighting cues, segmented-circle/wind information when available, and a conservative pattern plan.
The event scenario may use a simulated EP to drive night PEL and pattern work; brief the decision branch, not just the simulated field name.

events.overview: N4101 takes the VNAV method into the airplane. The standard is to show up with a usable chart and jet log, fly the route visually, keep timing/fuel/airspace ahead of the aircraft, and make destination, FMS, maintenance, and day-emergency decisions without letting local gouge replace current source checks.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: VFR chart preparation is complete only when the route can be flown in the cockpit without reinterpreting the plan: current chart, clean data boxes, checked checkpoint sequence, continuation fuel, and TOT math.

children.text: Use current sectional charts and verify expiration. Bring dividers, nav plotter, pencil, black pen, highlighters, and a shape template.
Select the target or final checkpoint first, then build the route with checkpoints that are prominent, identifiable from altitude, and normally spaced about 3 to 25 minutes apart.
Study each checkpoint from chart, imagery, and expected cockpit perspective. Prefer features with good horizontal development, uniqueness, and useful funneling or limiting features.
Avoid congested airspace, OLFs, controlled fields, alert areas, and other avoidable chart traps to the maximum practical extent.
Draw checkpoint circles about nickel-size, stop course lines at the circle edge, and keep markings readable rather than decorative.
Use true course and isogonic variation for the preferred magnetic-course calculation: TC minus easterly variation or TC plus westerly variation.
Measure center-to-center distances, round to the nearest 0.5 NM, and plan visual-navigation timing at 210 KGS, or 3.5 NM per minute.
Work continuation fuel backwards from destination and required reserves so every checkpoint has an abort-or-continue fuel gate.

items.text: Route management in the aircraft is a disciplined scan: fly stable altitude and airspeed, navigate with dead reckoning plus pilotage, identify checkpoints early, and update timing, fuel, divert, and radio work continuously.

children.text: Before leaving run-up, have charts, jet log, publications, frequencies, and destination data open and reachable.
Stabilize on altitude and airspeed prior to the first checkpoint. Trim matters because poor trim becomes heading drift, altitude drift, fuel imbalance, and fatigue.
Use clock-chart-ground: compare time, find the charted feature, then identify it outside. Look 2 to 5 minutes ahead and positively identify each checkpoint about 1 minute out.
Keep the chart oriented with aircraft track and scan wide; features off the nose are not the only useful references.
At each checkpoint, execute the 6 Ts: Time, Turn, Time, Transition, Twist, Talk.
Log ATA, turn to the new heading, restart timing if required, correct altitude for VFR cruising rules, set the heading bug to the next course, and give the required or desired ops check.
If a checkpoint does not appear, keep flying a deliberate plan. Confirm position with at least two references, avoid wandering, and climb to MSA if temporarily disoriented.

items.text: Standard time corrections protect ETA and TOT by changing groundspeed or distance flown. Make the correction early enough to matter, but do not trade away continuation fuel for cosmetic timing.

children.text: Off-course maneuvering changes distance. On a suitable route, turning 30 seconds past or before a checkpoint at 210 KGS produces about a 1.75 NM offset and can lose or gain about 1 minute.

For the proportional method, change groundspeed 1 knot for every second early or late and hold that speed for the number of minutes equal to groundspeed in NM per minute. At 210 KGS, use about 4 minutes.
For the 10 percent method, 10 percent of 210 KGS is 21 knots. Holding that adjustment for 10 minutes gains or loses 1 minute, or about 6 seconds per minute held.
Before correcting, decide whether the error came from wind, heading, airspeed, a prior course correction, or checkpoint identification.
If actual fuel is close to continuation fuel, a small timing error may be safer than an aggressive speed increase that forces an early abort.

items.text: Standard course corrections should be small, deliberate, and position-backed. A correction from an uncertain position usually makes the route worse.

children.text: First, aim for a feature on course and keep updating that reference as you approach.
Second, use funneling features between about 10 and 2 o'clock, such as roads, rivers, ridges, valleys, or power lines that lead toward the checkpoint.
Confirm your current position with at least two references before leaving planned heading.
If no visual correction feature works, calculate Standard Closing Angle as 60 divided by groundspeed in NM per minute.
At 210 KGS, use the Navigation FTI standard of 15 degrees. Hold SCA 1 minute per mile off course, or double the angle for half the time if leg length requires it.
After correcting, analyze the cause and adjust future headings or scan technique so the same drift does not repeat.

items.text: Airspace classification is not background trivia on a VNAV flight; it controls where you may go, what you must say, what speed limits apply, and whether the route needs to be changed before launch.

children.text: Class B requires explicit ATC clearance; Class C and Class D require two-way communication before entry.
Class E and G boundaries affect VFR weather requirements and controlled-airspace assumptions; read surface, 700-foot, and 1200-foot depictions carefully.
TRSA participation is not a separate airspace class, but it is treated as mandatory for CNATRA aircraft where applicable.

Special use airspace requires status and permission discipline: prohibited means do not enter, restricted requires controlling-agency authorization when active, and MOA/alert/warning areas demand route and lookout planning.
Below 10,000 feet MSL, plan around the 250 KIAS speed limit unless a specific exception applies.
Beneath Class B shelves or within 4 NM of a Class C/D primary airport at or below 2500 feet AGL, expect 200 KIAS limits.
Use current chart, NOTAM, TFR, and route-status checks; do not rely on a route from a prior student or prior date.

items.text: VFR field entry and departure require current airport information, correct airspace communication, and predictable pattern behavior.

children.text: For departure, tell tower or ground you are departing VFR, provide destination or direction as required, and comply with assigned heading, altitude, frequency, and transponder instructions.
At civilian fields, confirm whether you must activate the VFR flight plan through Flight Service after takeoff.
Before entering Class B, C, or D airspace, ensure the required clearance or two-way communication exists even if you are receiving radar advisories.
For towered arrivals, get ATIS or airport information first, then call with callsign, position, altitude, intentions, and information code.
For non-towered fields, monitor and broadcast on CTAF from about 10 NM to landing and again on downwind, base, final, and clear of runway as appropriate.
Use published pattern data, right-pattern markings, CTAF/UNICOM/FSS guidance, and visible traffic. Advisory information does not remove see-and-avoid responsibility.

items.text: Local cross-country SOP turns the VNAV plan into an approved squadron flight: know the current destination/alternate approval, weather limits, return-home priority, duty-chain coordination, and daily-inspection constraints before stepping.

children.text: Flight safety and timely execution of the approved plan outrank completing every training objective. Avoid creating a situation where weather, fuel, or maintenance prevents a safe return.
Fly only to the approved destination or alternate unless emergency authority or safety of flight requires a different decision.
Do not plan cross-country training into actual or forecast adverse weather that may preclude or excessively delay return.
If maintenance timing, daily inspection limits, or duty-day coordination may become a factor, brief the required duty-chain coordination before launch rather than discovering it after landing away.

items.text: FMS procedures support VNAV, but the visual chart and clearance remain controlling. Use the FMS to back up position, distance, and divert work without allowing it to replace pilotage.

children.text: Build or recall the route deliberately, verify waypoint sequence on the LEGS page, and confirm the active TO waypoint and active leg before using FMS cues.
Expect pending-route edits to require EXEC; erase unwanted modifications before execution.
Use FMS direct-to, nearest, and route data as aids for divert or abort decisions, but cross-check against the chart, airspace, weather, fuel, and field suitability.
Do not let a magenta line excuse flying through unbriefed airspace, weather, or an unapproved route change.

items.text: Emergency field selection for the flight is a live fuel, terrain, runway, and maintenance decision. Update it throughout the route instead of treating it as a preflight-only chart mark.

children.text: During chart study, identify suitable emergency fields within practical reach of each leg and note runway length, orientation, elevation, lighting, airspace, and likely pattern direction.
During ops checks every 15 to 20 minutes, update closest suitable divert and compare actual fuel against continuation fuel and bingo assumptions.
For a low-level engine malfunction, recovery is unlikely unless a suitable field is within about 3 NM. Fields inside the wingtip arc may be reachable with an immediate turn and climb.
A zoom from 240 KGS gains about 1300 feet; use it to improve options, but keep NATOPS emergency procedure and ejection decision points primary.

items.text: Destination maintenance and operating procedures are a preflight go/no-go item for away-field work: the destination must support the aircraft, the crew, and the next launch.

children.text: Before launch, confirm destination and alternate operating hours, runway suitability, fuel availability, contract fuel or emergency non-contract plan, parking, tie-down, security, and local operating procedures.
For strange-field operations, the PIC owns postflight and preflight inspection responsibility when normal support personnel or ground equipment are not available.
Know how oil will be checked and serviced, how the aircraft will be secured, who can move it if towing is required, and what maintenance or duty-chain call is required for a delay.
If destination support changes, update the route, fuel, and alternate plan before the aircraft is committed away from home field.

sections.title: Destination Maintenance Facilities and Operating Procedures

items.text: TOT is the exact planned arrival time at the final checkpoint, not a vague route estimate. Build it into the chart and then update it continuously from the actual route-start clock.

children.text: Put 0+00 in the first checkpoint data box, not at the departure airfield, and compute elapsed time cumulatively for each subsequent checkpoint.
At route start, note actual clock time so each checkpoint has a hard-time ETA.
At each checkpoint, compare ATA with planned elapsed time and decide early whether a time correction, course correction, or fuel-preserving acceptance is required.
Do not chase TOT so aggressively that the correction creates airspace, fuel, or route-control problems.

items.text: Any applicable day emergency on VNAV starts with aviate, navigate, communicate, then uses the chart, MSA/ERAA, divert fields, ATC, and NATOPS procedure to choose the recovery branch.

children.text: For temporary disorientation, climb to the leg MSA until position is regained; use the Five Cs if disorientation becomes significant: confess, climb, communicate, conserve, comply.
For total disorientation, inadvertent IMC, or aircraft malfunction, climb immediately to at least ERAA. In IMC, squawk 7700, contact ATC, and obtain an IFR clearance.
For lost communications, troubleshoot helmet, volumes, circuit breakers, frequency selection, previous frequencies, Guard, backup VHF, and survival radio before committing to lost-comm procedures.
For an unplanned PEL or divert, communicate with the field if able without delaying emergency procedures. The useful call is who you are, where you are, and what you want.
For low-level engine malfunction, the first reaction is climb to cope. Use chart, GPS, and NAVAIDs to maintain positional awareness and identify the nearest suitable recovery field.
If aborting in VMC, maintain terrain clearance, comply with VFR altitude restrictions if possible, squawk appropriately, maintain VMC, and contact the controlling agency when required.
If aborting into IMC, treat it as an emergency: climb to ERAA, squawk 7700, contact ATC, and fly the proper VFR altitude until receiving IFR clearance.

events.overview: F1201 is the formation Flight 0 rehearsal. Practice the physical brief setup, outbound and return flow, parade sequence, visual and radio communications, and emergency coordination until both Lead and Wing responsibilities can be executed without losing formation discipline.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Chair-fly the parade sequence in order and verbalize the checkpoint that confirms each position before moving to the next maneuver.
Wing should control wingtip separation, step-down, and bearing with small coordinated corrections while Lead remains predictable and monitors Wing's ability to continue.
Clear communications prevent confusion before it becomes a spacing problem.

children.text: Use the ATC call sign with outside agencies and the tactical call sign for inter-flight communication.
Brief primary and secondary UHF and VHF tactical frequencies before flight.
Lead handles outside-agency communications; Wing monitors and backs up Lead.
Wing is responsible for staying on the correct frequency and querying Lead if unsure.
Do not conduct formation check-ins on ATC frequencies unless directed; use tactical frequency to get well.
Lead must give Wing enough time to change frequencies before transmitting to the controlling agency.
Use positive check-ins after directed switches so both aircraft know the flight is together.
Use visual signals when they are clear and briefed.
Use radio calls in IMC, when there is confusion, or whenever a visual signal may be missed.
Lead should provide a stable platform during any radio or visual communication task.

items.text: Hand signals are formation commands. They must be passed where Wing can see them, acknowledged clearly, and backed up by radio when the situation is unclear.

children.text: Lead confirms Wing is in position, clears the area, passes the signal high and visible, then looks back for Wing's acknowledgment.
Wing acknowledges with a deliberate head nod or gives a no-head-shake if the signal is missed or unclear.
Lead executes only after acknowledgment unless the signal itself is an immediate safety-of-flight command.
Use radio calls in IMC, when a visual signal could be missed, or anytime confusion exists.
Do not force a visual-signal answer if aircraft control, spacing, or weather makes a radio call safer.

items.text: A Section PEL starts by giving the emergency aircraft the maneuvering room and authority it needs while preserving mutual support.

children.text: If Lead has the emergency, Lead should make a quick radio call so Wing can get separation.
If Wing has the emergency, Wing requests lead left or right.
Lead transfers lead verbally only after visual contact and separation make the transfer safe.
The new Wing transitions to perch.
New Wing clears the flight path, provides divert or field information, assists with procedures if requested, and monitors altitude, airspeed, VSI, and configuration.
Wing matches the emergency aircraft's configuration when remaining through the profile.
The emergency aircraft maneuvers and configures for high key.
Lead may kiss off Wing at any time.
If Wing remains through the ELP, Wing stays outside Lead's turn and waves off when directed, no lower than 300 ft AGL.
Normally, Wing can safely detach and monitor at high key.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Visual signals only work when Lead is predictable, Wing is in position, and both aircraft understand exactly when the signal is acknowledged and executed.

children.text: Lead first verbalizes the signal over ICS during training, confirms Wing is in position, clears the area, then passes the signal high and visible above the canopy rail.
Most signals are passed for about 3 seconds; the cruise signal uses a longer cadence.
Lead stops the signal, looks to Wing, confirms the head-nod acknowledgment, then executes smoothly.
If Wing gives a no-head-shake or there is confusion, Lead repeats the signal or clarifies by radio.
Run-up directs both aircraft to set the briefed run-up power and check safety-of-flight items.
Kiss-off releases Wing to separate for takeoff, breakup, detach, or landing as briefed.
Cruise directs Wing to move from parade to cruise; Wing acknowledges, slides to the 60-degree bearing line, sets the directed power, and calls ready.
Crossunder directs Wing to cross behind and below Lead after stabilizing aft with proper step-down.
Breakup and rendezvous starts the break sequence only after Wing acknowledges and Lead gives the kiss-off.
Lead change uses a distinct signal: Lead taps the helmet on the side away from Wing, then deliberately points to Wing.
The new Lead acknowledges, looks forward, and flies a stable platform.
The new Wing keeps eyes on the new Lead and preserves separation during the transition.

items.text: The formation maneuver set is a progression: establish spacing on departure, stabilize in parade, correct errors early, then use planned geometry for turns, crossunders, breakup and rendezvous, and underruns.

children.text: Line up with runway-side discipline and complete the Lineup Checklist before takeoff.
For interval takeoff, Wing delays 5 seconds after Lead begins the takeoff roll, then rejoins using controlled closure.
During running rendezvous, Wing keeps Lead slightly above the horizon, arrives on bearing line, and limits closure to a safe, briefed value.
Parade is built on the 45-degree bearing line, wingtip clearance, and step-down.
Wing corrects in A-B-C order: altitude, bearing, closure/separation.
In turns, Wing anticipates radius-of-turn effects: reduce power when Lead turns into Wing and add power when Lead turns away.
For a crossunder, Wing first moves aft and slightly down, verifies nose-to-tail clearance, then crosses behind Lead at a walking pace.
Wing never passes directly under Lead.
After crossing, reestablish bearing, separation, and step-down before moving back into normal parade.
For breakup and rendezvous, Lead starts from 200 KIAS, level flight, Wing in position, and clear airspace.
Wing breaks at Lead's 3/9 line, keeps Lead in sight, stabilizes in trail, then rejoins with Lead on the horizon.
If closure, aspect, or step-down becomes unsafe, underrun early instead of pressing a bad rendezvous.

events.overview: F2101 introduces the formation mindset before the airplane work becomes dense: Lead must provide a predictable platform, Wing must preserve sight and spacing, and both aircraft must use disciplined communications and small position corrections during departure, recovery, and basic formation maneuvering.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Formation departures and arrivals are built around predictable Lead actions, runway-side discipline, and enough spacing for Wing to correct without rushing.

children.text: Lead normally lines up on the downwind side so wake turbulence and prop wash move away from Wing.
Both aircraft complete the Lineup Checklist while crossing the hold-short line and center themselves on their assigned runway side.
Wing confirms Lead's runway side, then taxis forward until Wing's leading edge aligns with Lead's horizontal stabilizer trailing edge.
The runway must be at least 100 ft wide for an interval takeoff.
Lead passes the run-up signal; both aircraft set about 30% torque and check safety-of-flight items and engine instruments.
Wing visually inspects Lead and holds the thumbs-up until Lead acknowledges.
Lead gives the kiss-off and begins a maximum-power takeoff on the assigned side; Wing starts the takeoff roll 5 seconds later, creating about 1000 ft of spacing.
After takeoff, Lead flies the briefed departure and gives Wing a stable, predictable rejoin platform.
Local formation guidance uses about 80% torque and 160 KIAS until Wing joins; if a turn is required before join, keep the bank shallow enough for Wing to close safely.
Wing keeps Lead slightly above the horizon, manages closure, and moves inside a departure turn when that helps the rendezvous.
During a running rendezvous, keep closure controlled; the local event source limits closure to no more than 40 KIAS until joined.
Lead normally directs Wing to cruise for checks and weather, then brings Wing back to parade before entering tower or pattern airspace.
Use only the current SOP, course rules, and day-of brief for local routing, frequencies, and field-specific reporting points.
During recovery descents, Lead should remain stable and normally keep at least 15% torque; Wing may need idle power and speed brake to maintain position.
For the break or section approach, Lead plans the spacing problem early and gives Wing clear detach, break, or speed-brake direction.

items.text: Formation is a shared task, but responsibilities are different: Lead owns the platform and plan; Wing owns sight, position, and deconfliction.

children.text: The Designated Flight Lead is the administrative lead assigned for mission objectives and safe, orderly conduct.
The Formation Lead is the aircraft physically flying lead at that moment.
Formation Lead must make smooth, stable, predictable changes in power, heading, and altitude.
Lead keeps the flight in the assigned area, clear of clouds unless on an IFR clearance, and clear of other aircraft.
Lead must always know where Wing is and must execute the briefed sequence with proper visual or radio communications.
Keep Lead in sight and maintain flight-path deconfliction.
Maintain proper formation position and make small, timely corrections.
Comply with Lead's signals and give timely responses.
Provide mutual support by backing up navigation, communications, fuel awareness, and safety-of-flight decisions.
Everything takes longer in formation, especially frequency changes, checklist work, turns, and rejoins.
Lead must plan ahead for area boundaries, wind drift, sun angle, Wing workload, and how each maneuver sets up the next one.

items.text: Clear communications prevent confusion before it becomes a spacing problem.

children.text: Use the ATC call sign with outside agencies and the tactical call sign for inter-flight communication.
Brief primary and secondary UHF and VHF tactical frequencies before flight.
Lead handles outside-agency communications; Wing monitors and backs up Lead.
Wing is responsible for staying on the correct frequency and querying Lead if unsure.
Do not conduct formation check-ins on ATC frequencies unless directed; use tactical frequency to get well.
Lead must give Wing enough time to change frequencies before transmitting to the controlling agency.
Use positive check-ins after directed switches so both aircraft know the flight is together.
Use visual signals when they are clear and briefed.
Use radio calls in IMC, when there is confusion, or whenever a visual signal may be missed.
Lead should provide a stable platform during any radio or visual communication task.

items.text: Position corrections start with relative motion: Lead is the reference, and Wing fixes altitude, bearing, then closure in that order.

children.text: Altitude is the first correction because step-down protects separation.
Bearing line is second; acute means forward of the bearing line, sucked means aft of it.
Closure or separation is last; do not close distance until altitude and bearing are under control.
Vertical movement is primarily controlled with elevator.
Fore and aft movement is controlled with power.
Left and right movement is controlled with aileron.
Every correction needs a re-correction: add the input, stop the movement, then reset a middle value.
When Lead turns into Wing, Wing is on a smaller radius and must reduce power early or become acute.
When Lead turns away from Wing, Wing is on a larger radius and must add power early or become sucked.
Lead every turn with the required power change, then scan the whole aircraft instead of fixating on one checkpoint.

flashcardDecks.title: F4101 Discussion Items

events.overview: F4101 sets the contracts that make the remainder of the formation block predictable. Both aircraft must understand who owns the decision, how visual signals and cadence are acknowledged, how an abort preserves runway separation, and how Lead manages geometry and sun so Wing can remain safe and effective.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Lead and Wing share the sortie, but they do not share the same immediate job.

children.text: The Designated Flight Lead is administratively responsible for mission objectives and safe, orderly conduct.
The Formation Lead is the aircraft physically flying lead at the moment.
Lead must be smooth, stable, predictable, and directive.
Lead must keep the flight clear of clouds unless on an IFR clearance, clear of other aircraft, and within the assigned area or route.
Keep Lead in sight and maintain deconfliction.
Maintain proper position and correct early with small inputs.
Comply with Lead's signals and respond promptly.
Back up navigation, communications, fuel awareness, and safety decisions.

items.text: Hand signals are formation commands. They must be passed where Wing can see them, acknowledged clearly, and backed up by radio when the situation is unclear.

children.text: Lead confirms Wing is in position, clears the area, passes the signal high and visible, then looks back for Wing's acknowledgment.
Wing acknowledges with a deliberate head nod or gives a no-head-shake if the signal is missed or unclear.
Lead executes only after acknowledgment unless the signal itself is an immediate safety-of-flight command.
Use radio calls in IMC, when a visual signal could be missed, or anytime confusion exists.
Do not force a visual-signal answer if aircraft control, spacing, or weather makes a radio call safer.

items.text: An aborted takeoff in formation is a separation problem as much as an aircraft problem. Decide, stay on your side, and communicate as soon as aircraft control permits.

children.text: Brief abort contingencies before takeoff.
If aborting, execute the NATOPS abort procedure, maintain directional control, remain on the assigned runway side, and transmit intentions.
If Lead aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing normally aborts behind Lead while maintaining Wing's side; the 5-second interval should provide spacing.
If Wing aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing aborts on Wing's side and transmits once Lead is airborne and Wing is under control.
If either aircraft aborts after brake release, the aborting aircraft stays on its side and executes the abort.

The non-aborting aircraft recognizes the rapid line-of-sight change, selects maximum power, maintains side-of-runway discipline, and executes an individual takeoff unless separation cannot be maintained or it has its own emergency.
Wing must be prepared to avoid Lead if Lead loses directional control, including changing sides or leaving the prepared surface if required to prevent collision.
Aviate: control the aircraft.
Navigate: preserve runway-side separation and avoid the other aircraft.
Communicate: state intentions to the flight and tower when able.

items.text: Area and sun management are Lead responsibilities, but Wing should understand the plan so corrections and calls make sense.

children.text: Lead must know the assigned area boundaries and visualize how maneuver combinations will keep the flight inside them.
Wind affects ground track; Lead should plan turn direction and rollout timing before the edge of the area becomes urgent.
Formation tasks take longer than single-ship tasks, including radio changes, maneuvers, rejoins, and checklist work.
Lead should avoid prolonged straight-and-level or turn-into setups that force Wing to look into the sun.
Plan rollouts, crossunders, and maneuver sequencing to reduce Wing's sun exposure when practical.
Wing should call blind sun if Lead is temporarily lost in sun glare and then lag Lead's last known position.
Lead must be predictable and give Wing enough time to stabilize before the next maneuver.
If area, sun, or Wing position makes the next maneuver unsafe, use terminate or knock-it-off early.
