events.overview: F4102 focuses on maintaining separation and mission control when visual contact, geometry, or recovery conditions degrade. Prepare the immediate blind/lost-sight actions, coordinated configuration changes, flight-split responsibilities, and the communication and planning required for a section recovery away from home field.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Blind procedures are VMC procedures. The visual aircraft has deconfliction responsibility while the blind aircraft reports altitude and keeps looking.

children.text: Wing calls "blind" with altitude.
If Lead is visual, Lead directs Wing's eyes using clock position and high, level, or low references.
Wing continues to call "blind" or "visual" until Lead is reacquired.
If Wing calls visual, Lead directs the rejoin or continuation of training.
Lead transmits altitude, maneuvers predictably, and ensures at least 500 ft altitude separation without crossing altitudes.
Lead directs a rejoin at the briefed or alternate location.
Wing lags Lead's last known position, clears the flight path, follows directive instructions, and maintains altitude separation until visual.
TCAS may assist SA but is not the primary rejoin method.
If Wing is blind due to sun, Wing calls "blind sun" and lags Lead's last known position.
Lead calls continue only if deconfliction can be maintained; otherwise Lead calls knock-it-off.

items.text: Lost sight is an IMC procedure. Wing immediately transitions from formation references to instruments and creates predictable separation.

children.text: Transition to instrument scan and maintain aircraft control.
Call "lost sight" on the tactical frequency.
Smoothly reduce power about 10% to reduce closure risk.
Straight and level: Wing turns away for a 30-degree heading change, times for 30 seconds, then parallels Lead's heading.

Turns: the outside aircraft rolls wings level and transmits heading and altitude; the inside aircraft continues the turn for at least 30 degrees, then the outside aircraft turns to the assigned heading after 30 seconds.
Climbs or descents: Wing levels off, states altitude, and executes the applicable straight or turning lost-sight procedure while Lead continues to assigned altitude with at least 500 ft separation.
Inside the FAF, Wing turns away expeditiously, transitions to instruments, and calls lost sight.
Lead informs ATC and continues the approach.
Wing climbs to FAF or glideslope intercept altitude, proceeds to the MAP, and flies the missed approach unless ATC issues a new clearance.

items.text: Speed brake use as a section must be predictable because extension, retraction, pitch change, and closure all affect Wing at once.

children.text: Lead may use speed brake to increase descent rate or decelerate the formation.
During recovery descents, Lead should normally use at least 15% torque.
Wing may need idle power and speed brake to maintain position.
Speed brake effectiveness decreases at lower airspeeds, and extension or retraction creates pitch changes that must be countered.
If Wing is in parade, Lead may direct speed brake with the visual signal and a head-nod acknowledgment.
If Wing is in cruise, Lead should use clear radio calls such as standby speed brake and speed brake now.
Lead must remain stable and avoid ambiguous timing.
In cruise, Wing may combine power, pursuit curves, and speed brake to move between parade and cruise or hold position.
During the fan break, Wing may use idle power and speed brake at maneuver start to create spacing.
If Lead is turning and Wing has excessive closure, Wing may need idle power and speed brake to avoid passing ahead.

sections.title: Speed Brake Use As a Section

items.text: Dissolving the flight turns a formation into individual aircraft while preserving positive separation, ATC coordination, and clear responsibility.

children.text: Complete required formation training and any needed lead change before the split.
Lead assigns heading and altitude separation; local event source uses at least 30 degrees of heading separation and normally 500 ft of altitude separation.
Wing normally turns away and descends to the assigned heading and altitude.
Lead maintains the original altitude until Wing reports established.
Use clear readbacks for heading, altitude, area, and detach clearance.
Wing sets the appropriate transponder or TCAS configuration per the brief and current local procedure.
Lead coordinates with ATC when the flight is splitting and dissolves the formation only after aircraft are established in their assigned blocks or areas.
For later rejoin, Wing reports ready on the tactical frequency and Lead coordinates the join clearance.
Keep local area names, frequencies, and route-specific calls tied to the day-of brief, not memorized as universal procedure.

items.text: A section approach is a mutual-support recovery that requires Lead to fly a smooth approach and Wing to maintain visual contact, configuration awareness, and readiness to assume Lead.

children.text: Plan the approach, missed approach, configuration timing, and final separation before starting down the approach.
Weather must be at or above circling minimums, or 1000 ft and 3 SM if circling minimums are not published.
Bring Wing to parade, reduce airspeed, and configure the flight no later than the FAF; earlier may be needed in IMC or VFR on top.
Confirm configuration with a clear visual or radio response.
Lead positions the formation on final and normally flies 120 KIAS with Wing in parade until detached.
Wing mirrors Lead's configuration, maintains visual contact in IMC, and stays ready to assume Lead.
If the section misses approach, execute the published missed approach using normal hand signals or tactical frequency unless otherwise briefed.
If individual approaches are required, Lead coordinates separate squawks and normally sends the lower-fuel aircraft first.
Use current local SOP, IFG, and day-of brief for field-specific detach or landing-flow details.

items.text: Strange field operations start when the aircraft is away from normal support and the PIC must make sure the aircraft is inspected, serviced, secured, and ready for the next launch.

children.text: If mission requirements dictate an overnight stay and ground support equipment or personnel are not available, NATOPS makes the PIC responsible for postflight and preflight inspections.
Postflight starts with parking brake set, interior checked, gust lock engaged, and ejection-seat/CFS safety pins installed in both cockpits.

The exterior check looks for leaks, flap and speed-brake condition, gear and door condition, tire damage, brake-wear indicators, loose panels, covers, restraints, chocks, tie-downs, and static grounding as required.
Check oil with the dipstick 15 to 20 minutes after shutdown for the most accurate result.
Oil must be serviced within 30 minutes of shutdown; normal level is between ADD and MAX HOT, and oil at or below ADD must be serviced to MAX HOT.
Use the dipstick, not the sight glass, for the correct oil-level indication.
Secure the aircraft before leaving: canopy locked, external CFS doors closed and locked, baggage door latched and locked, avionics doors latched, and sun shields installed as required.
The wing and tail tie-down points are sufficient in normal conditions; secure the nose gear as well when windy or extreme conditions are anticipated.
If high winds are expected and time permits, move the aircraft to a hangar; NATOPS warns that winds above 80 knots can cause structural damage.
Before planning a strange field, confirm fuel, servicing, security, parking, hangar or tie-down support, and who can move the aircraft if the parking brake must be released for towing.

flashcardDecks.title: F4103 Discussion Items

events.overview: F4103 treats every emergency as both an aircraft problem and a formation problem. Lead and Wing must protect separation, assign tasks, select the safest recovery, and know when to dissolve the flight while supporting PEL, HEFOE, gear, IMC, or damaged-aircraft contingencies.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Treat a section emergency as both an aircraft problem and a formation-separation problem: fly the affected aircraft, communicate the malfunction, and establish clear Lead/Wing responsibilities.

Lead remains directive, protects the emergency aircraft, coordinates recovery, and dissolves or reconfigures the flight when formation adds risk; Wing maintains safe position and avoids compounding the emergency.
A Section PEL starts by giving the emergency aircraft the maneuvering room and authority it needs while preserving mutual support.

children.text: If Lead has the emergency, Lead should make a quick radio call so Wing can get separation.
If Wing has the emergency, Wing requests lead left or right.
Lead transfers lead verbally only after visual contact and separation make the transfer safe.
The new Wing transitions to perch.
New Wing clears the flight path, provides divert or field information, assists with procedures if requested, and monitors altitude, airspeed, VSI, and configuration.
Wing matches the emergency aircraft's configuration when remaining through the profile.
The emergency aircraft maneuvers and configures for high key.
Lead may kiss off Wing at any time.
If Wing remains through the ELP, Wing stays outside Lead's turn and waves off when directed, no lower than 300 ft AGL.
Normally, Wing can safely detach and monitor at high key.

items.text: HEFOE lets a NORDO aircraft communicate the affected system using visual signals.

children.text: Gain the other aircraft's attention first; the formation source uses a weeping signal before passing the affected system.
Use hand signals during day and flashlight signals at night if required.
The good-radio aircraft coordinates with ATC or tower and keeps the NORDO aircraft supported.
H: Hydraulics.
E: Electrical.
F: Fuel.
O: Oxygen.
E: Engine.

items.text: Emergency field selection is a suitability and energy problem: choose a field the aircraft can reach and land on, then keep updating the plan as energy changes.

children.text: Prefer the closest suitable hard-surface runway at least 3000 ft long.
If multiple fields are available, consider crash crew, medical support, runway surface, wind, obstacles, and recovery complexity.
Use charts, NAVAIDs, FMS NAV/TSD, and nearest-airport tools to judge distance.
Use the DME method to judge one field: one-half DME plus key altitude plus field elevation equals the approximate MSL altitude required.
Add 3000 ft for high key or 1500 ft for low key when deciding if current energy is sufficient.
Use the altitude method to compare several fields: subtract 3000 ft for high key or 1500 ft for low key from AGL altitude, then multiply by 2 for maximum glide distance in NM.
Best-glide planning from the Contact FTI is about 125 KIAS clean, with roughly 2 NM per 1000 ft of altitude in no-wind conditions.
A zoom from high energy can increase altitude; local source material cites about 1300 ft gained from 240 KGS.
If no suitable landing area exists, NATOPS and Contact FTI guidance favor ejection when possible rather than pressing an unsuitable off-field landing.
If ejection is not possible or malfunctions, an ELP to an unprepared surface or ditching may be the remaining option, with higher injury and egress risk.

items.text: Inadvertent instrument flight in formation requires Lead to fly instruments while Wing maintains parade and prepares for lost-sight execution if visual references fail.

children.text: Lead transitions to an instrument scan and determines the safest way to exit IMC.
Wing maintains parade position and scans Lead.
If unable to regain VMC, Lead ensures terrain clearance and coordinates an IFR clearance for the flight or individual clearances at Flight Lead discretion.
If Wing loses sight of Lead, Wing immediately executes lost sight procedures.
Lead must stay directive and predictable so ATC coordination and separation do not conflict.

items.text: A landing gear inspection is an emergency-support task, not a formation proficiency stunt. The inspection is flown only when it can be done without adding risk.

children.text: The aircraft with the unsafe indication notifies the other aircraft and ATC.
Climb to the published emergency orbit, delta pattern, or other local procedure before troubleshooting.
Request an airborne gear inspection if it will help the decision and can be done safely.
Wing follows the distressed aircraft and assists as directed.
Conduct the inspection at a minimum of 2000 ft AGL.
Use a discrete frequency when practical to reduce chatter and confusion.
The emergency aircraft communicates configuration, airspeed, altitude, and planned changes.
The inspecting aircraft reports position and intentions and avoids undue risk.
Use caution if visible damage could allow gear parts to depart the aircraft.
Student solos shall not join up to inspect landing gear.
Students shall not be at the controls during the landing gear inspection.
The emergency aircraft may ask Wing, chase, base, or RDO to help read checklists and troubleshoot.

items.text: Airborne damage is first an aircraft-control and deconfliction problem. The section does not rejoin just because both aircraft remain flyable.

children.text: Follow NATOPS procedures for the actual malfunction or damage.
If severe damage causes or may cause OCF, do not delay ejection beyond the safe envelope.
If damage is minimal, communicate, separate, maintain visual contact, and establish a deconfliction plan.
Use lateral, altitude, ground-reference, DME, or working-block separation as appropriate.
Do not rejoin the damaged aircraft as a flight.
Complete appropriate emergency checklists.
Consider assigning a chase or inspection aircraft if it can be done without adding risk.
Develop a recovery plan for both aircraft; if runway damage or FOD risk exists, consider separate airfields.
The damaged aircraft communicates if able, climbs to a safe altitude, and assumes Lead as necessary to assess the damage.
If forward visibility is lost or aircraft control is doubtful, controlled ejection may be required.
The good aircraft moves to perch and assists as required.

events.overview: F4104 is the advanced relative-motion event. Use pursuit geometry to control closure and position in cruise and Tail Chase, preserve step-down and energy, recognize unsafe trends early, and distinguish a normal terminate from the immediate safety response required by a knock-it-off.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Knock-it-off stops the maneuvering because safety is compromised or could be compromised.

children.text: Any flight member may initiate knock-it-off.
Use it for emergencies, traffic conflicts, blind situations, G-LOC or AGSM failure, area boundary concerns, or any developing unsafe condition.
The pilot calling knock-it-off should state the reason if able.
Lead maneuvers predictably, normally straight-and-level or with shallow bank.
Lead gives directive intentions and may state altitude and a reference heading for the flight.
Both aircraft prioritize separation and aircraft control before resuming any training objective.

items.text: Terminate stops an exercise or maneuvering for an expected or administrative reason; it is not the same as knock-it-off.

children.text: Lead normally initiates terminate, but Wing may request or initiate it.
Use terminate when the training objective is complete, the exercise is ending, or continuing would not be useful.
If the reason is safety-of-flight, call knock-it-off instead.
Lead remains predictable and transitions to a safe attitude.
Lead directs follow-on intentions, such as cleared to parade, continue, repeat, or recover.
Wing maintains deconfliction and does not rush the rejoin.

items.text: Cruise maneuvering teaches Wing to maintain position with pursuit geometry and lift-vector placement, not constant power chasing.

children.text: Lead signals cruise and holds a stable platform until Wing is established.
Wing acknowledges, slides to the 60-degree bearing line, sets the directed power, and calls ready.
Formation FTI references use about 80% torque above 10,000 ft and 70% torque below 10,000 ft before maneuvering; hold the PCL position rather than chasing torque changes with altitude.
Cruise position is about 60 degrees bearing, about 20 ft step-down, and 3 to 6 plane widths of spacing.
Lead is limited to no more than 120 degrees AOB and no less than 1G.
Wing uses lead, lag, and pure pursuit plus lift-vector placement to stay in the cruise cone.
Minor turns may need small power corrections; aggressive turns should be solved primarily with pursuit geometry.
Lead or Wing calls terminate.
Lead rolls level or establishes a predictable 30-degree AOB turn, stabilizes near 200 KIAS, and clears Wing to parade.
Wing maintains cruise spacing, anticipates acceleration or deceleration, and rejoins without losing step-down.

items.text: Tail Chase demonstrates lead, lag, and pure pursuit in dynamic maneuvering. Wing normally maintains 800-1000 feet in trail, offset from prop wash, and uses pursuit geometry instead of chasing position with power.
Do not conduct Tail Chase below 6000 feet AGL or within 500 feet of the bottom of the assigned block, whichever is higher; avoid less than 1 G, more than 6 G, or slower than 110 KIAS.
Split-S and Immelmann maneuvers are prohibited. Call knock-it-off for a safety deviation, then make Lead predictable and recover the formation deliberately.
Cruise maneuvering teaches Wing to maintain position with pursuit geometry and lift-vector placement while Lead provides a smooth, predictable maneuvering platform.

children.text: Lead passes the cruise signal and holds a stable platform until Wing is established.
Wing acknowledges, slides to the 60-degree bearing line, sets the directed power, and calls ready.
Formation references use about 80% torque above 10,000 ft and 70% torque below 10,000 ft before maneuvering; hold the PCL position instead of chasing every torque change.
Cruise position is built around the 60-degree bearing line, safe step-down, and enough range to maneuver without drifting through Lead's 6 o'clock.
Local Capstone source cues the scan as altitude, bearing, then closure: exhaust stack tangent to Lead's wing leading edge, ventral fin over the inboard aileron cutout, and pitot tube on the prop arc.
Lead may use level turns and vertical wingovers; the local supplement frames the work as basic level turns followed by vertical maneuvering.
Lead remains within safe maneuvering limits, including no more than 120 degrees AOB and no less than 1G.
Lead should let Wing stabilize before maneuvering and should start with predictable, wingman-considerate turns.
Wing should keep Lead above the canopy rail during vertical work and avoid using PCL as the primary correction for geometry errors.
Terminate or knock-it-off early if closure, step-down, sun, blind geometry, or energy state becomes unsafe.

items.text: The principle of lead is to create a safe, predictable training platform while still meeting mission and area requirements.

children.text: Lead makes smooth, stable, predictable changes in power, heading, and altitude.
Lead keeps the flight within the assigned area and complies with current course rules or clearances.
Lead maintains cloud and traffic clearance unless operating on an IFR clearance.
Lead always knows Wing's position and monitors Wing's energy, aspect, range, closure, heading crossing angle, and line of sight.
Formation tasks take longer than single-ship tasks, so Lead must plan turns, radio changes, checks, and rejoins early.
Lead must understand area boundaries, wind effects, and how maneuver combinations affect ground track.
Lead should manage sun position and avoid forcing Wing to stare through Lead into the sun when practical.
A tight, abrupt maneuver has little training value if Wing cannot safely maintain position.

events.overview: F4290 verifies that formation knowledge transfers across the entire stage. Review each maneuver with Lead/Wing responsibilities, geometry, communications, limits, completion cues, and common errors, then apply the same disciplined crew coordination to any assigned emergency procedure.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Treat any previously discussed maneuver as a review of contracts, checkpoints, and discontinue criteria rather than a list of isolated steps.

children.text: For departure work, review lineup, interval takeoff, section takeoff, initial rendezvous, and abort responsibilities.
For parade work, review A-B-C corrections, parade turns into and away, crossunder, breakup and rendezvous, underrun, and lead change.
For recovery work, review cruise-to-parade transition, speed brake coordination, section approaches, break spacing, NORDO recovery, and section missed approach.
For cruise maneuvering, review 60-degree bearing, step-down, lead/lag/pure pursuit, terminate, and knock-it-off criteria.
Brief the setup, the visual references, the correction priority, and the common unsafe trend for each maneuver.
Know which aircraft owns deconfliction at each point and when Lead must be directive.
Use terminate for expected training stops, knock-it-off for safety concerns, and underrun when a rendezvous geometry is unsafe.

items.text: Any emergency procedure means the student must show a repeatable review method, not invent an exhaustive list during the brief.

children.text: Start with aircraft control and the applicable NATOPS critical action or checklist.
Add the N/W/Cs that change the decision, timing, or crew coordination.
State whether the emergency is handled as individual aircraft, section support, lost sight, blind, NORDO, Section PEL, airborne damaged aircraft, or down-aircraft response.
Preserve formation separation before trying to preserve flight integrity.
Aviate: maintain aircraft control and execute the correct emergency procedure.
Communicate: use the correct aircraft call sign when one aircraft has the emergency, then be directive on tactical and ATC frequencies.
Separate: transfer lead, move to perch, detach, climb, turn away, or establish altitude separation as the emergency requires.
Recover: choose a suitable field or pattern, coordinate support, and avoid rejoining damaged aircraft unless specifically directed and safe.
